have no linkage between an output and any recorded clinical outcome. Where the sponsor cannot show a
data pathway from output to observable consequence, the monitoring program is aspirational and cannot
justify reduced premarket evidence. This should be an explicit gating question.
Detection latency must be shorter than harm accumulation. Where a degradation would produce harm
faster than the monitoring cadence could detect it, the trade is unavailable regardless of program quality.
Irreversibility  forecloses  the  trade. Where  the  harm  from  an  incorrect  output  cannot  be  undone,
postmarket detection is not a mitigation — it is an audit of damage already done.
I recommend CDRH state affirmatively that reduced premarket evidence is not available for devices in the
high-consequence, high-activity region of the risk grid, so that the flexibility is bounded on its face.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Calendar-based reassessment is mismatched to GenAI devices whose performance shifts discontinuously at the moment of a change rather than gradually over time, so time-based cadence alone may miss safety-relevant degradation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an event-driven reassessment cadence with a calendar floor (annual, more frequent for higher-risk devices), with triggers including model version/weight changes (manufacturer- or provider-initiated), prompt/instruction/output-template changes, retrieval corpus or knowledge source changes, input-distribution shifts beyond prespecified bounds, sampling configuration changes, and complaint or adjudicated-error thresholds.
positions.public_summary: Finds FDA's three postmarket evaluation approaches sensible and complementary, but recommends reassessment be event-driven rather than calendar-driven, with an annual calendar floor (more frequent for higher-risk devices). Proposes specific triggers including model, prompt, retrieval-corpus, sampling, input-distribution, and complaint/error thresholds.
positions.supporting_text:
The three approaches described are sensible and complementary. My substantive recommendation concerns
cadence: it should be event-driven with a calendar floor, not calendar-driven.
Calendar-based reassessment is poorly matched to a technology whose performance changes discontinuously
at the moment of a change rather than continuously with time. I recommend triggering events include, at
minimum: any change to the underlying model version or weights, whether initiated by the manufacturer or
the model provider; any change to system prompts, instructions, or output templates; any change to a retrieval
corpus or knowledge source; any measured shift in the input distribution beyond prespecified bounds; any
change in the deployed sampling configuration; and any accumulation of complaints or adjudicated errors
exceeding a prespecified threshold. A calendar floor — annual, or more frequent for higher-risk devices —
should catch slow drift that trips no discrete trigger.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket monitoring and reassessment triggers would be maintained as a process separate from the manufacturer's existing design-change procedures, and that such parallel processes tend to diverge over time.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define postmarket monitoring/reassessment triggers as change-control triggers within the manufacturer's quality management system, so the monitoring obligation is integrated with existing design-change procedures rather than run as a separate process.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts postmarket monitoring and reassessment triggers but asks FDA to define them as change-control triggers inside the manufacturer's quality management system, integrated with existing design-change procedures, arguing that separate, parallel monitoring processes tend to diverge over time.
positions.supporting_text:
From  a  quality-system  perspective  these  should  be  defined  as  change-control  triggers  within  the
manufacturer’s QMS, so that the postmarket monitoring obligation is integrated with existing design-change
procedures rather than maintained as a separate process. Parallel processes diverge.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Human review of every output is not feasible for high-throughput devices, so machine-based supervision is treated as unavoidable; the dominant risk is correlated failure when a supervisory agent is built on the same foundation model as the device, since it shares the same blind spots and its agreement may be misread as independent confirmation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Focus on making automated supervision trustworthy rather than on whether to permit it, including addressing model-family independence between the supervisory agent and the monitored device so that agreement is not credited as independent confirmation.
positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents as unavoidable at high output volumes, shifting the question to trustworthiness rather than permissibility. Warns of correlated failure when the supervisor shares the device's foundation model, since shared blind spots make its agreement look like false independent confirmation.
positions.supporting_text:
Automated supervision is probably unavoidable at the volumes involved — human review of every output is
not feasible for a high-throughput device — so the question is how to make it trustworthy rather than whether
to permit it.
... The dominant risk is correlated failure.  A supervisory agent built on the same foundation model as the
device it monitors shares that model’s blind spots. It will approve exactly the outputs that are wrong for
reasons the model family does not represent, and its agreement will be misread as independent confirmation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A supervisory agent built on the same model family as the device it monitors may share failure modes, and aggregate agreement metrics can mask near-zero sensitivity for serious errors; a monitoring program whose final judgment is machine-made contains no independent check.
positions.requested_fda_action: Accept machine supervisory agents as postmarket evidence only under conditions: require architectural independence (different model family and provider) or reported failure-mode correlation on a held-out error set with evidentiary credit scaled to demonstrated independence; require validation of the supervisor as a measuring instrument via harm-specific sensitivity against human adjudication, re-measured over time; and restrict the supervisor to triage with a human-adjudicated terminal endpoint.
positions.public_summary: Supports machine supervisory agents only for triage, not conclusions. Asks FDA to require supervisors built on a different model family and provider (or reported failure-mode correlation), validation of harm-specific sensitivity against human adjudication with periodic re-measurement, and a human-adjudicated final endpoint.
positions.supporting_text:
Architectural  independence  as  a  condition  of  evidentiary  use. A  supervisory  agent  offered  as
postmarket evidence should be built on a model of a different family and provider than the supervised
device. Where full independence is impractical, the sponsor should characterize and report the correlation
in failure modes between supervisor and device on a held-out error set, and the monitoring program’s
credit should scale with the demonstrated independence.
The supervisor is itself a measuring instrument and must be validated as one.  Report its sensitivity
for  the  specific  harms  of  interest  against  human  adjudication  on  a  sampled  basis  —  not  aggregate
agreement, which is dominated by the easy majority of correct outputs and can be high while sensitivity
for serious errors is near zero. Sensitivity must be re-measured over time, since the supervisor’s own
performance drifts.
The supervisor triages; it does not conclude.  Its appropriate role is prioritizing outputs for human
review and enabling broader sampling than humans could achieve unaided. The adjudicated endpoint
should  remain  human.  A  monitoring  program  whose  terminal  judgment  is  machine-made  has  no
independent check anywhere in the loop.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a machine-based supervisory agent performs postmarket monitoring, modifications to that agent alter the device's monitoring properties, and treating the supervisor as outside the device could leave such changes unassessed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat the supervisory agent as part of the device system for change-control purposes, so that changes to the supervisor trigger reassessment on the same terms as changes to the device itself.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts use of machine-based supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring but asks FDA to define the supervisor as part of the device system for change control, so modifications to the supervisor trigger the same reassessment as device modifications.
positions.supporting_text:
The supervisor is part of the device system  for change-control purposes. A change to the supervisory
agent changes the device’s monitoring properties and should trigger reassessment on the same terms as a
change to the device.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that framing postmarket monitoring as a shared ecosystem could be read as shared responsibility, diluting the manufacturer's complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting duties, even though clinicians, institutions, and societies (and health systems holding outcome data manufacturers lack) are valuable signal sources.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly that signal may come from any source but the duty to investigate and act remains with the manufacturer, and build postmarket roles on existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than a parallel structure.
positions.public_summary: Supports third-party roles in postmarket monitoring but asks CDRH to state explicitly that manufacturers retain complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting duties regardless of signal source, and to build on existing complaint and MDR structures rather than create a parallel framework.
positions.supporting_text:
The accountability principle can be stated simply, and I recommend CDRH state it: information may come
from anywhere; the duty to investigate and act remains with the manufacturer.  Clinicians, institutions,
and societies can be valuable sources of signal, and health systems in particular hold the outcome data
manufacturers lack. But a manufacturer that has arranged to receive signal from third parties has not thereby
delegated any portion of its complaint-handling, investigation, or reporting obligations, and the paper should
say so directly to prevent the shared-ecosystem framing from being read as shared responsibility.
I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a
parallel  structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states it is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event or device malfunction for a generative output, using the example of a clinically incorrect recommendation that a clinician recognizes and disregards; under a conventional reading this could imply that hallucinations are reportable malfunctions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Clarify, before postmarket monitoring can function for GenAI-enabled devices, how reportable events and malfunctions are defined for generative outputs, including cases where an incorrect output is caught by the clinician.
positions.public_summary: While not objecting to postmarket monitoring, the commenter flags an unresolved threshold question: what counts as a reportable event or malfunction for a generative output, including incorrect recommendations a clinician catches and disregards, and asks FDA to clarify before monitoring can operate.
positions.supporting_text:
That said, I  want to flag a gap that I believe requires attention before postmarket
monitoring can function at all for these devices:
It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a
clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction
occurred? Under a conventional reading, the device did not perform as intended, and a malfunction that could
cause or contribute to serious injury if it recurred is reportable — which would imply that hallucinations

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that new postmarket performance evaluation mechanisms for GenAI-enabled devices could duplicate existing postmarket infrastructure. They favor leveraging established complaint-handling and medical device reporting (MDR) systems.
positions.requested_fda_action: Build any postmarket monitoring approach for GenAI-enabled devices on the existing complaint-handling and MDR framework rather than establishing a separate, parallel reporting structure.
positions.public_summary: The commenter recommends that FDA's postmarket monitoring approach for GenAI-enabled devices build on existing complaint-handling and medical device reporting systems rather than establishing a parallel structure. The passage does not detail specific monitoring methods or cadence.
positions.supporting_text: I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a parallel  structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states it is unclear what counts as a reportable event or malfunction when a generative output is clinically incorrect but the clinician recognizes and disregards it, and argues this unresolved ambiguity underlies every element of the postmarket section.
positions.requested_fda_action: Asks CDRH to directly define what constitutes a reportable event for generative outputs, and suggests a distinct aggregate reporting channel in which caught errors are reported as rates rather than individual MDRs, to preserve signal without unmanageable event volume.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports the postmarket section's direction but says it rests on an unresolved question: whether a clinician-caught incorrect generative output is a reportable malfunction. Asks CDRH to define reportable events and consider aggregate, rate-based reporting of caught errors instead of individual MDRs.
positions.supporting_text: It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction occurred? ... This ambiguity is consequential and unresolved, and every element of Section VI depends on how it is settled. I recommend CDRH address it directly, and would suggest that the workable answer likely involves a distinct, aggregate reporting channel for caught errors — reported as rates rather than as individual MDRs — so that the signal is preserved without generating unmanageable individual-event volume.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that scaling re-evaluation to the apparent magnitude of a modification misses the key question of whether the locked premarket evaluation instrument still validly measures the changed device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but categorize post-deployment modifications according to whether the change invalidates the locked benchmark suite rather than by the size of the change.
positions.public_summary: Supports treating the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but proposes that change categorization turn on whether a modification invalidates the locked benchmark suite rather than on the magnitude of the change, since small changes may invalidate evaluation instruments.
positions.supporting_text: I support using the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline. The organizing principle I would propose for categorizing changes is this:  the question is not how large the change is, but whether the locked evaluation instrument remains valid for the changed device.  A small change that invalidates the benchmark suite requires more scrutiny than a large change that does not.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that post-deployment modifications be sorted by their actual potential to affect device outputs, and that a locked benchmark suite remain a valid measuring instrument for whatever change is made. Changes that introduce capabilities the suite does not probe are treated as beyond QMS-managed handling.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a three-tier change framework: Tier 1 (no re-benchmarking) for changes with no path to outputs; Tier 2 (full re-benchmarking against a locked suite within the QMS, no submission) for same-family model version updates, prompt/template changes within a validated structure, validated retrieval corpus refreshes, and sampling changes within a validated range, conditioned on passing at a prespecified non-inferiority margin with inspection-ready documentation; Tier 3 (premarket submission) for change of foundation model family or provider, intended use/user/scope expansion, new input or output modality, changes to agentic tool access or action scope, and any change that invalidates the locked benchmark suite.
positions.public_summary: Proposes three tiers: no re-benchmarking if outputs can't be affected; QMS-managed full re-benchmarking against a locked suite at a prespecified non-inferiority margin for same-family model, prompt, corpus, or sampling changes; premarket submission for model family/provider changes, scope/modality expansion, agentic action changes, or benchmark invalidation.
positions.supporting_text:
Tier 1 — no re-benchmarking.  Changes that cannot affect device outputs: user interface presentation, logging, analytics instrumentation, infrastructure changes with no path to the output. Documented under normal change control.
Tier 2 — full re-benchmarking against the locked suite, managed within the QMS, no premarket submission. Model version updates within the same family and provider; prompt or template modifications within  a  validated  structure;  retrieval  corpus  refreshes  drawing  on  a  validated  source  list;  sampling configuration changes within a validated range. The condition is that the device passes the complete locked benchmark  suite  at  a  prespecified  non-inferiority  margin,  with  results  documented  and  available  on inspection. Failure at any element converts the change to Tier 3.
Tier 3 — premarket submission.  Change of foundation model family or provider; expansion of intended use, intended user, or clinical scope; addition of a new input or output modality; any change to agentic tool access or action scope; and any change for which the locked benchmark suite is no longer a valid instrument — for example, a change that introduces capabilities the suite does not probe.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a sponsor can revise both the device and the benchmark instrument under a lower-tier (Tier 2) change pathway, non-inferiority testing against the revised benchmark becomes meaningless as an assurance of continued performance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the locked benchmark suite cannot be altered under the lower-tier change pathway, and treat any modification of the locked suite as a higher-tier (Tier 3) change requiring the corresponding level of review.
positions.public_summary: Accepts a tiered change-control approach but urges a safeguard: the locked benchmark suite must not be modifiable under the lower tier, since revising device and benchmark together makes non-inferiority meaningless; suite changes should always trigger the highest tier.
positions.supporting_text: The essential safeguard is that the benchmark suite itself cannot be modified within Tier 2.  If the sponsor can  revise  the  instrument  and  the  device  together,  non-inferiority  against  the  revised  instrument  is meaningless. Modification of the locked suite should always be a Tier 3 event.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the existing PCCP construct, which prespecifies the specific modification, methods, and impact assessment, does not work for generative devices because the change space is genuinely open — sponsors cannot enumerate future third-party model versions or prompt refinements in advance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an 'invariant-based' PCCP that locks what must remain true after any change rather than the changes themselves: an escrowed immutable benchmark suite, acceptance thresholds including subgroup thresholds and non-inferiority margin, an independent verification protocol run before changes reach users, rollback criteria and maximum time-to-rollback with technical demonstration, change categories defined by a tier boundary rather than enumeration, and documentation and notification obligations.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts change-control adaptation but says prespecifying modifications fails for generative devices with open change spaces. Proposes an 'invariant-based' PCCP locking escrowed benchmarks, subgroup acceptance thresholds and non-inferiority margins, independent pre-release verification, demonstrated rollback with time limits, tier-defined change categories, and notification duties.
positions.supporting_text:
The current PCCP construct prespecifies what will change  — the modification, the methods to implement and validate it, the impact assessment. For generative devices this fails, not because sponsors are unwilling but because the change space is genuinely open: a sponsor cannot enumerate in advance the model versions a provider will release or the prompt refinements that experience will suggest.
The adaptation is to invert what is locked. An invariant-based PCCP prespecifies not the change but what must remain true after any change:
The evaluation instrument — the complete benchmark suite, escrowed and immutable.
The acceptance thresholds, including subgroup-level thresholds and the non-inferiority margin.
The verification protocol — what is run, in what order, by whom, with what independence, before any change reaches users.
The  rollback  criteria  and  mechanism,  including  maximum  time-to-rollback  and  the  technical demonstration that rollback is achievable.
The  change categories in scope , defined by the Tier 2 boundary above rather than by enumeration of specific changes.
The documentation and notification obligations attaching to each change.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a sponsor can alter its benchmark suite at the same time it alters the device, the change-control construct becomes circular and yields no real assurance of continued safety or effectiveness.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the benchmark suite be locked and escrowed, and that any change to the suite itself be treated at the highest review tier (Tier 3) rather than managed at the sponsor's discretion.
positions.public_summary: Supports the change-control construct only if the benchmark suite is locked and escrowed, with any modification to the suite subject to the highest-tier review. Warns that sponsor-modifiable benchmarks make evaluation circular and provide no assurance, treating these safeguards as essential rather than optional.
positions.supporting_text: The construct depends entirely on the integrity of the locked instrument. If the sponsor can modify the benchmark suite while modifying the device, the whole thing is circular and provides no assurance at all. Escrow of the suite, and Tier 3 treatment of any change to it, are not optional features of this proposal — they are the proposal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Devices built on third-party foundation models may be exposed to provider-initiated model changes if the manufacturer cannot lock to a specific model version; the commenter treats the absence of version pinning and change notice as a design deficiency rather than an acceptable residual risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that GenAI-enabled devices relying on third-party models are expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that inability to pin (or use of a provider lacking pinning with change notice) must be remediated as a design control matter.
positions.public_summary: Endorses addressing third-party model changes but asks CDRH to go further: state that GenAI devices must run against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that inability to pin, or use of providers without pinning and change notice, is a design deficiency requiring correction.
positions.supporting_text: Treat version pinning as a design control expectation.  CDRH should state that a GenAI-enabled device relying on a third-party model is expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that the inability to pin — or reliance on a provider that does not offer pinning with change notice — is a design deficiency to be addressed, not a residual risk to be accepted. This is the single highest-leverage statement CDRH could make in this area, and it would immediately reshape provider offerings in the medical device segment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Device manufacturers relying on third-party foundation models may not have enough advance warning of developer-initiated model changes to complete re-evaluation before the change takes effect, and pinned model versions may be retired too quickly.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require contractual advance-notice provisions with a defined minimum notice period long enough to complete the referenced Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, plus a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.
positions.public_summary: Supports contractual mechanisms for third-party model changes but asks FDA to require defined minimums: an advance change-notice period long enough to complete Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, and a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.
positions.supporting_text: Require contractual change notice with a defined minimum period , sufficient to complete the Tier 2 re-benchmarking described above before a change takes effect, together with a minimum deprecation window for pinned versions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Contractual commitments from third-party hosted model providers cannot be verified in real time, so silent upstream model changes may go undetected in deployed devices.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should describe continuous 'canary' monitoring — a small fixed probe suite of inputs with known expected outputs run frequently against the live endpoint — as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device built on a third-party hosted model.
positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket monitoring of third-party model dependencies but asks FDA to go further: because supplier contracts cannot be verified in real time, CDRH should treat continuous high-frequency 'canary' probe testing against live endpoints as an expected monitoring element for hosted-model devices.
positions.supporting_text: Require continuous canary monitoring, because contracts cannot be verified in real time.  A small, fixed probe suite — a set of inputs with known expected outputs — executed against the live endpoint at high frequency  provides  direct  detection  of  silent  upstream  change.  This  is  inexpensive,  technically straightforward, and the only mechanism I am aware of that verifies rather than assumes endpoint stability. I recommend CDRH describe it as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device on a third-party hosted model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: When a foundation model provider deprecates a pinned version, the manufacturer's forced migration produces a device running on a materially different model; the commenter is concerned that the involuntary nature of the change could be used to justify reduced re-evaluation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Classify provider-forced model migrations as a Tier 3 (highest-scrutiny) change and explicitly foreclose lighter treatment because the migration was involuntary, while expecting manufacturers to address the contingency in design planning, including maintaining a validated fallback.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a tiered change-control approach but asks FDA to classify provider-forced foundation model migrations as the highest tier, explicitly rejecting lighter treatment because the change was involuntary, and to expect manufacturers to plan ahead with a validated fallback version.
positions.supporting_text: Treat provider-forced migration as a Tier 3 change. When a provider deprecates a pinned version and the manufacturer must migrate, the resulting device is running on a different model. That it was involuntary does not change what it is, and the paper should foreclose the argument that forced migrations warrant lighter treatment.  Manufacturers  should  be  expected  to  plan  for  this  contingency  —  including  maintaining  a validated fallback — as part of design planning rather than handling it as an emergency.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Manufacturers and CDRH currently have to infer dependency risk from third-party foundation model behavior rather than assess it directly, because model versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices are not documented in any standing record.
positions.requested_fda_action: Advance the Foundation Model Master File concept as a maintained, current record covering model versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices so dependency risk can be assessed directly.
positions.public_summary: Supports the voluntary Foundation Model Master File concept, stating it would be most valuable as a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices, enabling FDA and manufacturers to assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.
positions.supporting_text: I would also note that this is where a Foundation Model MAF (Question 25) would deliver the most value: a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices would let CDRH and manufacturers assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees with CDRH's assessment that foundation model developers have little incentive to voluntarily disclose safety-relevant limitations, since medical devices are a small revenue share and disclosure carries competitive and litigation exposure, so a purely voluntary MAF program is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own.
positions.requested_fda_action: Create the voluntary Foundation Model MAF program but pair it with a manufacturer-side default: where no MAF exists, the device manufacturer must independently generate and fund full model characterization (training data provenance as determinable, contamination assessment, known failure modes, version and deprecation practices, subgroup performance) or the submission is incomplete, thereby creating a procurement preference for models with MAFs.
positions.public_summary: Agrees with FDA that voluntary Foundation Model MAFs face weak developer incentives, but recommends creating the program anyway and adding a manufacturer-side default: absent an MAF, the manufacturer must independently fund full model characterization or the submission is incomplete, creating procurement pressure.
positions.supporting_text:
The paper's candor about the incentive problem is warranted. Foundation model developers serve markets in which  medical  devices  are  a  small  fraction  of  revenue;  disclosure  of  safety-relevant  limitations  carries competitive and litigation exposure; and a voluntary program asking them to document weaknesses for a regulator overseeing someone else's product is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own merits.
I nonetheless recommend CDRH create it, because the mechanism that makes it work is not the model developer's incentive — it is the device manufacturer's.
Pair  the  voluntary  MAF  with  a  manufacturer-side  default:  where  an  MAF  is  absent,  the  device manufacturer bears the full characterization burden for the underlying model. Training data provenance to  the  extent  determinable,  contamination  assessment,  known  failure  modes,  version  and  deprecation practices, subgroup performance characterization — all of it, generated independently at the manufacturer's cost, or the submission is incomplete.
That default creates a procurement preference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A Foundation Model MAF is only useful if it contains specific safety-relevant content (version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning) and is kept current; a one-time snapshot would not support contamination analysis or detection of developer-initiated model changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify the enumerated MAF content elements and impose a currency requirement obligating updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the voluntary Foundation Model MAF concept but asks FDA to specify content—model identity and version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning—and to require updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.supporting_text: Suggested MAF content: model identity and version lineage; training data cutoff date (essential for the contamination analysis under Question 10); versioning, change notification, and deprecation policy (essential for Question 24); known limitations and documented failure modes; safety training and refusal behavior; evaluation results the developer has generated; and any medical-domain-specific training or fine-tuning. A currency requirement — the MAF must be updated within a defined period of any model change — is what makes it useful rather than a snapshot.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a Foundation Model MAF could be misread as evidence of the safety or effectiveness of devices built on that model, displacing evaluation of the finished device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Explicitly frame the MAF as contextual information supporting, not substituting for, evaluation of the final user-facing device as configured for deployment, consistent with the paper's statement on the unit of evaluation.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the Foundation Model MAF concept but cautions it should never be treated as establishing a downstream device's safety or effectiveness. Endorses FDA's statement that the final user-facing device as deployed is the unit of evaluation, with MAFs serving only as context.
positions.supporting_text: I would add one caution: an MAF should never be treated as establishing the safety or effectiveness of any device built on the model. The paper's statement that the unit of evaluation is the final user-facing device as configured for deployment is correct and important, and the MAF should be framed as context for that evaluation, not as a partial substitute for it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Per-step accuracy metrics overstate end-to-end reliability for multi-step agentic devices, since compounding error across a sequence (e.g., 95% per step over ten steps yields roughly 60% task success) means step-level results do not reflect whether the completed task is performed correctly.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that acceptance criteria and evaluation for agentic GenAI-enabled devices must be defined and measured at the level of completed task/trajectory rather than individual step accuracy, anticipating that sponsors will otherwise submit easier-to-generate step-level metrics.
positions.public_summary: Commenter agrees agentic devices need distinct oversight but asks CDRH to state explicitly that acceptance criteria and evaluation be set at the completed-task (trajectory) level, not per-step accuracy, because compounding step errors make step-level metrics misleading for multi-step tasks.
positions.supporting_text: Trajectory-level  acceptance  criteria. Per-step  performance  is  a  misleading  summary  of  end-to-end reliability. A device that completes each step correctly 95% of the time completes a ten-step task correctly about 60% of the time, and that arithmetic is unforgiving as sequences lengthen. Acceptance criteria must be stated at the level of the completed task, and evaluation must measure task completion rather than step accuracy. I recommend CDRH state this explicitly, because step-level metrics are far easier to generate and will otherwise be offered.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic systems can take actions—tool calls, write operations, effects on external systems—whose consequences vary in reversibility, and unbounded or silently expanded action capability is not adequately controlled by existing framing.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take, each classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution, require explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions, and treat the inventory as a locked specification whose expansion is a Tier 3 change.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA require agentic device sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every possible action—tools, write operations, external systems affected—classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution, with explicit user confirmation for irreversible actions and inventory expansion treated as a Tier 3 change.
positions.supporting_text: Action inventory with irreversibility classification. I recommend sponsors submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take — every tool, every write operation, every external system it can affect — each classified by reversibility and by the consequence of erroneous execution. Irreversible actions should require explicit confirmation by a qualified user, and the inventory should be treated as a locked specification whose expansion is a Tier 3 change under the framework in Question 22.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic GenAI devices could hold broader tool permissions than their intended use requires, and the discussion paper risks creating a separate treatment that duplicates CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect agentic systems to operate under least-privilege tool access scoped per deployment, and cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations rather than developing a parallel framework.
positions.public_summary: Supports addressing agentic systems but recommends FDA specify least-privilege tool access, with permissions scoped per deployment to the narrowest set sufficient for the intended use, and cross-reference existing CDRH cybersecurity expectations instead of creating a parallel treatment.
positions.supporting_text: Least-privilege  tool  access. Agentic  systems  should  hold  the  narrowest  permissions  sufficient  for  the intended use, scoped per deployment. This is standard security practice and maps directly onto CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations; I recommend the paper cross-reference them rather than developing a parallel treatment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without audit logs capable of reconstructing the full agentic trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect — root cause analysis of harmful outcomes is impossible and corrective action becomes guesswork, and complaint-handling obligations discussed under Question 21 cannot be met.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make the adequacy of audit logging an explicit element of premarket review for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, rather than assuming it will be addressed postmarket.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports attention to agentic device oversight but asks FDA to make audit logging adequacy an explicit premarket review element rather than a postmarket assumption, arguing full trajectory reconstruction — inputs, tool calls, actions, model version — is necessary for root cause analysis and complaint
positions.supporting_text: Audit logging sufficient for post-hoc reconstruction. When an agentic system produces a harmful outcome, the investigation must be able to reconstruct the full trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts where available, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect. Without this, root cause analysis is not possible, corrective action is guesswork, and the complaint-handling obligations under Question 21 cannot be discharged. I recommend audit logging adequacy be an explicit premarket review element for agentic devices rather than a postmarket assumption.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that agentic devices are precisely where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish before market entry while compounding errors propagate fastest and are least reversible after deployment, making them a poor fit for trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should treat agentic GenAI-enabled devices as presumptively ineligible for the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway contemplated in Question 18.
positions.public_summary: Commenter warns that the proposed trade of premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring fits agentic devices poorly, since end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket while errors compound fastest and are least reversible. Recommends CDRH presumptively exclude agentic devices from that pathway.
positions.supporting_text: I would also note that the compounding-error arithmetic above interacts badly with the premarket-uncertainty trade proposed in Question 18. Agentic devices are where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket,  and  simultaneously  where  errors  propagate  fastest  and  are  least  reversible  postmarket.  I recommend CDRH treat agentic devices as presumptively outside the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that without an explicit, published mapping from risk tier to required evidence, the framework will lack predictability, and that a 'competency-based' approach may not in practice be the 'least burdensome' one.
positions.requested_fda_action: Publish the risk-tier-to-evidence mapping so sponsors can predict the level of evidence expected for a given risk tier.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts pairing the risk framework with the competency-based approach but asks FDA to publish an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping, arguing that predictability is what makes risk-based frameworks less burdensome and that otherwise "competency-based" and "least burdensome" may diverge.
positions.supporting_text: Publish  the  risk-tier-to-evidence  mapping. Predictability  is  the  mechanism  by  which  risk-based frameworks reduce burden. Without it, "competency-based" and "least burdensome" will not describe the same thing.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the proposed framework could create documentation and assessment artifacts that run parallel to, rather than build on, manufacturers' existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control procedures.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should ground the competency-based framework and modification re-evaluation in existing quality system and risk management infrastructure instead of creating separate artifacts, and should explain in the paper how the new framework elements relate to those existing requirements.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the framework's general direction but asks FDA to build on existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control rather than creating parallel artifacts, and to explain explicitly how the new framework elements relate to those existing requirements.
positions.supporting_text: Integrate with existing quality system and risk management infrastructure.  Manufacturers maintain ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and change control procedures under the QMSR. The framework should draw on these rather than establishing parallel artifacts, and the paper should state how the pieces relate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Several elements of the framework — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations reaching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the limits of existing statutory authority, and the paper defers the question.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should revisit and explicitly identify which proposed elements it can implement under current authorities and which would require new legislation, so stakeholders know which parts of the framework to build toward.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but urges CDRH to stop deferring the legal-authority question, noting that enforceable postmarket conditions, third-party recognition, and obligations on non-manufacturer foundation model developers may exceed current authorities and could require congressional action.
positions.supporting_text: Identify  which  elements  require  new  legal  authority. The  paper  expressly  defers  this  question.  I understand why, but I would encourage CDRH to return to it, because several proposals — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, obligations touching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the edge of existing authorities. Stakeholders assessing which parts of this framework to build toward would benefit from knowing which parts CDRH can implement and which would require Congress.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that the discussion paper is framed toward enabling market entry and worries the competency-based approach could be read as an authorization pathway rather than a genuine evaluation framework.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly that the competency-based framework contemplates the outcome that a given intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency-based framework but asks CDRH to state explicitly that it can conclude an intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so the approach is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.supporting_text: Preserve  the  option  to  say  no. The  paper's  framing  is  oriented  toward  enabling  market  entry, appropriately  so  given  its  purpose.  But  a  competency-based  framework  should  also  be  capable  of concluding  that  a  given  intended  use  is  not  currently  supportable  by  available  evidence.  I  would encourage CDRH to state that the framework contemplates that outcome, so that it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the framework's flexibility exceeds the supporting infrastructure: benchmarks that are not yet trustworthy, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, third-party foundation model dependencies manufacturers cannot control, and a nonexistent third-party assessment capacity.
positions.requested_fda_action: Sequence implementation so that the enabling infrastructure (trustworthy benchmarks, clear reportability rules, mechanisms for third-party model change control, and qualified third-party assessment capacity) is established before the flexible evidentiary pathways are relied upon.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the framework's general direction but argues its flexibility currently exceeds supporting infrastructure — untrustworthy benchmarks, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, uncontrollable third-party model dependencies, and absent third-party assessment capacity. Asks FDA to build that infrastructure before relying on flexible evidentiary pathways.
positions.supporting_text: My central concern is that the framework's flexibility currently outruns the infrastructure needed to make flexibility safe: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, postmarket monitoring whose reportability rules are unsettled,  third-party  model  dependencies  that  manufacturers  cannot  presently  control,  and  third-party assessment capacity that does not yet exist. Each of these is addressable, and several are addressable now. But the flexibility and the infrastructure should arrive in that order — infrastructure first — rather than the reverse.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that because complex models are opaque even to many developers and users, no party currently stands to be accountable when data breaches or inaccurate outputs used in health practice cause harm. This accountability vacuum is the central worry.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter asks that AI manufacturers be held financially and legally accountable for all failures, data problems, and harms caused by these devices, rather than leaving responsibility undefined.
positions.public_summary: Commenter argues model opacity leaves no accountable party when data breaches or inaccurate outputs cause harm in health practice. Beyond FDA's framing of preserving manufacturer accountability in postmarket roles, the commenter asks that AI manufacturers bear full financial and legal liability for all resulting harms.
positions.supporting_text: Finally, the "black box" nature of complex models where the actually workings of the AI remain unknown to most of the developers and users presents an issue where, if there were data breeches or inaccurate information used in health practices which results in harm, there currently is no-one who stands to be accountable for such things. The AI manufacturers need to be held financially and legally accountable for ALL screw ups, data issues, or harm that these devices may do.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter endorses pairing standardized benchmarking with risk-tiered clinical confirmation, but wants the resulting review process to be clear and streamlined, particularly for high-impact use cases.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt the competency-based evaluation model as described, and additionally establish clear, streamlined regulatory pathways for high-impact GenAI use cases.
positions.public_summary: Strongly supports CDRH's competency-based model combining standardized benchmarking with risk-tiered clinical confirmation, while urging FDA to additionally provide clear, streamlined review pathways for high-impact use cases. Supporting detail appears truncated in the passage.
positions.supporting_text: We strongly support CDRH’s competency-based evaluation model (integrating standardized benchmarking with risk-tiered clinical confirmation) and urge the Agency to ensure clear, streamlined pathways for high-impact use cases:

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that risk stratification under the two-axis framework could subject supervised, lower-consequence functions such as ambient documentation, EHR screening, and HCP-reviewed imaging second-reads to disproportionate premarket scrutiny.
positions.requested_fda_action: Explicitly place ambient scribing, EHR screening, and HCP-supervised imaging second-reads in lower-risk categories, and reserve the most intensive premarket evidence expectations for unmonitored autonomous execution.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the two-axis risk framework but asks FDA to calibrate it so ambient scribing, EHR screening, and HCP-supervised imaging second-reads are firmly classified as lower risk, with the most intensive premarket scrutiny reserved for unmonitored autonomous execution.
positions.supporting_text: Two-Axis Risk Calibration (Questions 1–6): Anchor ambient scribing, EHR screening, and HCP-supervised imaging second-reads firmly in lower-risk categories, reserving high-intensity premarket scrutiny for unmonitored autonomous execution.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that GenAI outputs involving numerical laboratory data may be imprecise or confabulated, and that safety-escalation behavior may be inadequately tested under the proposed benchmarking structure.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the competency benchmarking framework but give priority weight to the Safety Escalation (S.1) and Quantitative Analysis (E.3) competencies to ensure numerical precision and prevent confabulation in blood lab analysis.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency benchmarking approach but asks FDA to prioritize the Safety Escalation and Quantitative Analysis competencies, citing the need for numerical precision and prevention of confabulated outputs in blood laboratory analysis.
positions.supporting_text: Competency Benchmarking (Questions 7–10): Prioritize Safety Escalation (S.1) and Quantitative Analysis (E.3) to guarantee numerical precision and prevent confabulations in blood lab analysis.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Downstream device developers need access to safety-relevant information about upstream foundation models, while model developers need to protect proprietary information such as model weights.
positions.requested_fda_action: Fully operationalize the voluntary Foundation Model Device Master File mechanism so downstream developers can reference upstream model cards without requiring disclosure of proprietary model weights.
positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's voluntary Foundation Model Master File concept and asks that it be fully operationalized, so downstream device developers can reference upstream model cards without foundation model developers disclosing proprietary model weights. No further conditions stated.
positions.supporting_text: Voluntary Master Files (Question 25): Fully operationalize Foundation Model Device Master Files (MAFs) so downstream developers can leverage upstream model cards without exposing proprietary weights.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that governing model drift through repeated supplemental clearances would be burdensome, and that postmarket tools such as machine-based supervisory agents and adaptable change-control plans should be permitted instead.
positions.requested_fda_action: Allow machine-based supervisory agents in postmarket monitoring and authorize flexible Predetermined Change Control Plans under FD&C Act § 515C so that model drift can be managed without additional supplemental clearance submissions.
positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA's postmarket direction but asks it to go further: permit machine-based supervisory agents and flexible Predetermined Change Control Plans under FD&C Act § 515C so model drift can be managed without repeated supplemental clearance submissions.
positions.supporting_text: Postmarket Monitoring (Questions 18–24): Enable machine-based supervisory agents and flexible Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCPs) under FD&C Act § 515C to govern model drift without requiring burdensome supplemental clearances.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter wants the concepts in the discussion paper, particularly the Foundation Model Master File concept, to move from discussion to actionable policy, and wants clearance pathways for AI tools used under HCP supervision to be streamlined so that beneficial healthcare innovation is not delayed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Issue the discussion paper's concepts as formal Draft Guidance, establish streamlined clearance pathways for HCP-supervised AI tools, and operationalize the voluntary Foundation Model MAF program.
positions.public_summary: Supports the discussion paper's direction and urges FDA to convert it into formal Draft Guidance, to create streamlined clearance pathways for AI tools used under healthcare professional supervision, and to operationalize the voluntary Foundation Model Master File program. No specific objections stated.
positions.supporting_text: FDA should advance this discussion paper into formal Draft Guidance, establishing streamlined clearance pathways for HCP-supervised AI tools while operationalizing the Foundation Model MAF program to accelerate safe, life-saving healthcare innovation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the two axes capture severity and a proxy for autonomy but omit the probability that an incorrect output is actually acted upon, which is where generative systems differ most from previously regulated software.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add "detectability" — the likelihood an incorrect output is recognized before reliance — as an explicit third dimension, and treat reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, and output traceability as determinants of detectability rather than separate axes, preserving a usable two-dimensional grid.
positions.public_summary: Considers FDA's two axes necessary but insufficient because they omit the probability an incorrect output is acted upon. Recommends adding detectability as an explicit dimension, with reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, and traceability treated as determinants of detectability rather than separate axes.
positions.supporting_text: The two axes — device activity and the consequence of relying on an incorrect output — are necessary but not sufficient. Together they describe severity and a proxy for autonomy. They do not describe the probability that an incorrect output is acted upon , which is where generative systems differ most sharply from the software CDRH has regulated to date.... I recommend CDRH add detectability — the likelihood that an incorrect output is recognized as incorrect before it is relied upon — as an explicit dimension, and treat reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, and output traceability as determinants of detectability rather than as independent axes. This preserves a two-dimensional grid that remains usable in practice while giving the omitted variable a defined home.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without an explicit statement of how the two-axis risk framework relates to a manufacturer's existing ISO 14971 risk management file, manufacturers will assume they must maintain a second, FDA-specific risk taxonomy in parallel, creating documentation burden without a corresponding safety benefit.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should state explicitly how the two-axis framework relates to the ISO 14971 risk management file, and if the grid functions as a communication and triage tool drawing on the existing 14971 file rather than a separate analysis, say so.
positions.public_summary: The commenter accepts the two-axis risk framework but asks CDRH to state explicitly how it relates to existing ISO 14971 risk management files—ideally clarifying that the grid draws on that file rather than requiring a parallel, FDA-specific risk taxonomy and added documentation.
positions.supporting_text: I further recommend that CDRH state explicitly how this framework relates to a manufacturer’s existing ISO 14971 risk management file. If the answer is that the grid is a communication and triage device that draws on the 14971 file rather than a separate analysis, that should be said. Absent such a statement, manufacturers will reasonably assume they must maintain a second, FDA-specific risk taxonomy alongside the first, which produces documentation burden without a corresponding safety gain.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues directiveness is an emergent property of generative outputs that manufacturers can constrain but cannot guarantee, so classification resting on a binary 'non-directive' determination would require attestations no sponsor can honestly make.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat directiveness as a constrained and monitored property: require sponsors to specify a directiveness ceiling for the intended use, document technical controls, and report a measured escape rate from adversarial and representative evaluation sets, with classification conditioned on the escape rate meeting a prespecified bound and the escape rate tracked as a postmarket endpoint.
positions.public_summary: Accepts directiveness as a risk modifier but rejects binary classification, arguing directiveness is emergent and unverifiable at design time. Proposes sponsors specify a directiveness ceiling with technical controls and report a measured escape rate, with classification conditioned on that rate and monitored postmarket.
positions.supporting_text: Directiveness  of  a  generative  output  is  an  emergent  property  of  the  output,  not  a  design  input  the manufacturer controls or can verify at design time. A manufacturer can constrain it — through system prompts, output templates, refusal training, post-generation filtering — but cannot guarantee it. If regulatory classification turns on whether a function is “non-directive,” sponsors will be asked to attest to something no sponsor can honestly attest to... The more workable construction treats directiveness as a constrained and monitored property . A sponsor would specify a directiveness ceiling for the intended use, describe the technical controls enforcing it, and — critically — report a measured escape rate: the rate at which outputs exceeded the specified ceiling across an adversarial and representative evaluation set. Classification would then be based on the specified ceiling, conditioned  on  the  escape  rate  meeting  a  prespecified  bound,  with  escape  rate  becoming  a  postmarket monitoring  endpoint.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that treating patient-facing GenAI functions as categorically higher risk misidentifies the operative variable, which they describe as whether the user has a realistic path to verification at the moment of reliance rather than the user's abstract domain knowledge.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure the risk framework around the verification path — its availability, its latency, and whether the output's design supports or discourages verification — rather than the user category, and credit safeguards such as traceable citations with verifiable links, explicit uncertainty communication, and consequence-scaled prompts to seek confirmation instead of static boilerplate.
positions.public_summary: Cautions against categorically higher risk for patient-facing functions. Recommends FDA base risk on the user's realistic verification path — availability, latency, and whether output design supports verification — rather than user category, crediting traceable citations, uncertainty communication, and consequence-scaled confirmation prompts.
positions.supporting_text: I would caution against a categorical elevation of risk for patient-facing functions. ... The variable that actually distinguishes the two cases is not the user’s domain knowledge in the abstract but whether the user has a  realistic path to verification  at the moment of reliance. ... I recommend the framework attend to the verification path — its availability, its latency, and whether the output’s design supports or discourages it — rather than to the user’s category. Safeguards that meaningfully change the analysis include traceable citation to primary sources with verifiable links, explicit uncertainty communication, and a designed prompt to seek confirmation that scales with the consequence of the specific output rather than appearing as static boilerplate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts that the generalist/specialist distinction is analytically real but warns it is not enforceable in practice, since a manufacturer can label an intended user but cannot control which clinician actually opens the application. Labeling-only mitigations are said to have a poor track record in software.
positions.requested_fda_action: Distinguish explicitly among labeled intended user, technical enforcement of user scope, and foreseeable off-label user, and state which drives risk assessment. Assess risk against foreseeable use, giving mitigation credit only for demonstrated technical enforcement such as role-based access controls tied to institutional credentialing, not for labeling alone.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the generalist/specialist risk distinction as analytically real but calls it unenforceable through labeling. Asks CDRH to separate labeled intended user, technical enforcement, and foreseeable off-label user, and to assess risk against foreseeable use, crediting only demonstrated access controls tied to credentialing.
positions.supporting_text: This distinction is analytically real but creates an enforcement problem CDRH should confront directly. A manufacturer can label an intended user; it cannot control which clinician opens the application. ... If CDRH intends specialty scope to bear regulatory weight, the paper should distinguish between (a) labeled intended user, (b) technical enforcement of user scope, and (c) foreseeable off-label user, and should state which of the three drives the risk assessment. My recommendation is that risk be assessed against foreseeable use, with  credit  given  for  demonstrated  technical  enforcement  —  role-based  access  controls  tied  to institutional credentialing, for example — rather than for labeling alone. Labeling-only mitigations have a poor track record in software and should not be treated as risk-reducing here.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Single-turn or turn-level evaluation of a conversational device does not correspond to how the device is actually used, so risk that emerges across a conversation (drift from non-directive to action-directing output) goes unmeasured.
positions.requested_fda_action: State that for multi-turn devices the session, not the turn, is the unit of analysis; define intended use at the conversational level in terms of supported trajectories and boundaries; require trajectory-based multi-turn adversarial evaluation with a measured, bounded escape rate, and treat turn-level evaluation alone as insufficient.
positions.public_summary: Recommends FDA treat the session rather than the turn as the unit of analysis for multi-turn devices, defining intended use at the conversational level by supported trajectories and boundaries, and requiring trajectory-based adversarial evaluation with bounded escape rates; single-turn benchmarking alone insufficient.
positions.supporting_text: I recommend CDRH state that for multi-turn devices, the session, not the turn, is the unit of analysis  for both intended use and evaluation. Intended use should be defined at the conversational level, in terms of the range of trajectories the device is designed to support and the boundaries it is designed to hold. Evaluation should then be trajectory-based: multi-turn adversarial evaluation in which evaluators actively attempt to walk the device from non-directive information toward action-directing output, with the escape rate measured and bounded as described under Question 2. Single-turn benchmarking of a multi-turn device measures something that does not correspond to how the device is used... Turn-level evaluation of conversational devices should be treated as insufficient on its own regardless of how thorough it is.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without a prespecified trade-off between under- and over-escalation, sponsors can report both error rates after the fact and present whichever is more favorable as the primary endpoint. The commenter also notes the trade-off depends on deployment context and the capacity of the system receiving escalations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to prespecify an explicit asymmetric acceptance criterion (e.g., minimum sensitivity for escalation-warranted conditions plus a maximum acceptable over-escalation rate) with a clinical justification referencing the deployment context and receiving system capacity, and to have FDA assess that justification, not just the reported rates.
positions.public_summary: On escalation error trade-offs, the commenter proposes a procedural fix: rather than reconciling incommensurable error types, FDA should require sponsors to prespecify asymmetric acceptance criteria (minimum sensitivity plus maximum over-escalation rate) with context- and capacity-based clinical justification FDA reviews, foreclosing post hoc endpoint selection.
positions.supporting_text: My recommendation is procedural: rather than asking manufacturers to reconcile them, require that the trade-off be prespecified rather than discovered. A sponsor should state, before evaluation, an explicit asymmetric acceptance criterion — for example, a minimum  sensitivity  for  the  escalation-warranted  condition  together  with  a  maximum  acceptable  over- escalation rate — accompanied by a clinical justification for the chosen ratio that references the specific deployment context and the capacity of the receiving system. The justification, not just the numbers, should be part of the submission and should be assessed. Post hoc reporting of both rates without a prespecified trade-off allows the sponsor to characterize whichever result is more favorable as the primary endpoint, and CDRH should foreclose that.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that over-escalation harms — alert fatigue, resource diversion, and downstream harm to patients deprived of consumed capacity — are diffuse, delayed, and rarely attributed to the device, and so are systematically under-detected by the postmarket mechanisms described in Section VI.
positions.requested_fda_action: Give over-escalation greater weight in the evaluation of care escalation functions and strengthen postmarket approaches so they can detect diffuse, delayed harms that are not readily attributed to the device.
positions.public_summary: Comment argues over-escalation deserves more attention than it typically receives: its harms — alert fatigue, resource diversion, and downstream harm to patients whose capacity was consumed — are diffuse, delayed, and rarely attributed to the device, so FDA's described postmarket mechanisms systematically under-detect them.
positions.supporting_text: Over-escalation  deserves  more  attention  than  it  typically  receives.  Its  harms  —  alert  fatigue,  resource diversion, downstream harm to patients who did need the capacity consumed — are diffuse, delayed, and rarely attributed to the device. They are therefore systematically under-detected by exactly the postmarket mechanisms Section VI describes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts the competency-based framework as a useful organizing structure but warns that the physician-credentialing analogy carries an unstated assumption: licensure tolerates limited, non-exhaustive testing only because it sits within a system of continuous individual professional accountability, which a device does not reproduce.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the competency framing as the organizing structure for benchmarking, clinical confirmation, and monitoring, but state explicitly in the paper that the licensure analogy justifies the shape of the evidence rather than its quantity, and that the reduced-testing feature of credentialing does not transfer to devices.
positions.public_summary: Endorses the competency-based approach as a useful organizing structure, but asks FDA to state explicitly that the physician-licensure analogy justifies the shape, not the quantity, of required evidence, because credentialing's reduced testing depends on continuous individual accountability devices do not reproduce.
positions.supporting_text: Broadly, yes, and the paper’s framing is a genuine contribution. But the analogy carries an assumption that should be made explicit before it is relied upon... Physician credentialing is evidentiarily permissive — no exhaustive testing of every scenario — because it is embedded in a system of continuous individual accountability... A device inherits none of this. ... My recommendation is that CDRH retain the competency framing as an organizing structure — it maps cleanly  onto  benchmarking,  confirmation,  and  monitoring  —  while  explicitly  declining  to  import  its evidentiary permissiveness. The paper should state that the licensure analogy justifies  the shape  of the evidence, not the quantity, and that the reduced-testing feature of physician credentialing is a consequence of accountability structures the device context does not reproduce.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without an explicit, published mapping from risk tiers to required evidence, a competency-based approach would function as discretionary, case-by-case review rather than a predictable least-burdensome pathway.
positions.requested_fda_action: Publish a mapping table that specifies, for each cell or band of the risk grid, the minimum benchmarking elements, the minimum clinical confirmation tier from the Section V.C ladder, whether third-party involvement is expected, and the minimum postmarket monitoring configuration, with a documented justified deviation pathway but a stable published default.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency-based approach but argues it needs a published risk-tier-to-evidence mapping, otherwise it becomes discretionary case-by-case review. Asks CDRH to specify minimum benchmarking, clinical confirmation tier, third-party involvement, and postmarket monitoring per risk band, with a justified deviation pathway.
positions.supporting_text: A competency-based approach without a published risk-tier-to-evidence mapping is not a least-burdensome pathway. It is discretionary, case-by-case review with a new vocabulary. ... I recommend CDRH publish a mapping table specifying, for each cell or band of the risk grid: the minimum benchmarking elements required; the minimum acceptable clinical confirmation tier from the Section V .C ladder; whether third-party involvement is expected; and the minimum postmarket monitoring configuration. The mapping need not be rigid — a documented, justified deviation pathway should exist — but the default must be published and stable.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that the described robustness and reliability benchmarking addresses natural input variation but not adversarial or hostile input such as prompt injection via retrieved documents or patient-supplied text, instruction override, and jailbreak techniques that defeat scope constraints.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add adversarial/hostile input resistance as a distinct benchmarking element, treated as a security property rather than a robustness property, and cross-reference it to CDRH's premarket cybersecurity expectations.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the benchmarking structure but says it is missing adversarial input testing. Argues prompt injection, instruction override, and jailbreak resistance are security rather than robustness properties, and should form a distinct benchmarking element cross-referenced to CDRH premarket cybersecurity expectations.
positions.supporting_text: Adversarial and hostile input.  Robustness and reliability, as described, appear oriented toward natural variation in input... Generative devices additionally face adversarial input:  prompt  injection  through  retrieved  documents  or  patient-supplied  text,  instruction  override,  and jailbreak techniques that defeat scope constraints. This is a security property, not a robustness property, and it should  be  a  distinct  benchmarking  element  cross-referenced  to  CDRH’s  premarket  cybersecurity expectations.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Fabricated but plausible citations are a failure mode distinct from inaccurate content, and they undermine the user's ability to verify an output, turning an intended safeguard into a source of hazard.
positions.requested_fda_action: Include citation/provenance fidelity as a separately measured element within the benchmarking structure, rather than assuming it correlates with content accuracy.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the benchmarking framework but asks FDA to treat citation and provenance fidelity as a separately measured competency. Argues a fabricated yet plausible citation is a distinct failure mode that defeats user verification, and should not be assumed to track content accuracy.
positions.supporting_text: Provenance and citation fidelity.  Where a device cites sources, the correctness of the citation is a distinct failure mode from the correctness of the claim. A fabricated but plausible citation actively defeats the user’s verification path — it converts a safeguard into a hazard... Citation fidelity should be measured separately and should not be assumed to track content accuracy.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Scope maintenance testing that only checks whether a device stays within its intended scope misses how the device behaves at the scope boundary; sharp performance collapse accompanied by unchanged high confidence is more dangerous than graceful degradation and is not detectable through aggregate accuracy metrics.
positions.requested_fda_action: Include boundary behavior in the benchmarking structure by evaluating whether performance degrades gracefully with visible uncertainty at the edge of scope, rather than relying on aggregate accuracy or scope-adherence measures alone.
positions.public_summary: Supports the benchmarking framework but asks FDA to add evaluation of behavior at the edge of scope, distinguishing graceful degradation with visible uncertainty from sharp performance collapse paired with unchanged high confidence, which aggregate accuracy metrics do not reveal.
positions.supporting_text: Behavior at the edge of scope.  Scope maintenance measures whether the device stays in scope. Equally important is what it does at the boundary: whether performance degrades gracefully with visible uncertainty, or falls off sharply while confidence remains high. The latter is far more dangerous and is invisible to aggregate accuracy metrics.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is aware of ongoing AI evaluation and risk management standards work but states they lack current verified information on which specific standards are mature enough for regulatory recognition and does not want to cite one incorrectly.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recommends that CDRH directly survey the standards landscape and publicly state which externally developed standards it considers suitable for leveraging in benchmarking.
positions.public_summary: Commenter declines to identify specific external standards for benchmarking, citing lack of verified information on their maturity for regulatory recognition, and asks CDRH to survey the standards landscape itself and state which standards it considers suitable to leverage.
