positions.requested_fda_action: Establish/maintain the Foundation Model Master File as a standing, current record that documents model versioning, deprecation timelines, and change-notification practices so dependency risk can be assessed directly during review.
positions.public_summary: Comment sees the greatest value of a Foundation Model Master File in providing a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices, enabling CDRH and manufacturers to assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.
positions.supporting_text:
I would also note that this is where a Foundation Model MAF (Question 25) would deliver the most value: a
standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices would let
CDRH and manufacturers assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that foundation model developers have little intrinsic incentive to disclose safety-relevant limitations, since medical devices are a small share of their revenue and disclosure carries competitive and litigation exposure, so a purely voluntary MAF program is unlikely to attract broad participation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish the voluntary Foundation Model MAF program but pair it with a manufacturer-side default: absent an MAF, the device manufacturer must independently and at its own cost characterize the underlying model (training data provenance to the extent determinable, contamination assessment, known failure modes, version and deprecation practices, subgroup performance) or the submission is incomplete.
positions.public_summary: Agrees the voluntary MAF program faces a real incentive problem but recommends creating it anyway, paired with a default rule placing the full model-characterization burden (provenance, contamination, failure modes, versioning, subgroup performance) on manufacturers when no MAF exists, creating commercial pressure for developer participation.
positions.supporting_text:
The paper's candor about the incentive problem is warranted. Foundation model developers serve markets in
which  medical  devices  are  a  small  fraction  of  revenue;  disclosure  of  safety-relevant  limitations  carries
competitive and litigation exposure; and a voluntary program asking them to document weaknesses for a
regulator overseeing someone else's product is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own merits.
I nonetheless recommend CDRH create it, because the mechanism that makes it work is not the model
developer's incentive — it is the device manufacturer's.
Pair  the  voluntary  MAF  with  a  manufacturer-side  default:  where  an  MAF  is  absent,  the  device
manufacturer bears the full characterization burden for the underlying model. Training data provenance
to  the  extent  determinable,  contamination  assessment,  known  failure  modes,  version  and  deprecation
practices, subgroup performance characterization — all of it, generated independently at the manufacturer's
cost, or the submission is incomplete.
That default creates a procurement preference. Device manufacturers will strongly prefer model providers
that maintain a current MAF, because the alternative is expensive and often technically impossible. Providers
will then face a commercial reason to participate that has nothing to do with regulatory goodwill.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A Foundation Model MAF is only useful if it contains specific, safety-relevant items (version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, safety and refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning) and is kept current; a static snapshot would not support contamination analysis or timely detection of third-party model changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify a defined MAF content set covering model identity/version lineage, training data cutoff, versioning, change notification and deprecation policy, known limitations and failure modes, safety/refusal behavior, developer evaluation results, and medical-domain training. Impose a currency requirement obligating MAF updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.public_summary: Endorses Foundation Model Master Files, but specifies required content: model identity and version lineage, training data cutoff, versioning/change-notification and deprecation policy, known failure modes, safety and refusal behavior, developer evaluations, and medical fine-tuning; urges requiring updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.supporting_text:
Suggested MAF content: model identity and version lineage; training data cutoff date (essential for the
contamination analysis under Question 10); versioning, change notification, and deprecation policy (essential
for Question 24); known limitations and documented failure modes; safety training and refusal behavior;
evaluation results the developer has generated; and any medical-domain-specific training or fine-tuning. A
currency requirement — the MAF must be updated within a defined period of any model change — is what
makes it useful rather than a snapshot.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a Foundation Model Master File could be misread as evidence establishing the safety or effectiveness of devices built on that model, displacing evaluation of the device itself.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should explicitly frame the MAF as contextual information supporting, not substituting for, evaluation of the final user-facing device as configured for deployment, consistent with the paper's stated unit of evaluation.
positions.public_summary: Endorses the paper's position that the final deployed device is the unit of evaluation, and cautions that a Foundation Model Master File should be framed only as context for device evaluation, never as evidence of a device's safety or effectiveness.
positions.supporting_text:
I would add one caution: an MAF should never be treated as establishing the safety or effectiveness of any
device built on the model. The paper's statement that the unit of evaluation is the final user-facing device as
configured for deployment is correct and important, and the MAF should be framed as context for that
evaluation, not as a partial substitute for it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Per-step accuracy metrics overstate end-to-end reliability for multi-step agentic devices, since 95% per-step accuracy yields roughly 60% success across a ten-step task, and error compounding worsens as sequences lengthen.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that acceptance criteria for agentic GenAI-enabled devices be set at the level of the completed task, with evaluation measuring task completion rather than step accuracy.
positions.public_summary: Commenter endorses attention to agentic devices but urges FDA to state explicitly that acceptance criteria and evaluation address completed-task performance rather than per-step accuracy, citing compounding error across multi-step sequences and the ease of generating step-level metrics.
positions.supporting_text:
Trajectory-level  acceptance  criteria. Per-step  performance  is  a  misleading  summary  of  end-to-end
reliability. A device that completes each step correctly 95% of the time completes a ten-step task correctly
about 60% of the time, and that arithmetic is unforgiving as sequences lengthen. Acceptance criteria must be
stated at the level of the completed task, and evaluation must measure task completion rather than step
accuracy. I recommend CDRH state this explicitly, because step-level metrics are far easier to generate and
will otherwise be offered.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that an agentic device's scope of actions can expand incrementally—adding tools, write operations, or affected external systems—moving a deployment from low to high risk without any regulatory event marking the transition.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take, each classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution; require explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions; and treat the inventory as a locked specification whose expansion constitutes a Tier 3 change under the Question 22 change framework.
positions.public_summary: Supports the agentic and change-control framework but asks FDA to require an enumerated inventory of all system actions classified by reversibility and consequence of error, explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions, and treatment of scope expansion as a Tier 3 change.
positions.supporting_text:
Action inventory with irreversibility classification. I recommend sponsors submit an enumerated inventory
of every action the system can take — every tool, every write operation, every external system it can affect
— each classified by reversibility and by the consequence of erroneous execution. Irreversible actions should
require explicit confirmation by a qualified user, and the inventory should be treated as a locked specification
whose expansion is a Tier 3 change under the framework in Question 22. Uncontrolled expansion of an
agent's action scope is the most likely path from a low-risk deployment to a high-risk one without any
regulatory event marking the transition.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic GenAI devices could hold broader tool permissions than their intended use requires; the commenter views least-privilege, per-deployment scoping as standard security practice already reflected in CDRH cybersecurity expectations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect agentic systems to hold the narrowest permissions sufficient for the intended use, scoped per deployment, and cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations rather than creating a parallel treatment in the paper.
positions.public_summary: Supports addressing agentic autonomy but asks FDA to specify least-privilege tool permissions scoped to each deployment and intended use, and to cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations instead of developing a separate, parallel treatment in the discussion paper.
positions.supporting_text:
Least-privilege  tool  access. Agentic  systems  should  hold  the  narrowest  permissions  sufficient  for  the
intended use, scoped per deployment. This is standard security practice and maps directly onto CDRH's
existing cybersecurity expectations; I recommend the paper cross-reference them rather than developing a
parallel treatment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without audit logs capturing the full agentic trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect — root cause analysis of harmful outcomes is impossible and corrective action becomes guesswork. The commenter states this also prevents discharging the complaint-handling obligations discussed under Question 21.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make the adequacy of audit logging an explicit premarket review element for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, rather than treating it as an assumed postmarket capability.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's attention to agentic oversight but asks FDA to require audit logging that reconstructs full agentic trajectories — inputs, tool calls, actions, model version and configuration — as an explicit premarket review element, arguing root cause analysis and complaint handling otherwise fail.
positions.supporting_text:
Audit logging sufficient for post-hoc reconstruction. When an agentic system produces a harmful outcome,
the investigation must be able to reconstruct the full trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts
where available, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect.
Without this, root cause analysis is not possible, corrective action is guesswork, and the complaint-handling
obligations under Question 21 cannot be discharged. I recommend audit logging adequacy be an explicit
premarket review element for agentic devices rather than a postmarket assumption.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that compounding errors in agentic devices make end-to-end performance hardest to establish premarket while errors propagate fastest and are least reversible after deployment, so accepting greater premarket uncertainty is particularly ill-suited to this device category.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should treat agentic GenAI-enabled devices as presumptively ineligible for the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway that relies on greater postmarket monitoring.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the postmarket-reliance concept generally but argues it fits agentic devices poorly, since their end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket and errors compound fastest and are least reversible. Recommends CDRH presumptively exclude agentic devices from any reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.
positions.supporting_text:
I would also note that the compounding-error arithmetic above interacts badly with the premarket-uncertainty
trade proposed in Question 18. Agentic devices are where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish
premarket,  and  simultaneously  where  errors  propagate  fastest  and  are  least  reversible  postmarket.  I
recommend CDRH treat agentic devices as presumptively outside the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that without an explicit, published mapping from risk tier to required evidence, the competency-based framework will lack predictability and will not in practice be least burdensome.
positions.requested_fda_action: Publish the mapping between risk tiers and the corresponding level of premarket evidence expected, so sponsors can anticipate evidence requirements.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a risk-based, competency-based evidence framework but asks FDA to publish an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping, arguing that without such predictability the approach will not in practice be least burdensome.
positions.supporting_text:
Publish  the  risk-tier-to-evidence  mapping. Predictability  is  the  mechanism  by  which  risk-based
frameworks reduce burden. Without it, "competency-based" and "least burdensome" will not describe the
same thing.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the proposed competency-based framework could create artifacts parallel to the risk management, design control, and change control documentation manufacturers already maintain under ISO 14971 and the QMSR.
positions.requested_fda_action: Build the framework on existing quality system and risk management infrastructure rather than requiring separate parallel artifacts, and explain in the paper how the new elements relate to established QMSR and ISO 14971 processes.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but asks FDA to ground it in existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control procedures instead of creating parallel artifacts, and to clarify in the paper how these elements relate.
positions.supporting_text:
Integrate with existing quality system and risk management infrastructure.  Manufacturers maintain
ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and change control procedures under the QMSR. The framework
should draw on these rather than establishing parallel artifacts, and the paper should state how the pieces
relate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter notes that the paper defers the question of statutory authority, yet several proposals — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations reaching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — may sit at or beyond the limits of CDRH's existing authorities.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should return to and identify explicitly which elements of the framework it can implement under current authority and which would require new legislation from Congress, so stakeholders know which parts to build toward.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but urges CDRH to stop deferring the legal-authority question, arguing that enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations on non-manufacturer foundation model developers may require congressional action; stakeholders need that clarity.
positions.supporting_text:
Identify  which  elements  require  new  legal  authority. The  paper  expressly  defers  this  question.  I
understand why, but I would encourage CDRH to return to it, because several proposals — enforceable
postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, obligations touching
foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the edge of
existing authorities. Stakeholders assessing which parts of this framework to build toward would benefit
from knowing which parts CDRH can implement and which would require Congress.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that the discussion paper's competency-based framing is oriented toward enabling market entry and worries it may be read as an authorization pathway rather than a genuine evaluation framework capable of a negative conclusion.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that the competency-based framework contemplates the outcome that a given intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency-based framework in principle but asks CDRH to state explicitly that it can conclude an intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.supporting_text:
Preserve  the  option  to  say  no. The  paper's  framing  is  oriented  toward  enabling  market  entry,
appropriately  so  given  its  purpose.  But  a  competency-based  framework  should  also  be  capable  of
concluding  that  a  given  intended  use  is  not  currently  supportable  by  available  evidence.  I  would
encourage CDRH to state that the framework contemplates that outcome, so that it is understood as an
evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's central concern is that the framework's regulatory flexibility outpaces the supporting infrastructure: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, third-party foundation model dependencies manufacturers cannot currently control, and non-existent third-party assessment capacity.
positions.requested_fda_action: Sequence the approach so that the enabling infrastructure — trustworthy benchmarks, clear postmarket reportability rules, mechanisms for third-party model dependency control, and qualified third-party assessment capacity — is established before the flexible evidentiary pathways are relied upon.
positions.public_summary: The commenter accepts the framework's direction but argues its flexibility currently outruns necessary infrastructure — untrustworthy benchmarks, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, uncontrollable third-party model dependencies, and absent third-party assessment capacity — and asks FDA to build that infrastructure before relying on flexible pathways.
positions.supporting_text:
My central concern is that the framework's flexibility currently outruns the infrastructure needed to make
flexibility safe: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, postmarket monitoring whose reportability rules are
unsettled,  third-party  model  dependencies  that  manufacturers  cannot  presently  control,  and  third-party
assessment capacity that does not yet exist. Each of these is addressable, and several are addressable now. But
the flexibility and the infrastructure should arrive in that order — infrastructure first — rather than the
reverse.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the two-axis framework (device activity and consequence of an incorrect output) as a sound but incomplete basis for GenAI risk assessment, because it can assign identical risk positions to functions whose real-world risk differs substantially depending on oversight and deployment context.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework to incorporate three additional dimensions: traceability of the output to source data, the availability and effectiveness of downstream human oversight, and the temporal context of deployment (real-time clinical decision versus asynchronous review).
positions.public_summary: Calls the two-axis risk framework a sound starting point but insufficient for GenAI. Asks FDA to add three dimensions: output traceability to source data, availability and effectiveness of downstream human oversight, and temporal deployment context (real-time versus asynchronous review).
positions.supporting_text: To start, the two-axis framework is a sound starting point but is insufficient for GenAI. It omits three dimensions that are critical for real-world assessment: (a) traceability of the output to source data, (b) the availability and effectiveness of downstream human oversight, and (c) the temporal context of deployment (real-time clinical decision vs. asynchronous review). A GenAI function that generates a patient-facing summary with no clinician intermediary poses fundamentally different risk than one that produces a draft note for clinician review, even if both occupy the same position on the two-axis grid.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter considers the two-axis framework (device activity and consequence of incorrect output) insufficient to describe the actual risk surface of GenAI-enabled devices, because it omits how much human oversight exists at the point of output delivery and whether outputs can be traced to verifiable source data.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the framework to four axes by adding (3) degree of human oversight available at output delivery, from fully autonomous to mandatory clinician review, and (4) traceability of output to verifiable source data, from fully traceable to opaque; align with IMDRF's lifecycle management framework treating human oversight as a distinct governance dimension.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's two-axis risk framework but asks that it be expanded to four axes, adding degree of human oversight at output delivery (autonomous to mandatory clinician review) and traceability of outputs to verifiable source data, citing alignment with IMDRF lifecycle management concepts.
positions.supporting_text: Recommendation to FDA: Expand the framework to a four-axis model: (1) device activity (current Axis 1), (2) consequence of incorrect output (current Axis 2), (3) degree of human oversight available at the point of output delivery (ranging from fully autonomous to mandatory clinician review), and (4) traceability of output to verifiable source data (ranging from fully traceable to opaque/generative). This four-axis model would better capture the actual risk surface of GenAI-enabled devices and align with IMDRF's lifecycle management framework, which emphasizes human oversight as distinct a governance dimension

positions.stakeholder_concern: Existing PCCP practice requires pre-specifying modifications in concrete terms, but GenAI foundation models evolve in ways that cannot be fully predicted in advance, making granular pre-specification unworkable.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain pre-specification but allow it at a higher level of abstraction: permit PCCPs that authorize foundation model updates conditioned on meeting stated competency benchmarks, passing specified safety evaluations, and staying within defined performance deviation bounds from the authorized baseline.
positions.public_summary: Supports retaining PCCP pre-specification for GenAI devices but urges FDA to permit it at a higher level of abstraction—authorizing foundation model updates that meet specified competency benchmarks, pass safety evaluations, and remain within defined performance deviation bounds from the authorized baseline.
positions.supporting_text: The PCCP Framework requires pre-specification of modifications, but GenAI foundation models evolve in ways that cannot be fully predicted. The solution is not to abandon pre-specification but to pre-specify at a higher-level of abstraction. Rather than specifying “the model will be retrained with X additional images,” the PCCP for a GenAI-enabled device should specify that the foundation model may be updated provided the updated model meets the following competency benchmarks, passes the following safety evaluations, and does not exceed the following performance deviation bounds from the authorized baseline.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's concern is that modification types for GenAI devices vary widely (retraining, foundation model version updates, prompt engineering adjustments) and cannot be exhaustively prespecified, so change control should not depend on enumerating change categories. They describe an architecture whose lifecycle governance controls remain constant across all such modifications.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize a change-agnostic AI lifecycle governance layer as the basis for managing post-deployment modifications, comprising continuous QMS oversight (design controls, CAPA, change management, documentation), ISO 14971-aligned risk management, human-in-the-loop oversight with escalation paths, cybersecurity (secure by design, threat monitoring, incident response), and transparency/labeling on intended use, limitations, performance, and updates.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the need for change control but proposes that, rather than prespecifying modification categories, FDA rely on a change-agnostic lifecycle governance layer—QMS oversight, ISO 14971 risk management, human-in-the-loop escalation, cybersecurity, and transparency—that stays constant across retraining, foundation model updates, and prompt changes.
positions.supporting_text: I have already created for an architecture's governance framework that operates at exactly this level of abstraction. The AI lifecycle management controls apply across all the steps I created in my architecture in order to provide continuous QMS oversight (design controls, CAPA, change management, documentation), risk management (ISO 14971 aligned), human oversight (HITL throughout with escalation paths), cybersecurity (secure by design, threat monitoring, incident response), and transparency and labeling (intended use, limitations, performance, updates). This governance layer is change-agnostic and it applies regardless of whether the modification is a retraining event, a foundation model version update, or a prompt engineering adjustment. The key is that the governance controls remain constant even as the specific modifications vary.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Traditional PCCPs require pre-specification of exact modifications, which the commenter views as ill-suited to the unpredictability of how GenAI-enabled devices evolve.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish a new 'Performance-Bounded PCCP' category that pre-specifies continuing competency benchmarks, maximum acceptable deviation from the authorized baseline, monitoring methodology, rollback protocol, and cumulative impact tracking, allowing in-bounds modifications without a new submission while out-of-bounds deviations trigger rollback or a new submission.
positions.public_summary: Supports PCCP-based change control but asks FDA to create a 'Performance-Bounded PCCP' that pre-specifies continuing benchmarks, allowable deviation limits, monitoring, rollback, and cumulative-impact tracking instead of exact modifications, with out-of-bounds performance triggering rollback or a new submission.
positions.supporting_text: Create a new PCCP category called "Performance-Bounded PCCP" for GenAI-enabled devices. Unlike a traditional PCCP that pre-specifies the exact modifications, a "Performance-Bounded PCCP" would pre-specify: (1) the competency benchmarks the device must continue to meet after any modification, (2) the maximum acceptable performance deviation from the authorized baseline across each benchmark dimension, (3) the monitoring methodology for detecting deviations, (4) the rollback protocol if deviations are detected, and (5) the cumulative impact tracking methodology. Any modification that keeps the device within the performance bounds may be implemented without a new submission. Any modification that causes the device to fall outside the bounds triggers either a rollback or a new submission. This approach accommodates the unpredictability of GenAI evolution while maintaining the principle that FDA authorizes the safety and effectiveness envelope, not the specific technical implementation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter considers the two-axis framework (device activity and consequence of an incorrect output) necessary but insufficient, because it omits factors that determine whether an incorrect output actually reaches and harms a patient, including irreversibility, speed of harm, realistic detection and rescue, degree of system authority, whether human review is meaningful rather than nominal, and dependence on local environmental and workflow conditions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework to explicitly incorporate irreversibility, time to harm, opportunity for detection and rescue, system authority (observe/recommend/direct/coordinate/execute), quality of human review including automation bias and workload effects, and environmental dependence such as image quality, connectivity, latency, staffing, and local workflow.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's two-axis risk framework as necessary but insufficient, urging explicit added dimensions: irreversibility, time to harm, realistic detection and rescue, degree of system authority (observe through execute), whether human review is meaningful or nominal, and dependence on local environmental and workflow conditions.
positions.supporting_text:
Device activity and the consequence of relying on an incorrect output are necessary but insufficient. CDRH
should also account explicitly for:
• Irreversibility: Can the clinical act be stopped or undone without added harm?
• Time to harm: How quickly can an incorrect output cause injury?
• Opportunity for detection and rescue: Is there a realistic, validated safeguard before harm occurs,
and can the local team rescue the patient?
• System authority: Does the function observe, recommend, direct, coordinate, or execute an action?
• Human review quality: Is review contemporaneous and meaningful, or merely nominal because of
workload, speed, interface design, or automation bias?
• Environmental dependence: Does performance depend on image quality, connectivity, latency,
instruments, local workflow, staffing, or patient anatomy?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter treats directiveness as a graded procedural continuum of authority rather than a binary or two-point distinction, spanning observation/summarization, recommendation, action direction, bounded conditional execution, and autonomous sequencing of actions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a five-level continuum of device authority (observe/summarize, recommend, direct, conditionally execute a bounded task, autonomously sequence or perform actions) and scale required evidence and safeguards with both the level of authority and the consequence of an incorrect output.
positions.public_summary: Commenter proposes replacing a binary or narrow directiveness distinction with a five-level continuum of device authority—observe/summarize, recommend, direct, conditionally execute a bounded task, autonomously act—and asks that required evidence and safeguards escalate with both authority and consequence.
positions.supporting_text:
A useful procedural continuum is: (1) observe or summarize; (2) recommend; (3) direct an action; (4)
conditionally execute a bounded task; and (5) autonomously sequence or perform actions. Evidence and
safeguards should escalate with both authority and consequence.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that nominal human oversight may be credited as a risk mitigation even when the deployment design gives the clinician insufficient time or information to detect and correct erroneous outputs.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should not assign low-risk classification based on the mere presence of a human in the loop, and should instead account for whether the clinician realistically has the time and information needed to catch and correct errors.
positions.public_summary: Comment on the risk framework: classification should not treat a nominally "in the loop" clinician as risk-reducing. The commenter asks FDA to consider whether the design actually affords the clinician enough time and information to detect and correct errors.
positions.supporting_text:
A system should not be classified as low
risk merely because a clinician is nominally "in the loop" when the design leaves that clinician little time or
information to detect and correct an error.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Risk in multi-turn conversational and agentic systems can accumulate across a sequence of exchanges or actions even when each individual output looks acceptable, including drift beyond the stated intended use.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require evaluation at the level of realistic conversational and action trajectories, explicitly assessing cumulative anchoring, repeated overconfidence, premature closure, tool selection, and migration beyond the intended use.
positions.public_summary: Supports trajectory-based evaluation for multi-turn and agentic systems, noting risk can accumulate across a sequence even when individual outputs seem safe. Asks FDA to require testing of realistic conversational and action trajectories, covering anchoring, overconfidence, premature closure, tool selection, and drift beyond intended use.
positions.supporting_text:
For multi-turn or agentic systems, risk can emerge across a sequence even when no single output appears
dangerous. Evaluation should include realistic conversational and action trajectories, cumulative
anchoring, repeated overconfidence, premature closure, tool selection, and migration beyond the
intended use.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter holds that the harms from under-escalation and over-escalation are not interchangeable, so combining or netting them would obscure meaningfully different error consequences.
positions.requested_fda_action: Evaluate under-escalation and over-escalation as separate, distinct error directions rather than aggregating them into a single performance measure.
positions.public_summary: The commenter agrees with FDA's premise that escalation errors are not commensurable and recommends that under-escalation and over-escalation be assessed separately, as distinct error directions, rather than combined into a single aggregated performance measure. No further detail provided.
positions.supporting_text:
Under- and over-escalation should be evaluated separately because their harms are not
interchangeable.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts the competency-based approach only if 'competency' is assessed for the complete device operating in its intended environment rather than for a foundation model in isolation, and considers FDA's benchmarking domains incomplete for real-world clinical and procedural settings.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define competency at the level of the full device in its deployment environment and expand device benchmarking to include perception and spatial/temporal reasoning, uncertainty calibration, abstention and escalation, robustness to corrupted or adversarial inputs, rare anatomy/complications/equipment faults/workflow interruptions, subgroup and site generalizability, communication with the surgeon and OR team, error recovery and safe degradation on component or network failure, and, for agentic systems, adherence to explicit authority, tool, and stop boundaries.
positions.public_summary: Finds the competency-based approach useful only if competency is assessed for the complete device in its intended environment, not a standalone foundation model, and asks FDA to broaden benchmarking to cover perception, calibration and escalation, robustness, rare events, team communication, safe degradation, and agentic authority

positions.stakeholder_concern: Public benchmarks may be compromised by training-data contamination, saturation, or weak construct validity, so benchmark scores alone may not indicate real-world safety or effectiveness.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to demonstrate that chosen benchmarks measure the competencies specific to the intended use and predict performance in representative workflows, and support use of protected test sets and independent assessment to limit optimization to the test.
positions.public_summary: Comment agrees benchmarking has a role but says public benchmarks alone are inadequate where contamination, saturation, or weak construct validity is plausible. Asks FDA to require sponsor evidence linking benchmarks to intended-use competencies and representative workflows, with protected test sets and independent assessment.
positions.supporting_text:
Public benchmarks alone are inadequate where training-data contamination, saturation, or weak construct
validity is plausible. Sponsors should demonstrate that benchmarks measure the competencies required
by the intended use and predict performance in representative workflows. Protected test sets and
independent assessment can reduce optimization to the test.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts that clinical confirmation can be tiered by risk, but holds that lower-rigor approaches (retrospective review, silent deployment) are only suitable for bounded observational functions, while systems that direct or execute invasive actions require prospective evaluation under clinically realistic conditions, including deliberately constructed stress scenarios such as degraded visualization, uncommon anatomy, device conflict, missing data, and urgent conversion.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require, for high-risk surgical or invasive-action functions, staged confirmation comprising simulation and cadaveric/preclinical evaluation, staged clinical introduction, and prospective study, with stress-condition testing; the IDEAL and IDEAL Robotics frameworks are offered as models covering progressive evaluation, human factors, learning curves, and long-term monitoring.
positions.public_summary: Supports risk-proportionate clinical confirmation but would limit retrospective or silent deployment to bounded observational functions. Urges that systems directing or executing invasive actions undergo prospective, stress-condition testing, with simulation, cadaveric/preclinical work and staged introduction modeled on IDEAL and IDEAL Robotics frameworks.
positions.supporting_text:
Retrospective evaluation or silent deployment may be appropriate for bounded observational functions.
Systems that direct or execute invasive actions should require prospective evaluation under clinically
realistic conditions before routine use. Testing should include both ordinary cases and deliberately
constructed stress conditions: degraded visualization, blood or smoke in the field, uncommon anatomy,
unexpected motion, device conflict, missing data, delayed communication, and urgent conversion or
bailout.
High-risk surgical confirmation should include simulation and cadaveric or preclinical evaluation where
appropriate, followed by staged clinical introduction and prospective study. The IDEAL framework for
surgical innovation and the IDEAL Robotics recommendations provide useful models for progressive
evaluation, human factors, learning curves, and long-term monitoring.

positions.stakeholder_concern: For devices intended to support clinicians, evaluating the device in isolation may not capture how errors are caught or missed in practice, including automation bias, overreliance, workload, takeover time, skill retention, team communication, and variation by user experience level.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that safety and effectiveness be evaluated for the human-AI team in addition to the device alone, with specified measures such as user recognition of erroneous, uncertain, or out-of-scope outputs, automation bias and complacency, cognitive workload, time and information available for takeover, skill retention, team task allocation, and outcomes across user experience levels.
positions.public_summary: Supports human-AI team evaluation but asks FDA to go further than device-alone assessment for clinician-support products, specifying measures including user detection of erroneous or out-of-scope outputs, automation bias, cognitive workload, takeover time, skill retention, team communication, and outcomes by user experience level.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Using the care likely to occur without the device as the comparator could allow a device to lock in substandard care where the local baseline is poor.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit counterfactual/baseline comparators but, for high-risk functions, require evidence of both comparative benefit and an absolute minimum safety floor rather than relative improvement alone.
positions.public_summary: Accepts comparators based on care likely to occur without the device, but warns this could entrench substandard local baselines. Asks FDA to require, for high-risk functions, evidence of both comparative benefit and an absolute safety floor.
positions.supporting_text:
The comparator should reflect the care likely without the device, but a device should not be permitted to
institutionalize substandard care merely because the local baseline is poor. For high-risk functions, the
evidentiary question should include both comparative benefit and an absolute safety floor.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Synthetic data generated by models trained on similar data may reproduce the same omissions and biases that an evaluation is meant to uncover, so it cannot stand in for representative clinical data in high-consequence procedural applications.
positions.requested_fda_action: Limit synthetic data to a supplemental role for rare events and controlled perturbations, and require sponsors to report real and synthetic dataset performance separately, document how each dataset was generated or selected, and demonstrate representativeness across patient, clinician, institution, equipment, and resource settings.
positions.public_summary: Accepts synthetic data as a supplement for rare events and controlled perturbations but not as a substitute for representative clinical data in high-consequence procedural uses, warning generators may replicate the biases under evaluation; asks FDA to require separate real/synthetic reporting and documented representativeness.
positions.supporting_text:
Synthetic data can supplement testing for rare events and controlled perturbations, but they should not
substitute for representative clinical data in high-consequence procedural applications. A generator
trained on similar data may reproduce the same omissions and biases that an evaluation is intended to
detect. Sponsors should separately report performance on real and synthetic datasets, describe how each
was generated or selected, and demonstrate representativeness across relevant patient, clinician,
institution, equipment, and resource settings.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Independent evaluation is seen as appropriate for high-risk devices, but only if independence is genuine—covering financial ties, conflicts of interest, technical access, and the ability to report safety findings publicly.
positions.requested_fda_action: Provide for independent third-party involvement in high-risk benchmarking, clinical confirmation, cybersecurity review, and postmarket audit, and define independence criteria addressing financial relationships, conflicts of interest, access to necessary technical information, and freedom to publish or report safety findings.
positions.public_summary: Supports independent third-party involvement, but would extend it beyond benchmarking and clinical confirmation to cybersecurity review and postmarket audit for high-risk devices. Asks FDA to define independence criteria covering financial relationships, conflicts of interest, technical access, and freedom to report safety findings.
positions.supporting_text:
Independent third parties should have a role in high-risk benchmarking, clinical confirmation,
cybersecurity review, and postmarket audit. Independence criteria should address financial relationships,
access to necessary technical information, conflicts of interest, and freedom to publish or report safety
findings.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Accepting greater premarket uncertainty in exchange for postmarket monitoring is only defensible where errors can be caught and corrected; where harm occurs before review or rescue is uncertain, monitoring cannot substitute for premarket evidence.
positions.requested_fda_action: Limit the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway to low-consequence functions with readily reviewable outputs, reversible errors, and robust detection and correction mechanisms, and exclude functions that can direct or execute invasive actions or cause harm before meaningful review.
positions.public_summary: Supports greater postmarket reliance only conditionally: for low-consequence functions with readily reviewable outputs, reversible errors, and robust detection and correction. Says it cannot substitute for premarket evidence where functions direct or execute invasive actions, harm precedes review, or rescue is uncertain.
positions.supporting_text:
Greater reliance on postmarket monitoring may be reasonable for low-consequence functions when
outputs are readily reviewable, errors are reversible, and robust detection and correction mechanisms
exist. It is not an adequate substitute for premarket evidence when a function can direct or execute an
invasive action, when harm can occur before meaningful review, or when rescue is uncertain.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Postmarket surveillance limited to adverse outcomes would miss the operational, human-interaction, and drift signals that precede harm, including out-of-scope use, overrides, near misses, automation bias, technical/interface failures, and subgroup or site-level performance differences.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand postmarket monitoring expectations to capture a specified set of data elements (version/configuration history, out-of-scope use, subgroup and site performance, overrides and abstentions, near misses and failed takeovers, data-quality and latency failures, automation bias and skill degradation, case-mix shifts), and tie reassessment cadence to risk with defined triggers such as model, workflow, hardware, dataset, or foundation-model changes, new settings or populations, unexpected performance signals, and changes in intended user or autonomy level.
positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket performance evaluation but urges broader scope than adverse outcomes: version and configuration history, out-of-scope use, subgroup and site performance, overrides, near misses, technical and interface failures, automation bias, and case-mix shifts, with risk-based cadence and defined change triggers.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter sees value in contributions of data and domain expertise from clinicians, institutions, registries, and professional societies for postmarket monitoring, but is concerned that such multi-stakeholder participation could dilute the manufacturer's responsibility.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure postmarket monitoring roles so that outside stakeholders can supply data and clinical expertise while manufacturer accountability remains clearly undiluted.
positions.public_summary: The commenter supports involving clinicians, institutions, registries, and professional societies in postmarket monitoring as contributors of data and domain expertise, on the condition that such participation does not dilute the manufacturer's accountability. No specific structural mechanism is proposed in the passage.
positions.supporting_text:
Clinicians, institutions, registries, and professional
societies can contribute data and domain expertise, but participation must not diffuse manufacturer
accountability.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Concern that supervisory AI agents used to monitor deployed GenAI devices could themselves be unvalidated, and that shared failure modes or correlated errors between supervisor and supervised models could allow degradation to go undetected.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit machine-based supervisory agents as an aid to postmarket monitoring only if the agent itself is evaluated for sensitivity, specificity, independence, failure modes, and susceptibility to correlated error.
positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents as an aid to postmarket monitoring, but conditions their use on validation of the supervisory agent itself, including sensitivity, specificity, independence, failure modes, and susceptibility to correlated error with the monitored device.
positions.supporting_text:
Machine-based supervisory agents may assist monitoring, but should not become an unvalidated AI
system policing another AI system. Their sensitivity, specificity, independence, failure modes, and
susceptibility to correlated error should be evaluated.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Changes to third-party foundation models can be initiated outside the device manufacturer's control, yet the manufacturer must remain accountable for detecting and managing them; certain change types (authority, clinical scope, refusal behavior, tool use, subgroup performance) could materially affect safety without review.
positions.requested_fda_action: Confirm manufacturer responsibility for third-party model changes and expect contractual terms (advance notice, version access, change documentation, incident sharing, ability to suspend updates) plus technical controls against unreviewed model substitution. Require PCCPs to define bounded change categories, validation methods, acceptance criteria, rollback, and user notification, and treat changes to authority, clinical scope, refusal behavior, tool use, or vulnerable-subgroup performance as presumptively requiring FDA review.
positions.public_summary: Supports change-control and PCCP approaches for third-party foundation models, but urges specifics: manufacturers stay responsible; contracts must require advance notice, version access, incident sharing, and update suspension; technical controls must block unreviewed substitution; and changes to authority, scope, refusal behavior, tool use, or subgroup performance
positions.supporting_text:
A manufacturer must remain responsible for detecting and managing changes in any third-party foundation
model on which its device depends. Contracts should require advance notice, version access, change
documentation, safety-relevant incident sharing, and the ability to suspend an update. Technical controls
should prevent unreviewed model substitution. Predetermined change control plans should define
bounded change categories, validation methods, acceptance criteria, rollback procedures, and user
notification. Changes that alter authority, clinical scope, refusal behavior, tool use, or performance in
vulnerable subgroups should presumptively require FDA review.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Voluntary Foundation Model Master Files may be useful for review efficiency only if kept current and technically meaningful, but developers may have weak incentives to disclose safety-relevant information voluntarily.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should consider expecting access to an adequate Master File or equivalent documentation whenever a sponsor materially relies on a third-party model, with content covering version history, data provenance, known limitations, cybersecurity, update practices, refusal/content-control behavior, tool-use architecture, subgroup performance, incident reporting, and contractual allocation of change-management duties.
positions.public_summary: Supports the Foundation Model Master File as a review-efficiency tool if kept current and technically meaningful, listing content such as provenance, cybersecurity, update practices, and contractual change-management duties. Suggests FDA consider expecting such documentation, rather than voluntary disclosure, where sponsors materially depend on third-party models.
positions.supporting_text:
A Foundation Model Master File could improve review efficiency if it is current, technically meaningful, and
available for regulatory reliance. Relevant content includes version history, training and evaluation data
provenance, known limitations, cybersecurity, update practices, refusal and content-control behavior,
tool-use architecture, subgroup performance, incident reporting, and the contractual allocation of change-
management duties. Because developers may have weak incentives to disclose safety-relevant
information voluntarily, CDRH should consider whether access to an adequate Master File or equivalent
documentation should be expected when a sponsor relies materially on a third-party model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic devices can take multi-step autonomous actions, use tools, and potentially delegate to sub-agents with limited opportunity for human review; nominal human supervision may not actually mitigate risk if the supervisor lacks training, attention, authority, information, or time to intervene.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require for agentic devices explicit machine-readable and human-understandable definitions of permitted actions and tools, confirmation steps for consequential actions, validated stop/abstention/fail-safe states, immutable time-synchronized audit logs, detection of unauthorized delegation or emergent sub-agents, safe behavior during loss of data/instruments/power/connectivity, realistic takeover testing, and clear labeling of permitted and prohibited capabilities; credit human supervision as risk mitigation only when the supervisor is demonstrably able to intervene effectively.
positions.public_summary: Comment accepts FDA's focus on agentic devices but seeks specific mandatory controls: defined permitted actions and tools, confirmation for consequential actions, validated stop and fail-safe states, immutable audit logs, detection of unauthorized delegation, resilience and takeover testing, and labeling.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Concern that liability for GenAI-related harm will fall by default on the clinician closest to the patient rather than being allocated according to who actually controls safety-relevant design, deployment, and model behavior.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an explicit tiered allocation of responsibility: manufacturers for design, validation, labeling, updates, monitoring and known defects; deploying institutions for local validation, credentialing, workflow integration, maintenance, staffing, data governance and safety-signal response; clinicians for reasonable use within competence; and foundation-model/infrastructure providers for duties proportionate to their control over safety-relevant behavior and changes.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts shared postmarket roles but urges FDA to specify tiered responsibility: manufacturers for design, validation, updates, monitoring; institutions for local validation, credentialing, workflow, safety-signal response; clinicians for reasonable use within competence; foundation-model providers proportionate to control—so liability does not default to bedside clinicians.
positions.supporting_text:
Responsibility should not default to the surgeon standing closest to the patient. The manufacturer should
remain responsible for design, validation, labeling, updates, monitoring, and known or knowable defects. A
deploying institution should be responsible for local validation, credentialing, workflow integration,
maintenance, staffing, data governance, and response to safety signals. Clinicians should remain
responsible for reasonable use within their competence and for acting on information that can realistically
be evaluated. Foundation-model and infrastructure providers should have duties proportionate to their
control over safety-relevant behavior and changes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Aggregated performance estimates may mask clinically meaningful failures in specific subgroups or deployment contexts, so evidence limited to average performance would be insufficient.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect sponsors to submit evidence spanning demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, varying resource levels, workflows, and user experience, and to report disaggregated results rather than only pooled performance.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA require generalizability evidence spanning demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, resource levels, workflows, and user experience, with disaggregated reporting so that aggregated performance does not conceal clinically meaningful subgroup failures.
positions.supporting_text:
CDRH should expect evidence across relevant
demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, resource levels,
workflows, and user experience. Performance aggregation should not conceal clinically meaningful
subgroup failures.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that clinicians, operating-room staff, patients, patient advocates, and representatives of rural and lower-resource settings may be consulted too late or only nominally, after design decisions are fixed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Ensure these stakeholders participate in defining intended use, acceptable tradeoffs, evaluation endpoints, transparency, and postmarket monitoring, with participation documented, compensated where appropriate, and occurring early enough to influence design rather than merely validate a finished product.
positions.public_summary: Supports stakeholder roles in oversight but asks that clinicians, OR professionals, patients, advocates, and rural or lower-resource representatives help define intended use, tradeoffs, endpoints, transparency, and postmarket monitoring, with documented, compensated involvement early enough to shape design.
positions.supporting_text:
Practicing clinicians, operating-room professionals, patients, patient advocates, and representatives of
rural and lower-resource settings should participate in defining intended use, acceptable tradeoffs,
evaluation endpoints, transparency, and postmarket monitoring. Their participation should be
documented, compensated where appropriate, and occur early enough to affect design rather than merely
validate a completed product.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that responsibility for safety-relevant model behavior and changes may not align with who actually controls those elements, since foundation model and infrastructure providers can initiate changes affecting device safety.
positions.requested_fda_action: Allocate obligations to foundation-model and infrastructure providers in proportion to their control over safety-relevant behavior and changes, rather than relying solely on device manufacturer accountability or voluntary disclosure.
positions.public_summary: The commenter argues that regulatory duties should be allocated to foundation-model and infrastructure providers in proportion to their control over safety-relevant behavior and model changes, rather than resting solely with device manufacturers or depending on voluntary disclosure by upstream developers.
positions.supporting_text: Foundation-model and infrastructure providers should have duties proportionate to their control over safety-relevant behavior and changes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Commercial contracts between foundation model developers and device manufacturers can obscure who actually controls the model and shift risk to downstream users; FDA cannot fix adjacent legal issues such as privacy, IP, reimbursement, or malpractice, but opacity about control should not persist.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require device documentation and labeling that disclose how control over the model and its changes is distributed among parties, rather than permitting contractual arrangements to leave that distribution undisclosed.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts that FDA cannot resolve privacy, employment, intellectual property, reimbursement, or malpractice questions, but urges FDA to require device documentation and labeling disclosing how control is distributed among parties, so contractual opacity does not shift risk downstream.
positions.supporting_text: FDA cannot resolve every question of privacy, employment, intellectual property, reimbursement, or malpractice. It can, however, require device documentation and labeling that make the distribution of control visible rather than allowing contractual opacity to shift risk downstream.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Concern that GenAI-enabled surgical systems developed and validated mainly in well-resourced academic hospitals on narrow patient, device, procedure, and care-team populations will not deliver the promised expansion of access to expertise, and that aggregate performance figures can mask clinically meaningful subgroup failures.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should expect validation evidence spanning relevant demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, varying resource levels, workflows, and user experience levels, and should require subgroup-level performance reporting rather than accepting aggregated results.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the evidence framework but urges FDA to require validation across demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, resource levels, workflows, and user experience, with subgroup-level reporting so aggregated performance does not conceal clinically meaningful failures.
positions.supporting_text: The promise of GenAI-enabled surgery includes expanding access to expertise. That promise will not be realized if systems are developed and validated primarily in wealthy academic hospitals, on a narrow range of patients, devices, procedures, and clinical teams. CDRH should expect evidence across relevant demographic groups, anatomy and disease severity, community and rural settings, resource levels, workflows, and user experience. Performance aggregation should not conceal clinically meaningful subgroup failures.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter endorses a risk-proportionate regulatory posture but emphasizes that firm safeguards are needed at the threshold where software moves from providing information to directing or performing physical action.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a framework that scales oversight to risk while imposing firm, non-negotiable safeguards for functions that direct user action or execute physical actions.
positions.public_summary: Endorses a risk-proportionate approach in general, but asks that firm safeguards apply specifically where software begins to direct user action or perform physical action. The brief statement does not detail how such thresholds should be defined or implemented.
positions.supporting_text: The strongest framework will combine risk-proportionate innovation with firm safeguards at the points where software begins to direct or perform physical action.

positions.stakeholder_concern: For procedural and surgical applications, the commenter is concerned that evaluating the device in isolation misses how the deployed human-AI system actually performs, and that risk assessment omits factors such as the authority granted to the system, irreversibility of actions, time to harm, and opportunity for rescue.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should evaluate the deployed human-AI system rather than the device alone, explicitly incorporate authority, irreversibility, time to harm, and rescue into risk assessment, require realistic clinical confirmation, preserve manufacturer accountability, and require versioned, representative, auditable evidence across the product life cycle.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts FDA's direction but asks that, for procedural and surgical applications, evaluation address the deployed human-AI system and explicitly account for authority, irreversibility, time to harm, and rescue, with realistic clinical confirmation, preserved manufacturer accountability, and versioned, auditable lifecycle evidence.
positions.supporting_text: For procedural and surgical applications, CDRH should evaluate the deployed human-AI system; explicitly account for authority, irreversibility, time to harm, and rescue; require realistic clinical confirmation; preserve manufacturer accountability; and demand versioned, representative, and auditable evidence throughout the product life cycle.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's stated concern is that traditional software validation approaches are insufficient for open-ended GenAI systems, and views the paper's risk-based plus competency-based framework as an appropriate response aligned with a Total Product Lifecycle approach.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific change is requested; the commenter endorses the discussion paper's overall direction and its combined risk-based and competency-based framework.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses the discussion paper overall, describing it as consistent with a Total Product Lifecycle approach and correctly recognizing that traditional software validation is insufficient for open-ended generative AI. Supports the combined risk-based and competency-based framework without requesting specific changes.
positions.supporting_text: Overall, I think this is one of the most thoughtful FDA discussion papers published to date on GenAI regulation and it aligns well with a Total Product Lifecycle (TPLC) approach. It appropriately recognizes that traditional software validation approaches are insufficient for open-ended GenAI systems and introduces a risk-based + competency-based framework.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states the paper only briefly references multiple-function products and does not adequately address platforms combining medical and non-medical GenAI functions, shared foundation models serving both regulated and non-regulated functions, potential contamination or influence between their outputs, segregation requirements, or architecture recommendations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Provide explicit multiple function device product examples, boundary control expectations, and evidence requirements demonstrating independence between regulated and non-regulated functions.
positions.public_summary: Comment finds FDA's treatment of multiple-function products insufficient for platforms mixing medical and non-medical GenAI functions on shared foundation models. Asks FDA to add explicit examples, boundary control expectations, segregation/architecture guidance, and evidence demonstrating independence between regulated and non-regulated functions.
positions.supporting_text:
1. Missing Explicit Multiple Function Device Product (MFDP) Considerations
Although FDA briefly references multiple-function products, the discussion does not
sufficiently address:
•Medical + non-medical GenAI functions in the same platform
•Shared foundation models servicing both regulated and non-regulated functions
•Contamination or influence between regulated and non-regulated outputs
•Segregation requirements
•Architecture Recommendations inclusion Medical + non-medical GenAI functions
This is particularly important for platforms like where some functions could be medical-
device functions while others remain non-device administrative functions.
Recommendation
FDA should provide:
•Explicit MFDP examples
•Boundary control expectations
•Evidence requirements demonstrating independence between regulated and non-
regulated functions

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that the discussion paper mentions guardrails and prompt injection but does not sufficiently integrate cybersecurity into the competency framework, specifically omitting model poisoning, retrieval database attacks, prompt injection effects on clinical outputs, adversarial attacks, agentic tool abuse, and LLM supply chain security.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add a dedicated cybersecurity competency area to the benchmarking structure, or explicitly align the framework with FDA cybersecurity guidance, SBOM expectations, IEC 81001-5-1, and the NIST AI RMF.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the benchmarking competency structure but finds cybersecurity underrepresented, citing gaps on model poisoning, retrieval database attacks, prompt injection effects on clinical outputs, adversarial attacks, agentic tool abuse, and LLM supply chain security. Requests a dedicated cybersecurity competency area or explicit alignment with existing standards.
positions.supporting_text:
2. Cybersecurity is Underrepresented
The paper references guardrails and prompt injection but cybersecurity requirements are not
sufficiently integrated into the framework.
Particularly absent:
•Model poisoning
•Retrieval database attacks
•Prompt injection impact on clinical outputs
•Adversarial attacks
•Agentic tool abuse
•LLM supply chain security
Recommendation
Add a dedicated cybersecurity competency area or explicitly align with:
•FDA Cybersecurity Guidance
•SBOM expectations
•IEC 81001-5-1
•NIST AI RMF

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that the paper mentions communication quality and automation bias but does not explicitly link them to traditional human factors engineering requirements, leaving usability considerations insufficiently prominent in the evaluation framework.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make human factors validation a standalone evaluation pillar, and evaluate user trust calibration, overreliance, alert fatigue, automation bias, and explainability effectiveness for GenAI systems.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the evaluation framework's direction but argues human factors are underemphasized and not tied to traditional human factors engineering requirements. Recommends making human factors validation a standalone evaluation pillar covering trust calibration, overreliance, alert fatigue, automation bias, and explainability effectiveness.
positions.supporting_text:
3. Human Factors / Usability Not Prominent Enough
The paper discusses communication quality and automation bias. However, it does not
explicitly connect them to traditional human factors engineering requirements.
For GenAI systems FDA should evaluate:
•User trust calibration
•Overreliance
•Alert fatigue
•Automation bias
•Explainability effectiveness
Recommendation
Human factors validation should become a standalone evaluation pillar.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that most healthcare GenAI systems will not rely on foundation models alone but on retrieval-augmented generation, clinical knowledge repositories, guideline retrieval systems, and enterprise databases, and that the discussion paper insufficiently addresses retrieval quality, source governance, knowledge base drift, and citation accuracy.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define validation expectations separately for each architectural layer: the foundation model, the retrieval layer, the orchestrator layer, and the final clinical output.
positions.public_summary: Commenter argues the paper focuses too narrowly on foundation models and overlooks retrieval-augmented architectures, including retrieval quality, source governance, knowledge base drift, and citation accuracy. Asks FDA to set separate validation expectations for the foundation model, retrieval layer, orchestrator layer, and final clinical output.
positions.supporting_text:
4. Lack of Clear Treatment for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Most healthcare GenAI systems will not rely solely on foundation models.
Instead, they will rely upon:
•RAG architectures
•Clinical knowledge repositories
•Guideline retrieval systems
•Enterprise databases
The discussion focuses heavily on foundation models but insufficiently addresses:
•Retrieval quality
•Source governance
•Knowledge base drift
•Citation accuracy
Recommendation
FDA should define validation expectations separately for:
•Foundation model
•Retrieval layer
•Orchestrator layer
•Final clinical output

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds that the discussion paper raises questions about statistical rigor but offers no practical path forward on sample size determination, confidence intervals, performance thresholds, or statistical significance for open-ended outputs.
positions.requested_fda_action: Provide concrete statistical guidance, including consideration of non-inferiority and Bayesian approaches, risk-adjusted performance thresholds, and measures of human-AI team effectiveness.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts FDA's framing but says the paper poses statistical questions without answers, lacking practical methods for sample size, confidence intervals, thresholds, and significance for open-ended outputs. Recommends FDA consider non-inferiority and Bayesian approaches, risk-adjusted thresholds, and human-AI team effectiveness measures.
positions.supporting_text:
5. Statistics and Acceptance Criteria Remain Vague

One major weakness is that the document does not provide practical approaches for:
•Sample size determination
•Confidence intervals
•Performance thresholds
•Statistical significance for open-ended outputs
FDA raises the question but does not suggest a path forward.
Recommendation
Consider:
•Non-inferiority approaches
•Bayesian approaches
•Risk-adjusted performance thresholds
•Human-AI team effectiveness measures

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the discussion paper understates the risk of agentic systems, which can execute actions, trigger workflows, modify records, and interact with connected systems, making single-step validation insufficient.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require action approval checkpoints, tool-use verification, audit trails, rollback capabilities, and runtime supervision before high-risk autonomous deployment.
positions.public_summary: Comment accepts FDA's attention to agentic AI but argues the paper understates its risk, since such systems execute actions, alter records, and interact with connected systems. Recommends requiring approval checkpoints, tool-use verification, audit trails, rollback, and runtime supervision before high-risk autonomous deployment.
positions.supporting_text:
6. Agentic AI Requires Stronger Controls
Agentic AI is discussed but I think the risk is greater than portrayed.
Agentic systems can:
•Execute actions
•Trigger workflows
•Modify records
•Interact with connected systems
Single-step validation is insufficient.
Recommendation
Require:
•Action approval checkpoints
•Tool-use verification
•Audit trails
•Rollback capabilities
•Runtime supervision
before high-risk autonomous deployment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Third-party foundation model providers can change models without the device sponsor's involvement, causing overnight behavioral change, performance drift, and altered safety profiles, so FDA-cleared evidence may no longer reflect deployed device behavior. The commenter characterizes this as the biggest practical regulatory challenge.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should strongly consider requiring locked model versions, mandatory model version traceability, supplier quality agreements, triggered revalidation criteria, and PCCP provisions specific to foundation-model updates.
positions.public_summary: Agrees with FDA that third-party foundation model updates are a major challenge, calling it the biggest practical regulatory problem. Asks FDA to go further by considering locked model versions, version traceability, supplier quality agreements, triggered revalidation criteria, and foundation-model-specific PCCP provisions.
positions.supporting_text:
7. Third-Party Foundation Model Change Management
This is probably the biggest practical regulatory challenge.

The paper recognises that foundation model providers may change their models without
sponsors initiating updates.
For medical device manufacturers, this creates a major regulatory problem because:
•Behaviour may change overnight
•Performance may drift
•Safety profiles may change
•FDA-cleared evidence may no longer reflect deployed behaviour
Recommendation
FDA should strongly consider:
•Locked model versions
•Mandatory model version traceability
•Supplier quality agreements
•Triggered revalidation criteria
•PCCP-specific provisions for foundation-model updates

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter, a psychiatry resident, states the two-axis framework does not appropriately capture the risk of GenAI-enabled software functions, and points to prior instances and court cases involving generative AI providing false information as evidence that risk from medical advice must be defined objectively.
positions.requested_fda_action: Develop clear and objective methods for assessing the risk of any medical advice generated by GenAI-enabled functions, rather than relying on the proposed two-axis framework as described.
positions.public_summary: A resident physician in psychiatry states the proposed two-axis framework does not adequately capture GenAI software risk, citing past cases of generative AI providing false information, and calls for clear, objective methods for assessing the risk of medical advice.
positions.supporting_text:
It does not appropriately capture the risk related to the Gen-AI enabled software
function.As a resident physician in the psychiatry space, it is imperative that we
are able to define clear and objective methods for the risk of the anything medical
advice made. Clearly we have always had several cases of issues and court
cases where the generativeAI is indicated and gave false information.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that action-directing outputs conveying any medical knowledge or guidance may be relied upon without users understanding the continued need for human mental health professionals, including therapists, counselors, and hotline specialists, not only physicians.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that action-directing GenAI functions involving any medical knowledge or guidance carry a clear message to users, addressed to patients and to non-physician mental health providers, emphasizing continued reliance on human professionals rather than an AI model.
