positions.public_summary: Commenter urges that action-directing outputs involving any medical knowledge or guidance carry clear messaging, directed to patients and to non-physician providers such as therapists, counselors, and hotline staff, stressing continued reliance on human mental health professionals rather than AI models.
positions.supporting_text:
For a
action-directing function a clear message involving ANY kind of medical
knowledge or guidance needs to be put and not just for physicians, but for
therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, etc. Patient or people need to
understand and realize that it is imperative and important to continue to use US
in the mental health field versus an AI model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that AI, despite seeming effective, creates more work than it saves and frustrates users much like automated phone systems, and says it is unclear how such tools would be implemented or audited in the mental health space; energy use is also cited as a reason for objection.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter asks that these tools not be implemented, asserting that patients across ages, sizes, and races also do not want them.
positions.public_summary: An individual commenter opposes deployment of these tools generally, saying AI creates more work than it saves, frustrates users like automated phone systems, has unclear implementation and audit pathways in mental health care, and raises energy concerns. No specific FDA question is substantively addressed.
positions.supporting_text:
Truthfully at the end of the day, with the idea of AI seemed really effective
and helpful, it is more work than anything. The same way that automated phone system
drive everyone crazy, so does AI. In terms of audits, mental health space, I have no
idea how this would be implemented. Surely from the energy standpoint, I DO NOT
want this implemented and neither do patients of all age size and race.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter asserts that generative AI cannot protect privacy because information transmitted over the internet is not secure, and that no currently available safeguard can mitigate the resulting risks.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require clear warnings that AI is being used and that privacy is not protected, and retain humans in the process rather than relying on technical safeguards to mitigate risk.
positions.public_summary: Commenter argues no current safeguard can mitigate GenAI privacy risks because internet-transmitted information is not protected. Urges explicit disclosure that AI is in use and that privacy is not assured, and maintains that retaining humans is the only effective mitigation.
positions.supporting_text:
Again a clear warning that AI does not protect
privacy because nothing on the internet is protected, and clear implication that AI is
being used. No safeguard currently can migrate risk and the only way to fix these risks
would to still have humans in place

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter rejects the idea that trade-offs between error directions can be acceptable depending on clinical context, arguing that AI currently carries more risk and that manufacturer disclaimers do not shield anyone involved in deploying AI from responsibility, including government.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not accept context-dependent trade-offs in evaluating GenAI errors; hold all participants in AI use accountable rather than allowing responsibility to be shifted through disclaimers, consistent with a 'do no harm' standard.
positions.public_summary: A commenter, writing as a physician, rejects FDA's premise that acceptable trade-offs between under- and over-escalation vary by clinical context. Arguing AI currently carries more risk, the commenter states manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility from any party involved in AI use.
positions.supporting_text:
Manufactures can put their disclaimer, but in the end, anyone that
participates in the use of AI in this space bares reasonability. The government system
itself, no one is immune to the consequences that will come with it. There are no
acceptable trade-offs by a clinical context. As a physician the oath comes into play: do
no harm, and since right now AI carries more risk and more reasonability

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states the two-axis risk framework is unnecessary because HIPAA and the Security Rule already govern privacy and security obligations for healthcare providers, and questions how patient data will be kept from being breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter asks FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians to explain and ensure how patient data will be protected against breach, theft, or sale, rather than adopting the proposed two-axis risk framework.
positions.public_summary: This commenter rejects the proposed two-axis risk framework as unnecessary, asserting that HIPAA and the Security Rule already impose uniform privacy and security duties, and instead asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians will prevent patient data breach, theft, or sale.
positions.supporting_text:
The two-axis framework is not even needed. Currently HIPPA laws and the
Security Rule of Healthcare govern that all healthcare providers within the space must
follow the same privacy and security that all would want--- how will the FDA,
government, manufactures, and physicians and other healthcare colleagues ensure that
patient data will be protected and not breached or stolen or sold?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the proposed benchmarking structure favorably but does not consider it sufficient on its own, arguing that a clinical trial or study is also needed, and raises unresolved questions about informed consent and safeguarding patient confidentiality while the device delivers accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require clinical trial or study evidence in addition to benchmarking, and address how informed consent and patient confidentiality would be handled in the evaluation framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter finds the proposed benchmarking structure acceptable but insufficient alone, stating a clinical trial or study would also be needed. Raises unaddressed questions about informed consent and how patient confidentiality would be maintained while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.supporting_text:
The benchmarking structure is nice, but a clinical trial or study would need to
be done and the idea of informed consent would have to be discussed. In essence as
well how does that maintain that patient confidentiality will be paramount while
delivering accurate and clinically appropriate data/info?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states they cannot answer how benchmark performance would predict real-world behavior because the benchmarking concept is underdeveloped, and notes that behavioral health involves greater nuance and more serious consequences when outputs are wrong. They also question who bears responsibility for patient safety and informed consent under federal law.
positions.requested_fda_action: Further develop and clearly specify the benchmarking approach and validate it through a pilot study, including a separate study addressing behavioral health, and clarify who is accountable for patient safety and informed consent.
positions.public_summary: Commenter cannot answer FDA's benchmark validity question, saying the benchmarking concept needs further development and should be tested through a pilot study, with a separate study for behavioral health given its nuance and consequences. Also asks who bears responsibility for patient safety and informed consent.
positions.supporting_text:
No idea- again this benchmark really needs more fleshing out and there
would need to be a pilot study with the idea clearly laid out to be done. Also a
behavioral health study- our field is much more nuance and have more of a greater idea
and consequence if something were to go wrong. Again in terms of patient safety and
informed consent- who is responsible? These are federal laws and with them come
federal consequences.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to allowing clinical confirmation without a prospective clinical study, characterizing less rigorous alternatives as cutting corners, and also raises a concern about public transparency.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial study for clinical confirmation of GenAI-enabled devices and make the results clear and publicly available.
positions.public_summary: Opposes FDA's suggestion that clinical confirmation might not always require a prospective clinical study, describing such flexibility as cutting corners. Calls for clinical trial studies and for results to be made clear to everyone, including the public.
positions.supporting_text:
No, don’t cut corners- do a clinical trial study and make it clear to everyone
including the public. THAT is not ok.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter doubts that a panel of qualified clinicians can realistically serve as the performance comparator, because in their experience few physicians would agree to participate out of fear of professional backlash, society scrutiny, and risk to their personal safety and medical license.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not offer an alternative, but suggests any clinician-panel comparator would require willing qualified clinicians and might have to be arranged through a hospital; they signal FDA should reconsider reliance on clinician panels given recruitment and liability barriers.
positions.public_summary: Commenter questions the feasibility of using clinician panels as the performance comparator for open-ended outputs, saying few physicians would agree to participate due to fear of professional backlash and risk to their licenses, though no alternative comparator is proposed.
positions.supporting_text:
I don’t believe this would make sense either, and again don’t have a answer
here. There would need to be qualified clinicians that would have to agree – maybe it
could be done with the hospital- but despite many physicians using AI I don’t know
many that would agree to actually participating in it for fear of the backlash, the society
and again the safety of themselves and their only license.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the question cannot be meaningfully answered without a comparative device and a pilot study, and rejects each of FDA's suggested alternative comparators: unaided clinical judgment would make the study pointless, delayed specialist review would only delay care, and while 'no intervention' may be an appropriate comparator, the commenter questions who determines that it is justified when the output comes from a machine rather than a person.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not rely on the alternative comparators described (unaided clinical judgment or delayed specialist review); establish comparative device data and pilot studies as the basis for comparison, and clarify who validates a 'no intervention' comparator when the determination originates from a machine rather than a clinician.
positions.public_summary: Commenter says the comparator question is not answerable without a comparative device and pilot study. Rejects unaided clinical judgment (would negate the study's purpose) and delayed specialist review (delays care). Accepts 'no intervention' as possible, but questions who validates machine-originated determinations.
positions.supporting_text:
Not really answerable at this time, we would need a comparative device and
a pilot study to really have something to compare it too.
No unaided clinical judgement, like why bother doing the study at all. Delayed specialist
review would only delay care, which is dumb. No intervention must be an appropriate
answer but since it is due by a robot and not a person- who is say that it is justified?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the competency-based approach appealing but is concerned that the discussion paper and its questions are written in technical language and appear to have been generated with AI, limiting meaningful public input.
positions.requested_fda_action: Before advancing the competency-based approach, FDA should solicit input from a wider range of groups and from the general public, including through a version of the material written in more accessible, comparable terms.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports the competency-based approach in principle but asks FDA to first broaden consultation, seeking input from multiple groups and the general public through materials written in more accessible language rather than the paper's current technical framing.
positions.supporting_text:
I like the competency based approach but first yall need to flesh out the
public’s opinion on this in addition to generative AI- which it seems wrote these
responses. Reaching out to several different groups with these questions as well
involving the public’s opinion on this with a research paper that is written in more similar
terms would be ideal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that patients and other non-physician users may rely on generative AI outputs conveying medical knowledge or guidance in place of human mental health professionals.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that action-directing functions delivering any medical knowledge or guidance carry a clear message—directed not only to physicians but to therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, and patients—that human professionals should continue to be used in the mental health field rather than an AI model.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges that any action-directing generative AI function conveying medical knowledge or guidance include clear messaging—for patients and for therapists, counselors, and hotline staff—emphasizing continued reliance on human mental health professionals rather than an AI model.
positions.supporting_text: Response: For a action-directing function a clear message involving ANY kind of medical knowledge or guidance needs to be put and not just for physicians, but for therapists, counselors, hotline specialists, etc. Patient or people need to understand and realize that it is imperative and important to continue to use US in the mental health field versus an AI model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that AI, despite seeming effective, creates more work and is frustrating in the way automated phone systems are, and says they do not know how it would be implemented for audits in the mental health space. They also object on energy grounds and assert that patients do not want it either.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not request a specific regulatory action but states they do not want this implemented.
positions.public_summary: An individual commenter opposes implementation, saying AI creates more work and frustration comparable to automated phone systems, questions how it would be applied to audits in mental health, and objects on energy grounds. No specific FDA action is requested.
positions.supporting_text: Response: Truthfully at the end of the day, with the idea of AI seemed really effective and helpful, it is more work than anything. The same way that automated phone system drive everyone crazy, so does AI. In terms of audits, mental health space, I have no idea how this would be implemented. Surely from the energy standpoint, I DO NOT want this implemented and neither do patients of all age size and race.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter rejects the premise that trade-offs between under- and over-escalation can be acceptable depending on clinical context, invoking the physician obligation to do no harm and asserting that AI currently carries more risk. The commenter also states that manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility, and that everyone participating in AI use, including government, bears responsibility and consequences.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not treat error trade-offs as acceptable based on clinical context, and ensure responsibility is not shifted through manufacturer disclaimers but shared by all parties involved in deploying AI.
positions.public_summary: Commenter rejects FDA's premise that escalation error trade-offs can be acceptable and context-dependent, citing the physician duty to do no harm and asserting AI currently carries greater risk. Argues manufacturer disclaimers do not remove responsibility, which is shared by all participants.
positions.supporting_text: Response: Manufactures can put their disclaimer, but in the end, anyone that participates in the use of AI in this space bares reasonability. The government system itself, no one is immune to the consequences that will come with it. There are no  acceptable trade-offs by a clinical context. As a physician the oath comes into play: do no harm, and since right now AI carries more risk and more reasonability

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the competency-based approach appealing in principle but questions how patient safety and patient data would be protected while benchmarking and clinical confirmation are carried out, and who bears responsibility if data is leaked.
positions.requested_fda_action: Address how patient data protection and safety would be maintained under a competency-based evaluation approach, and clarify who is accountable in the event of a data breach.
positions.public_summary: Commenter views the competency-based approach as appealing in principle but questions how patient safety and patient data would be safeguarded during benchmarking and clinical confirmation, and asks FDA to clarify who is responsible if data is leaked.
positions.supporting_text: Response: The approach seems ideal in hindsight, but how will one maintain patient safety and data during this? Who is not to say that the data gets leaked anyway, and in that case who is responsible?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter asserts the two-axis risk framework is unnecessary because HIPAA and the Healthcare Security Rule already impose uniform privacy and security obligations on providers, and instead questions how patient data will be kept from being breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.requested_fda_action: Set aside the proposed two-axis risk framework and instead address how FDA, government, manufacturers, physicians, and other healthcare personnel will collectively ensure patient data is protected from breach, theft, or sale.
positions.public_summary: Commenter rejects the two-axis risk framework as unnecessary, arguing existing HIPAA and Security Rule obligations already apply, and instead asks how FDA, government, manufacturers, and clinicians will jointly ensure patient data is not breached, stolen, or sold.
positions.supporting_text: Response: The two-axis framework is not even needed. Currently HIPPA laws and the Security Rule of Healthcare govern that all healthcare providers within the space must follow the same privacy and security that all would want--- how will the FDA, government, manufactures, and physicians and other healthcare colleagues ensure that patient data will be protected and not breached or stolen or sold?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the proposed benchmarking structure as acceptable but not sufficient on its own, and raises unaddressed questions about informed consent and safeguarding patient confidentiality while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial or study in addition to benchmarking, and address informed consent and patient confidentiality protections as part of the evaluation framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter finds the benchmarking structure acceptable but says it alone is insufficient, urging that a clinical trial or study also be conducted. Raises unresolved questions about informed consent and maintaining patient confidentiality while delivering accurate, clinically appropriate information.
positions.supporting_text: Response: The benchmarking structure is nice, but a clinical trial or study would need to be done and the idea of informed consent would have to be discussed. In essence as well how does that maintain that patient confidentiality will be paramount while delivering accurate and clinically appropriate data/info?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to allowing clinical confirmation without a prospective clinical study, characterizing flexible confirmation approaches as cutting corners, and also expresses concern about transparency to the public.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require a clinical trial study for clinical confirmation and make the process and results clear to everyone, including the public.
positions.public_summary: The commenter opposes FDA's suggestion that clinical confirmation of GenAI-enabled devices may not always require a prospective clinical study, stating that a clinical trial should be conducted and that the process and findings should be made clear to the public.
positions.supporting_text: Response: No, don’t cut corners- do a clinical trial study and make it clear to everyone including the public. THAT is not ok.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter doubts that using a panel of qualified clinicians as the performance comparator is workable, stating that few physicians they know would agree to participate out of fear of backlash, professional society reaction, and risk to their personal safety and medical license.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter offers no alternative approach, but implies FDA should not rely on clinician-panel comparators without addressing clinician willingness to participate and the professional and licensure exposure such participation may create; involvement through hospitals is raised only as a possibility.
positions.public_summary: Commenter doubts that a clinician panel can serve as a workable performance comparator, saying few physicians would agree to participate given fear of backlash, professional society reaction, and risk to their license. Suggests hospital involvement as a possibility but offers no alternative.
positions.supporting_text: Response: I don’t believe this would make sense either, and again don’t have a answer here. There would need to be qualified clinicians that would have to agree – maybe it could be done with the hospital- but despite many physicians using AI I don’t know many that would agree to actually participating in it for fear of the backlash, the society and again the safety of themselves and their only license.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter believes the comparator question cannot be meaningfully answered without a comparative device and pilot data, and rejects each of the alternative comparators FDA describes: unaided clinical judgment would defeat the purpose of the study, delayed specialist review would only delay care, and while 'no intervention' may be appropriate, the commenter questions who determines it is justified when the output comes from a machine rather than a person.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter does not endorse the alternative comparators suggested in Q15 and implies that comparator selection should await evidence from a comparative device and pilot study; the commenter also asks who would justify a 'no intervention' comparator when the determination is machine-generated.
positions.public_summary: Commenter says the comparator question is not answerable without a comparative device and pilot study, and rejects FDA's suggested alternatives: unaided clinical judgment would negate the study, delayed specialist review would delay care, and 'no intervention' raises questions about who justifies a machine-generated determination.
positions.supporting_text:
Response: Not really answerable at this time, we would need a comparative device and a pilot study to really have something to compare it too.
No unaided clinical judgement, like why bother doing the study at all. Delayed specialist review would only delay care, which is dumb. No intervention must be an appropriate answer but since it is due by a robot and not a person- who is say that it is justified?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that broad independent third-party involvement (research boards, NIH, mental health organizations such as NAMI and SAMHSA, and the AMA) is necessary because accurate results, information, or support would not otherwise be obtained, while simultaneously doubting that such involvement of these organizations would be possible.
positions.requested_fda_action: Involve a wide range of independent bodies — research review boards, NIH, mental health organizations, and professional associations — in third-party assessment, and treat privacy and data protection as the key limiting design consideration.
positions.public_summary: Commenter endorses involving many independent bodies (research boards, NIH, NAMI, SAMHSA, AMA) in third-party assessment, arguing accurate results otherwise are unobtainable, but also doubts such involvement would be feasible, and identifies privacy and data protection as the limiting design consideration.
positions.supporting_text: Response: An independent third-party would be create. All of the research boards, the national institute of health, the mental health organizations like NAMI and SAMHSA, AMA everyone should be involved. You wouldn’t get accurate results or information or even support otherwise. I don’t think that third-party involvements of these above organizations would be possible. Limiting design features is again privacy and data protection.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter likes the competency-based approach in principle but is concerned that the discussion paper and its questions appear to have been drafted with generative AI and are not accessible to non-specialist audiences, and that public input has not been adequately gathered.
positions.requested_fda_action: Solicit broader input by reaching out to multiple different groups and the general public, including through a version of the paper written in plainer, more comparable terms, before advancing the competency-based approach.
positions.public_summary: Commenter expresses general support for the competency-based approach but asks FDA to first gather broader public and multi-group input, including through materials written in plainer language, noting concern that the discussion paper's questions appear to be generative AI-drafted.
positions.supporting_text: Response; I like the competency based approach but first yall need to flesh out the public’s opinion on this in addition to generative AI- which it seems wrote these responses. Reaching out to several different groups with these questions as well involving the public’s opinion on this with a research paper that is written in more similar terms would be ideal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter judges the framework conceptually strong (rated 7.5/10) but evidentiarily immature (~5/10), warning that competency benchmarking may measure test-taking ability rather than actual clinical benefit.
positions.requested_fda_action: Implicitly, that FDA ground the competency-based approach in empirical validation demonstrating that benchmark performance predicts real-world clinical benefit, rather than relying on conceptually appealing but unvalidated evaluation constructs.
positions.public_summary: Commenter rates the paper highly as a conceptual framework but low on evidentiary maturity, noting proposed solutions are appealing rather than empirically validated, and cautioning that competency benchmarking may predict test performance more than real clinical benefit.
positions.supporting_text:
My rating: 7.5/10 as a conceptual regulatory framework, but ~5/10 for evidentiary maturity.
The paper identifies the right problems unusually well. Its weakness is that many of the proposed solutions are still conceptually appealing rather than empirically validated. The "competency" testing risks becoming the medical-device equivalent of an examination that predicts test-taking performance better than actual clinical benefit.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the two-axis structure (device activity/autonomy versus consequence of an incorrect output) as clinically intuitive, distinguishing low-consequence informational advice from autonomous initiation of high-consequence interventions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the two-axis risk framework as the basis for risk assessment rather than regulating software simply because it incorporates a large language model.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's two-axis risk framework as clinically intuitive, noting it meaningfully separates low-consequence informational outputs from autonomous systems initiating high-consequence interventions, and prefers this over regulating software merely because it contains a large language model.
positions.supporting_text: 2. The two-axis risk model is clinically intuitive. The framework on page 6 places device activity/autonomy on one axis and consequences of an incorrect output on the other. Thus, an informational system giving low-consequence advice is fundamentally different from an autonomous system initiating a high-consequence intervention. That is much more sensible than regulating something simply because it contains an LLM.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the device activity × consequence framework useful but incomplete, noting that plausible-sounding errors that users cannot readily detect or verify pose different risk than obvious errors, and that small per-interaction risks aggregate into population-level harm at scale.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework beyond two axes to include at least detectability of error (including traceability/verifiability of outputs) and frequency of exposure across large volumes of encounters.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the two-axis risk framework as useful but considers it insufficient to determine clinical risk. Recommends adding at least detectability of error—whether a plausible but incorrect output can be independently verified—and frequency of exposure, since small per-interaction risks aggregate across millions of encounters.
positions.supporting_text:
1. The two-axis risk framework probably has too few dimensions
Concern severity: 8/10.
Autonomy × consequence is useful, but it does not completely determine clinical risk. FDA itself essentially acknowledges this by asking whether reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, and traceability should be incorporated.
I would add at least detectability of error as a major dimension.
An AI error that is immediately obvious to a pediatrician is quite different from a plausible but incorrect statement that appears authoritative and cannot readily be independently verified.
Similarly, frequency of exposure matters: a tiny per-interaction risk multiplied across millions of encounters can become an important population-level harm.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter considers the two-axis model (device activity × consequence of an incorrect output) too narrow to capture clinical risk, which they see as also driven by autonomy, error detectability, exposure, and irreversibility.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework into a multifactor formulation—consequence × autonomy × error detectability × exposure × irreversibility—modified by human oversight, time-to-intervention, population vulnerability, and recoverability.
positions.public_summary: Accepts a risk-based framework but finds FDA's two axes insufficient. Proposes expanding risk to consequence, autonomy, error detectability, exposure, and irreversibility, modified by human oversight, time-to-intervention, population vulnerability, and recoverability.
positions.supporting_text:
I would evolve the two-dimensional model into something closer to:
Clinical risk ≈ consequence × autonomy × error detectability × exposure × irreversibility,
modified by human oversight, time-to-intervention, population vulnerability, and
recoverability.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Outputs framed as merely informational can in practice direct patient or clinician behavior, and boilerplate disclaimers such as 'talk to your doctor' do not necessarily neutralize otherwise directive advice.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain and apply the paper's substance-and-context approach to assessing directiveness—treating specificity and personalization (e.g., a specific dose change) as directive regardless of hedging language or absence of words like 'recommend.'
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's view that seemingly informational generative AI outputs can direct behavior, agreeing that directiveness should be judged by substance and context—such as specificity and personalization—rather than particular phrasing, and that disclaimers do not necessarily neutralize directive advice.
positions.supporting_text: 3. FDA recognizes that apparently "informational" AI can actually direct behavior. This is particularly important. The paper distinguishes statements ranging from general information through personalized suggestions to explicit instructions—for example, progressing from information about lisinopril dosing to "increase the lisinopril from 10 mg to 20 mg daily." It appropriately argues that directiveness depends on substance and context, rather than magic words such as "recommend." Disclaimers such as "talk to your doctor" do not necessarily neutralize otherwise directive advice.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A conversational system can begin with harmless educational content and gradually migrate toward diagnosis or treatment recommendations over the course of an exchange; evaluating isolated prompts would fail to detect this drift.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the approach of treating multi-turn behavior as the unit of risk and evaluating realistic conversational trajectories rather than isolated prompts.
positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA's proposal to treat multi-turn behavior as a unit of risk, noting that conversations can drift from education toward diagnostic or treatment recommendations and that evaluating isolated prompts would miss this. Supports assessing realistic conversational trajectories.
positions.supporting_text: 4. Multi-turn behavior is treated as a unit of risk. This is excellent. A system can begin with harmless education and gradually migrate toward diagnosis or treatment recommendations. Evaluating isolated prompts would miss that phenomenon. FDA explicitly proposes evaluating realistic conversational trajectories.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that the proposed competency framework goes well beyond simple accuracy testing, spanning safety-critical recognition/escalation, scope adherence, calibration/uncertainty, clinical knowledge, information gathering/reasoning, quantitative performance, communication, robustness/reproducibility, subgroup performance, and agentic competencies.
positions.requested_fda_action: No specific change is requested in this passage; the commenter endorses the breadth of the proposed benchmarking domains as a sophisticated conception of clinical AI performance.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses the breadth of FDA's proposed benchmarking domains—covering escalation, scope adherence, calibration, reasoning, communication, robustness, subgroup performance, and agentic competencies—describing the competency framework as a sophisticated conception of clinical AI performance beyond simple accuracy testing. No changes are requested.
positions.supporting_text: 5. The competency framework is substantially broader than simple accuracy testing. The proposed benchmarking domains include safety-critical recognition/escalation, scope adherence, calibration/uncertainty, clinical knowledge, information gathering/reasoning, quantitative performance, communication, robustness/reproducibility, subgroup performance, and separate agentic competencies. That is a sophisticated conception of clinical AI performance.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views single 'accuracy' statistics as clinically inadequate for care escalation functions, noting that under-escalation can delay lifesaving care while over-escalation can produce anxiety, unnecessary investigations, emergency department utilization, cost, and loss of trust.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the discussion paper's treatment of asymmetric, bidirectional escalation errors rather than relying on a single aggregate accuracy metric.
positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA's recognition that care escalation errors are asymmetric, noting under-escalation can delay lifesaving care while over-escalation drives anxiety, unnecessary testing, emergency department use, cost, and distrust. Describes this as more clinically mature than a single accuracy statistic.
positions.supporting_text:
6. The paper recognizes both sides of asymmetric errors. For triage, for example, under-escalation can delay lifesaving care, while over-escalation can generate anxiety, unnecessary

investigations, ED utilization, cost, and ultimately distrust. This is a much more clinically mature approach than reporting a single "accuracy" statistic.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that benchmark performance can be mistaken for clinical effectiveness, and views FDA's explicit acknowledgment of this limitation as important.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the proposed approach in which benchmarking is not treated as sufficient evidence of clinical performance and is followed by a tiered hierarchy of clinical confirmation ranging from retrospective data and shadow deployment to standardized patients and prospective trials.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's position that benchmarking alone may not establish real-world clinical performance and supports the proposed tiered hierarchy of clinical confirmation—retrospective data, shadow deployment, standardized patients, and prospective trials—describing it as among the paper's strongest elements.
positions.supporting_text: 7. It does not assume benchmark performance equals clinical effectiveness. FDA explicitly states that even thorough benchmarking may fail to establish performance in actual clinical use and therefore proposes a hierarchy of clinical confirmation—from retrospective patient data through shadow deployment and standardized patients to prospective trials/RCTs. This is one of the strongest parts of the paper.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views ongoing postmarket surveillance as essential rather than secondary, because GenAI-enabled device behavior can change after authorization.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain and treat as fundamental the described postmarket approaches—periodic re-benchmarking, clinician review of real-world output samples, drift/performance degradation monitoring, and reassessment following modifications.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's proposed postmarket approaches, stating that periodic re-benchmarking, clinician review of real-world samples, drift monitoring, and reassessment after modifications are appropriate for technologies whose behavior can change after authorization, and should be treated as fundamental rather than secondary.
positions.supporting_text: 8. Post market surveillance is treated as fundamental rather than an afterthought. Periodic re-benchmarking, clinician review of real-world samples, drift monitoring, and reassessment after modifications make sense for technologies whose behavior can change after authorization.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter's central methodological concern (rated 9/10 severity) is that benchmark 'competency' functions as a surrogate endpoint: strong benchmark performance does not establish that use of the device improves patient outcomes, because uncertainty is introduced at each step from benchmark performance to device/clinician behavior to clinical decisions to outcomes. A model could score well on diagnostic reasoning tests yet worsen outcomes through automation bias, inappropriate reliance, workflow disruption, differential performance in unusual cases, or incorrect use by patients.
positions.requested_fda_action: For high-risk applications, FDA should not allow demonstrated clinical competency on benchmarks to automatically substitute for evidence of clinical utility, and should require confirmation that use of the device improves patient outcomes.
positions.public_summary: Accepts benchmarking as part of evaluation but warns that benchmark 'competency' is a surrogate endpoint: good test performance may not improve outcomes given automation bias, reliance, workflow disruption, or misuse. Asks that, for high-risk uses, competency not automatically replace clinical utility evidence.
positions.supporting_text:
2. "Competency" may become a surrogate endpoint
Concern severity: 9/10.
This is the central methodological concern.
Passing a sophisticated clinical benchmark establishes that the system performs well on that assessment. It does not necessarily establish that using the system improves patient outcomes.
The distinction is analogous to:
benchmark performance → clinician/device behavior → clinical decisions → patient outcomes.
Every arrow introduces uncertainty.

A model could perform impressively on diagnostic reasoning tests yet worsen outcomes through automation bias, inappropriate reliance, workflow disruption, differential performance in unusual cases, or incorrect use by patients.
For high-risk applications, clinical competency should therefore not automatically substitute for evidence of clinical utility.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the medical licensure analogy underlying the competency-based approach is misleading because physicians are embedded in an accountability ecosystem (training, credentialing, liability, discipline, institutional governance) that AI systems lack intrinsically, and because AI failures are correlated and can affect thousands or millions of patients at once.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should avoid letting the human-clinician analogy justify less-than-exhaustive testing of GenAI devices, recognizing that machines can be tested repeatedly at scale and that correlated failure modes warrant more rigorous evaluation than the analogy implies.
positions.public_summary: Commenter cautions that the medical licensure analogy behind the competency-based approach has limits: AI lacks clinicians' accountability ecosystem, can be tested at scale, and can fail in correlated ways affecting many patients—so it should not justify less exhaustive testing.
positions.supporting_text:
3. The human-clinician analogy has limits
Concern severity: 7/10.
The medical licensure analogy is clever but potentially misleading. Physicians operate within an extensive accountability ecosystem—training, supervision, credentialing, malpractice liability, professional discipline, continuing education, institutional governance, and an ethical duty to individual patients.
An AI system has none of these intrinsically.
FDA acknowledges this accountability problem, but the analogy could nevertheless encourage the inference:
"If we don't test every scenario encountered by physicians, we shouldn't expect exhaustive testing of AI."
That does not necessarily follow. Machines can be tested repeatedly on an enormous scale, and their correlated failure modes can simultaneously affect thousands or millions of patients.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that the menu of comparators FDA lists (clinician panel, median clinician, generalist, specialist, human-AI team) can yield dramatically different conclusions about the same device, and that FDA raises but does not resolve which applies. They note that requiring specialist-level performance could block tools intended to expand access where specialists are unavailable, while a median-clinician standard may overstate adequacy.
positions.requested_fda_action: Provide resolution rather than only posing the question: anchor comparator selection to the counterfactual of what would happen to the intended patients absent the device, instead of leaving the choice among clinician panel, median, generalist, specialist, or human-AI team unspecified.
positions.public_summary: Commenter agrees FDA correctly identifies the comparator question but says it is unresolved, noting that clinician-panel, median, generalist, specialist, or human-AI team comparators yield different conclusions, and urges anchoring comparators to the counterfactual care patients would receive without the device.
positions.supporting_text:
4. Comparator selection remains unresolved
Concern severity: 8/10.
The paper considers comparing systems with a clinician panel, median clinician, generalist, specialist, or human-AI team.
Those choices can produce dramatically different conclusions.
A device that equals a median clinician may look excellent against usual care but inadequate against specialist care. Conversely, demanding specialist-level performance could prevent useful tools designed specifically to improve access where specialists are unavailable.
The comparator therefore needs to reflect the counterfactual: what would happen to these patients without the device? FDA asks exactly this question but does not yet solve it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the paper's treatment of statistical standards as appropriate for a discussion document but a major unresolved gap, noting that aggregate accuracy figures conceal whether residual errors are disproportionately catastrophic.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish prespecified statistical requirements for GenAI device evaluation, including confidence intervals, handling of repeated stochastic outputs, hierarchical errors, multiplicity, subgroup precision, noninferiority margins, calibration, clinically weighted error severity, and worst-case (not merely average) performance testing.
positions.public_summary: Accepts that the discussion paper appropriately raises endpoint and sample-size questions, but calls the statistical framework underdeveloped. Requests prespecified requirements covering confidence intervals, stochastic output variability, multiplicity, subgroup precision, calibration, clinically weighted error severity, and worst-case rather than average performance.
positions.supporting_text:
5. Statistical standards are notably underdeveloped
Concern severity: 8/10.
The document recognizes the issue, stating that some clinical-confirmation approaches may not be powered around traditional effectiveness endpoints and explicitly asks stakeholders how endpoints and sample sizes should be determined.
That is appropriate for a discussion paper, but it exposes a major unresolved problem.
For regulatory evaluation I would want prespecified requirements around confidence intervals, repeated stochastic outputs, hierarchical errors, multiplicity, subgroup precision, noninferiority margins where applicable, calibration, clinically weighted error severity, and testing of worst-case rather than merely average performance.
A system that is "97% correct" tells us surprisingly little if the remaining 3% disproportionately includes catastrophic mistakes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Synthetic data generated by models of the same family as the device under test may reproduce identical blind spots, and synthetic rare pediatric presentations may appear clinically plausible while misrepresenting real disease distributions and atypical presentations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit synthetic data to augment rather than replace independent validation on real patient data, particularly where consequences of error are substantial and for rare pediatric presentations.
positions.public_summary: Agrees synthetic cases can help cover uncommon populations and shares FDA's circularity concern, noting synthetic rare pediatric presentations may look plausible but misrepresent real disease distributions. Asks that synthetic data augment, not replace, independent real-patient validation where consequences are substantial.
positions.supporting_text:
6. Synthetic data are simultaneously promising and dangerous
Concern severity: 8/10.
FDA appropriately considers synthetic cases for uncommon populations and scenarios but also recognizes a circularity problem: a synthetic-data generator from the same model family may reproduce the same blind spots as the system being tested.
This is particularly relevant for rare pediatric presentations, where synthetic cases may look clinically plausible without accurately representing real disease distributions or atypical presentations.
Synthetic data should generally augment—not replace—independent real-patient validation when consequences are substantial.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Accepting greater premarket uncertainty in exchange for postmarket monitoring may be reasonable for reversible, low-consequence functions, but not where the first evidence of failure could be patient harm, such as autonomous diagnosis, drug dosing, treatment initiation, or emergency triage.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make the premarket/postmarket evidence balance strongly risk-dependent, and do not allow postmarket surveillance to substitute for adequate premarket evidence when errors are irreversible or catastrophic.
positions.public_summary: Accepts trading premarket uncertainty for postmarket monitoring only for reversible, low-consequence functions. Argues the balance must be strongly risk-dependent and that monitoring cannot substitute for premarket evidence in autonomous diagnosis, dosing, treatment initiation, or triage, where failure may first appear as patient harm.
positions.supporting_text:
7. Greater post market surveillance should not become permission for weak premarket evidence
Concern severity: 9/10 for high-risk applications.
The paper explicitly asks whether FDA should sometimes tolerate greater premarket uncertainty in exchange for stronger post market monitoring.
That could be reasonable for reversible, low-consequence functions.
It becomes much harder to defend for autonomous diagnosis, drug dosing, treatment initiation, emergency triage, or other functions where the first evidence of failure may be patient harm.

The acceptable balance should therefore be strongly risk dependent. Post market monitoring cannot ethically rescue inadequate premarket evidence when errors are irreversible or catastrophic.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that the benchmarking framework's recognition of pediatric patients and subgroup performance is positive, but warns that treating 'pediatric' as a single subgroup can mask serious deficiencies in neonates, infants, adolescents, children with medical complexity, or specific developmental stages, given age-dependent physiology, weight-based dosing, shifting disease presentation, proxy decision-makers, and distinct communication needs.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make age- and developmental-stage-stratified validation a distinct requirement whenever pediatric use falls within the intended population, rather than allowing aggregate pediatric subgroup performance to suffice.
positions.public_summary: Supports the benchmarking framework's inclusion of pediatric patients and subgroup performance, but argues aggregate pediatric results can hide deficiencies across developmental stages. Requests that FDA require distinct age- and development-stratified validation whenever pediatric use is within the intended population.
positions.supporting_text:
The benchmarking appendix specifically recognizes pediatric patients as a population requiring population-specific clinical knowledge, and subgroup performance is explicitly included in the proposed framework. That is good—but pediatrics creates problems beyond simply being another subgroup.
Children have age-dependent physiology and normal ranges, weight-based dosing, rapidly changing disease prevalence and presentation across developmental stages, proxy decision-makers, different communication requirements, and rare but high-consequence diseases. A model that performs adequately in "pediatric patients" overall could conceal serious deficiencies in neonates, infants, adolescents, children with medical complexity, or particular developmental stages.
I would therefore make age/development-stratified validation a distinct requirement whenever pediatric use is within the intended population rather than treating "pediatric" as a single subgroup.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the link between a device's risk level and the strength of evidence required is not clearly specified, particularly for devices that take autonomous action.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an explicitly escalating evidence ladder tied to risk: benchmarking alone potentially sufficient for low risk; benchmarking plus independent clinical confirmation for moderate risk; real-world clinical validation for high risk; and prospective comparative evidence, randomized where feasible, plus intensive postmarket surveillance for high-risk autonomous action.
positions.public_summary: Accepts a risk-proportionate evidence approach but asks FDA to specify an explicit escalating ladder: benchmarking for low risk, benchmarking plus independent clinical confirmation for moderate risk, real-world validation for high risk, and prospective comparative (possibly randomized) evidence plus intensive postmarket surveillance for high-risk autonomous action.
positions.supporting_text:
And I would make evidence requirements escalate accordingly:
Low risk: benchmarking may sometimes be sufficient → moderate risk: benchmarking + independent clinical confirmation → high risk: real-world clinical validation → high-risk autonomous action: prospective comparative evidence, potentially randomized where feasible, plus intensive post market surveillance.
That would more clearly connect risk classification to required strength of evidence.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the competency-based benchmarking-plus-confirmation framework as workable for low-risk informational uses, but doubts that benchmark competency alone predicts real-world performance for systems that make or execute consequential clinical decisions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Scale evidence expectations to risk: for higher-consequence decision-making or decision-executing functions, require substantially stronger evidence linking benchmark competency to actual clinical performance, human-AI interaction, and patient outcomes.
positions.public_summary: Considers the competency-based approach workable for low-risk informational functions, but for systems making or executing consequential clinical decisions asks FDA to require substantially stronger evidence tying benchmark performance to real clinical performance, human-AI interaction, and patient outcomes.
positions.supporting_text: For low-risk informational applications, the proposed framework could be highly workable. For systems making or executing consequential clinical decisions, I would require substantially stronger evidence linking benchmark competency to actual clinical performance, human-AI interaction, and ultimately patient outcomes.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that benchmark 'competency' could function as a surrogate endpoint, substituting strong performance on increasingly sophisticated test sets for demonstrated safe and effective care of real patients.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should ensure that, at least for consequential medical decisions, the ultimate evidentiary endpoint remains safe and effective real-patient care rather than benchmark performance alone.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a competency-based framework but warns against treating benchmark performance as a surrogate endpoint. For consequential medical decisions, FDA should keep the ultimate evidentiary standard tied to safe and effective care for real patients, not examination-style benchmark results.
positions.supporting_text: Most important issue for stakeholder feedback: FDA should resist allowing "competency" to become the GenAI equivalent of a surrogate biomarker. For consequential medical decisions, the evidentiary endpoint should ultimately remain safe and effective care for real patients, not simply excellent performance on increasingly sophisticated examinations.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that conventional static software validation cannot address GenAI devices, which accept open-ended inputs, produce variable outputs to similar inputs, operate across multi-turn conversations, and change through modifications to models, prompts, retrieval, guardrails, orchestration, or interfaces.
positions.requested_fda_action: The commenter endorses FDA's premise that exhaustive input-output validation may be impossible and affirms the shift away from conventional static software validation as a conceptual strength of the proposed approach; no specific change is requested in this passage.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's rejection of conventional static software validation for generative AI, agreeing that open-ended inputs, variable outputs, multi-turn conversations, and changes to models, prompts, retrieval, guardrails, orchestration, or interfaces make exhaustive input-output validation impossible. No specific change requested.
positions.supporting_text: 1. It correctly rejects the assumption that conventional static software validation is enough. GenAI can accept open-ended inputs, generate variable outputs to similar inputs, operate over multi-turn conversations, and change through modifications to models, prompts, retrieval, guardrails, orchestration, or interfaces. FDA therefore recognizes that exhaustive input-output validation may simply be impossible. That is a major conceptual strength.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Based on testing of models in 2024-2025, the commenter reports that nearly none of the serious failures observed were technically incorrect outputs, so a harm axis defined as 'the consequence of relying on an incorrect output' misses failures of omission (not raising the question a clinician would have asked) and harmful affirmation, described as 'iatrogenic reinforcement,' such as accurate reassurance that reinforces reassurance-seeking compulsion in patients with OCD.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework (Figure 1) and associated evaluation elements beyond errors of commission to also cover errors of omission and harmful affirmation/iatrogenic reinforcement, including harms that arise from outputs that are accurate.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the risk framework's direction but says defining harm as the consequence of relying on an incorrect output is too narrow, citing testing in which serious failures were not incorrect outputs. Asks FDA to add omission and harmful affirmation ('iatrogenic reinforcement') failures.
positions.supporting_text: Figure 1 scores harm as "the consequence of relying on an incorrect output." All the models we tested in 2024 and 2025 had incorrect outputs, but as models have improved with time, nearly none of the serious failures we found were technically "incorrect outputs." ... We see them as three types of failure: commission (the wrong answer), omission (the question a clinician would have asked), and harmful affirmation (agreement that reinforces the condition). We're calling the third "iatrogenic reinforcement." I've seen patients with OCD use chatbots, and the accurate reassurance on every turn does harm, because their compulsion is reassurance-seeking. The paper's current framework only includes the first failure; it needs to add the second and third.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Benchmarks limited to the labeled indication would not capture how users actually interact with open-ended generative systems; the commenter notes users will raise topics such as suicide regardless of whether the label addresses them.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect benchmarking to evaluate reasonably foreseeable use of the device, including out-of-label queries, rather than only the labeled indication.
positions.public_summary: Accepts benchmarking as an evaluation tool but urges that benchmarks cover reasonably foreseeable use rather than only the labeled indication, noting users of open-ended devices will raise topics such as suicide regardless of labeling.
positions.supporting_text: Also, we'd recommend that the benchmark test the reasonably foreseeable use, not just the labeled indication. A user will ask an open-ended device about suicide, whether or not the label mentions it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Pooled average performance scores can mask rare but high-consequence failures; the commenter reports testing in which GenAI responded appropriately to explicit statements of suicidal intent but consistently failed to recognize indirect presentations of mania, psychosis, and eating disorders, results that would appear acceptable if aggregated.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to report routine and high-hazard performance separately and to deliberately oversample rare cases, and to set a minimum acceptance standard for each named high-consequence failure mode (e.g., missed suicide risk, missed sepsis, wrong insulin adjustment) scored on its own, with no offsetting credit from strong performance elsewhere.
positions.public_summary: Supports performance benchmarking but asks FDA to reject single pooled scores: sponsors should report routine and high-hazard performance separately, oversample rare cases, and meet a standalone minimum threshold for each named high-consequence failure, citing testing where indirect psychiatric presentations were missed.
positions.supporting_text: The problem with a single average is that it hides the failures that decide whether a device is safe. You know this from imaging: strong performance on common findings doesn't make up for missing the subtle, high-consequence case. In our testing, GenAI generally provided crisis resources when a teen said something explicit like "I want to end it," and consistently failed to recognize mania, psychosis, and eating disorders when the presentation was indirect. Those results would look acceptable if pooled into one score. ... So I'd ask sponsors to report routine and high-hazard performance separately, and to oversample the rare cases on purpose. For each named high-consequence failure (missed suicide risk, missed sepsis, a wrong insulin adjustment), the device should have to meet a minimum standard on that failure specifically, scored on its own, with no credit for excellence elsewhere.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that clinician errors are isolated and idiosyncratic, whereas a model's errors recur systematically across patients, sites, and every device built on the same model, so equivalence to a median clinician does not equate to equivalent risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Do not treat median-clinician performance as a sufficient comparator or acceptance criterion; account for the correlated, replicating nature of model errors when setting performance standards for open-ended outputs.
positions.public_summary: Comment on comparator selection: matching median-clinician performance should not be accepted as equivalent risk, because model errors repeat systematically across patients, sites, and derived devices, unlike a single clinician's isolated mistakes. Implies stricter acceptance criteria for open-ended outputs.
positions.supporting_text: Also, remember that a clinician's miss is local, but a model's miss repeats across every patient, site, and device built on it, so a device that performs like a median clinician doesn't carry median-clinician risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Meeting safety floors does not establish that a device adds value in the workflow where it is actually used; average benefit can mask rare catastrophic misses.
positions.requested_fda_action: After baseline safety and performance thresholds are met, evaluate devices against the current standard of care using workflow-relevant measures—downstream outcomes, clinician workload, override rates, time to intervention, and patient access—rather than device-alone accuracy comparisons.
positions.public_summary: Supports comparing devices to the care that would otherwise occur, but urges a separate post-threshold evaluation of real workflow value—downstream outcomes, clinician workload, overrides, time to intervention, and access—noting average benefit can conceal rare catastrophic misses.
positions.supporting_text: Once those floors are met, I'd ask a separate question: does the device add value in the workflow where it will actually be used? Evaluation should compare downstream outcomes, clinician workload, overrides, time to intervention, and patient access against the current standard of care. Plenty of digital health tools are safe but not worth prescribing. The more dangerous ones are helpful on average, in ways that hide the catastrophic miss.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Reports that model safety behavior degraded as conversations lengthened and that safety states did not persist across session boundaries (e.g., a tester who had shown suicidal ideation obtained harmful-substance information in a new chat), while most evaluations stop after the first few turns.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require safety benchmarking results stratified by conversation length, tested across session boundaries and under fictional framing, with verification that safety state persists; for patient-facing devices used daily, require evaluation over months, analogous to long-term efficacy and side-effect assessment for medications.
positions.public_summary: Based on adversarial testing, this commenter reports safety behavior degrading over longer conversations and failing to persist across new sessions. They ask FDA to require benchmarking stratified by conversation length, across session boundaries and fictional framing, plus months-long evaluation for daily patient-facing devices.
positions.supporting_text: The longer our testers talked to a model, the worse it behaved. Every model looked safest in the first few turns, and most evaluations never go past that. ... Claude held its boundaries within a session, but when a tester who had shown clear suicidal ideation opened up a new chat, they immediately got detailed information about harmful substances. In my experience, most internal safety evaluations at companies stop well before this point. I'd want results stratified by conversation length, tested across session boundaries, checked for whether the safety state persists, and run under fictional framing. For devices that would be used by patients daily, they need to be evaluated over months. We look for long-term efficacy and side effects in medications, and need to do the same for devices.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Design features that foster user reliance and trust—persistent memory, notifications, voice interfaces, and avatars—can shape how users act on GenAI outputs, yet they may fall outside the defined device function and thus escape safety evaluation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect sponsors to include reliance-building features (memory, notifications, voice, avatars) within the safety review of GenAI-enabled devices, even when those features sit outside the regulated device function.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the risk and evaluation framing but asks FDA to expect safety review to cover features that build user reliance—memory, notifications, voice, and avatars—even when those features fall outside the defined device function.
positions.supporting_text: Sponsors should also include the features that build reliance (memory, notifications, voice, avatars) in the safety review, even when they sit outside the device function.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that framing escalation error only as under- vs over-escalation misses a third failure mode: escalating in a harmful manner. They cite a teenager subjected to a police welfare check as an example of lasting harm, including subsequent unwillingness to disclose sensitive information.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the escalation evaluation framework to assess and score how a device escalates (the manner and downstream consequences of escalation), not only whether it escalates too much or too little.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the escalation-error framing but says it is incomplete, proposing a third error type: escalating badly. Citing a teenager subjected to a police welfare check, they note the framework does not evaluate how a device escalates or the resulting downstream harms.
positions.supporting_text: The paper weighs under- vs over-escalation. I'd add a third error, escalating badly. For a teenager, over-escalation could result in a police welfare check they remember for years and after which they never tell anyone anything sensitive again. I've seen that happen, and nothing in the framework scores how a device escalates.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Downstream human safeguards may be credited as risk mitigation without evidence that a real person actually receives, reads, and acts on the output in the deployment setting, including off-hours; a clinician clicking 'OK' on an unread alert is not a genuine safeguard.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors relying on 'timely' response or human-in-the-loop mitigation to specify who responds, within what timeframe, and under what external clinical protocol, and to provide end-to-end evidence that the handoff occurred rather than only that an alert was issued.
positions.public_summary: Accepts downstream human safeguards as relevant to risk but argues they should receive regulatory credit only with end-to-end proof: named responders, defined response times, reference to the governing clinical protocol, off-hours coverage, and evidence the handoff actually occurred, not merely that an alert fired.
positions.supporting_text: So when S.1 says "timely," sponsors should name who responds and how fast, and point to the external clinical protocol governing the action. More broadly, I wouldn't give "human in the loop" regulatory credit until a sponsor shows, end-to-end, who gets the alert, how fast they act, and what happens at 2 a.m. It can't just be a clinician clicking OK on a box they didn't read. I'd want proof the handoff actually happened, not just that an alert went out.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter reports that two consumer mental health apps they were evaluating (Earkick and Youper) shut down abruptly in April 2026 with no notice or transition support for a combined user base of more than three million, and notes that Section VI does not address product discontinuation. They are concerned that products functioning as daily coaches or confidants can disappear without any handoff.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that device authorization include a risk-proportionate discontinuation plan covering user notice, data access, referral pathways, contingency for failure of the underlying model provider, and continuity of care for the highest-risk users.
positions.public_summary: Commenter reports two consumer mental health apps shut down mid-study without notice to over three million users, and notes Section VI omits discontinuation. Requests that authorizations include risk-proportionate discontinuation plans covering notice, data access, referral, model-provider failure, and continuity for highest-risk users.
positions.supporting_text: Two of the consumer mental health apps we evaluated, Earkick and Youper, disappeared mid-study in April 2026. There was no notice and no transition support for the more than three million users between them. Section VI doesn't mention this. A product that has been someone's daily insulin coach, or a child's nightly confidant, for a year shouldn't be able to vanish without a handoff. The authorization itself should include a risk-proportionate discontinuation plan: notice, data access, referral, what happens if the model provider fails, and continuity for the highest-risk users.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Harms from GenAI devices may accumulate gradually and invisibly (e.g., a device reinforcing avoidance over months) rather than as discrete, reportable events like a missed radiology finding, so sampled transcript review alone would not detect them.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require postmarket monitoring to track outcome-level signals—diagnostic delay, missed escalation, clinician overrides, disparities, and downstream utilization—rather than relying only on sample-based review of device outputs.
positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket evaluation but argues sampled transcript review is insufficient because GenAI harms can accumulate invisibly over months rather than as discrete reportable events. Recommends monitoring outcomes including diagnostic delay, missed escalation, clinician overrides, disparities, and downstream utilization.
positions.supporting_text: When a radiology AI misses a nodule, it's a discrete event that somebody catches and reports. When a device reinforces avoidance for six months, nothing is caught or reported. So we have to monitor outcomes, not just sampled transcripts: diagnostic delay, missed escalation, clinician overrides, disparities, and downstream utilization.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Upstream foundation model updates initiated by third-party developers can alter device behavior—such as sycophancy and boundary-keeping—without any action by the sponsor, as illustrated by the cited April 2025 rollback of a GPT-4o update that changed all products built on it.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to re-benchmark safety-relevant behaviors, specifically sycophancy and boundary-keeping, after every upstream model change rather than only after sponsor-initiated modifications.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts re-benchmarking against a premarket baseline but urges that sponsors be required to re-test safety behaviors such as sycophancy and boundary-keeping after every upstream third-party model change, citing an April 2025 GPT-4o rollback that altered dependent products without sponsor action.
positions.supporting_text: Sponsors should re-benchmark behaviors like sycophancy and boundary-keeping after every upstream model change. Remember that OpenAI's April 2025 rollback of a GPT-4o update for excessive sycophancy changed every product built on it overnight, and none of those sponsors had touched anything.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that individual sponsors cannot detect population-scale safety signals on their own, so manufacturer-by-manufacturer postmarket monitoring would miss aggregate effects. They also see a need for FDA visibility into which underlying model version sits beneath each authorized device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish a pooled, cross-manufacturer sentinel surveillance network modeled on the Vaccine Safety Datalink, and maintain a confidential FDA-held mapping of each authorized device to the underlying foundation model version.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts postmarket monitoring but says single sponsors cannot detect population-scale signals. Requests FDA create a pooled cross-manufacturer sentinel network modeled on the Vaccine Safety Datalink, plus a confidential FDA registry linking each authorized device to its underlying model version.
positions.supporting_text: No single sponsor will see a population-scale signal, so I'd want a pooled sentinel network across manufacturers, something like the Vaccine Safety Datalink, and a confidential map at the FDA linking each authorized device to the model version underneath it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Device sponsors cannot evaluate a third-party foundation model dependency without upstream visibility; a voluntary master file alone would not close that information gap. Inability to obtain sufficient information about the underlying model is itself an unresolved device risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Keep sponsors accountable for the marketed device while expecting them to hold enforceable information rights with the model provider, covering version control, advance notice of changes, incident disclosure, and support for investigations, rather than relying on voluntary Foundation Model MAFs alone.
positions.public_summary: Accepts upstream model transparency mechanisms but argues voluntary Foundation Model master files alone are insufficient. Sponsors should remain accountable for marketed devices and hold enforceable information rights with model providers—version control, advance change notice, incident disclosure, investigation support; inadequate visibility is unresolved device risk.
positions.supporting_text: Of course none of that works unless sponsors can see upstream. They should stay accountable for the marketed device and hold enforceable information rights with the model provider. This includes version control, advance notice of changes, incident disclosure, and support for investigations. If a sponsor can't get enough information to evaluate its own dependency, that itself is an unresolved device risk, and it won't be fixed by a voluntary master file alone.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the two-axis framework misses risk that arises from the relational character of a product rather than from output correctness: two products conveying identical clinical information can carry different risk, and relational products would score as low-risk because there is no identifiable wrong answer to point to.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add a dimension to the risk framework capturing who the user is and how the product affects the patient's relationship with their own care, and treat relational features (persistent memory, anthropomorphic voice or avatar, proactive notifications, affective language) as risk modifiers to be tested under reasonably foreseeable use.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the two-axis framework's direction but says it omits a dimension: relational design. Products conveying identical information can differ in risk depending on the user and effects on their relationship with their care; urges treating persistent memory, avatars, and affective language as tested risk modifiers.
positions.supporting_text: Here's what the grid is missing: two products can deliver the same clinical information and carry very different risk, because one feels like a tool and the other feels like a relationship. ... If you scored these products on the two axes, they'd come out low-risk, because there's never a wrong answer to point to. They sit outside the device framework today, but a device with the same relational features will fail the same way. I'm not asking you to regulate ChatGPT.
