positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic and distributed GenAI systems can take multi-step autonomous actions and exchange information across components, so the commenter is concerned that autonomy be bounded, permissions constrained, supervision not self-referential, and that safety-relevant causal chains remain reconstructable after the fact.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require, for agentic and distributed systems, enforceable operational scope, least-privilege access, bounded autonomy, safe information exchange, safe interruption, and risk-proportionate reconstruction of safety-relevant causal chains, with independent or diversely implemented supervision where risk warrants and it is practicable.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA impose specific controls on agentic and distributed GenAI devices: enforceable scope, least privilege, bounded autonomy, safe information exchange, safe interruption, and reconstruction of safety-relevant causal chains, with independent or diversely implemented supervision where risk warrants and is practicable.
positions.supporting_text:
9.  For agentic and distributed systems, require enforceable scope, least privilege, bounded
autonomy, safe information exchange, independent or diversely implemented supervision
where risk warrants and practicable, safe interruption, and risk-proportionate reconstruction of
safety-relevant causal chains.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without a defined record of the specific AI configuration that shapes device behavior, it is difficult to trace what was evaluated, authorized, deployed, and subsequently changed, including changes originating with third-party model or component suppliers.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add a risk-proportionate AI System Bill of Materials (AI-SBOM) as a supplemental record linked to existing design, supplier, product-BOM, and cybersecurity-SBOM records, identifying the behavior-shaping AI configuration across evaluation, authorization, deployment, and change, without duplicating existing component records.
positions.public_summary: Supports the change-control direction but asks FDA to add a risk-proportionate AI System Bill of Materials as a supplemental record, linked to existing design, supplier, product-BOM, and cybersecurity-SBOM records, identifying the behavior-shaping AI configuration evaluated, authorized, deployed, and changed, without duplicating existing records.
positions.supporting_text:
6.  Add a risk-proportionate AI System Bill of Materials (AI-SBOM) as a supplemental record linked
to existing design, supplier, product-BOM, and cybersecurity-SBOM records where applicable,
identifying the behavior-shaping AI configuration that was evaluated, authorized, deployed, and
changed without duplicating established component records.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter treats verifiable identity and provenance of system components—models, agents, tools, data sources, policies, users, and the humans who grant approvals—as safety-relevant controls rather than purely IT or security matters.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize identity and provenance tracking across models, agents, tools, data sources, policies, users, and approving humans as safety controls within the evaluation and oversight framework for GenAI-enabled devices.
positions.public_summary: Brief recommendation, offered without elaboration, that FDA treat identity and provenance of models, agents, tools, data sources, policies, users, and approving humans as safety controls—framing these traceability measures as safety-relevant rather than only security or IT concerns.
positions.supporting_text:
5.  Treat identity and provenance as safety controls for models, agents, tools, data sources, policies,
users, and approving humans.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that data generated or derived by GenAI-enabled devices—prompts, conversations, inferences, embeddings, memory, tool results, and safety evidence—may be handled without defined governance over its lifecycle.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require explicit governance for all collected and derived data, addressing purpose, access, retention, correction, deletion, reuse, and transfer.
positions.public_summary: Recommends FDA require explicit lifecycle governance for data collected or derived by GenAI-enabled devices—prompts, conversations, inferences, embeddings, memory, tool results, and safety evidence—covering purpose, access, retention, correction, deletion, reuse, and transfer. The passage does not otherwise evaluate FDA's proposals.
positions.supporting_text:
7.  Require explicit governance for collected and derived data—including prompts, conversations,
inferences, embeddings, memory, tool results, and safety evidence—covering purpose, access,
retention, correction, deletion, reuse, and transfer.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that characterizing a GenAI function requires more dimensions than device activity and consequence of an incorrect output, including whether the system merely communicates, supports a device function, directs care, or acts with clinical consequences.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should characterize GenAI functions using an expanded set of properties: intended purpose, output recipient, degree of personalization, directiveness, effective opportunity for qualified review, authority to act, time to harm, reversibility, integration with clinical systems or devices, persistence of memory or state, and ability to change after deployment.
positions.public_summary: Accepts risk characterization in principle but asks FDA to expand beyond the two axes, adding properties such as output recipient, personalization, directiveness, opportunity for qualified review, authority to act, time to harm, reversibility, system integration, memory persistence, and post-deployment changeability.
positions.supporting_text:
FDA should characterize the function using intended purpose, output recipient, degree of
personalization, directiveness, effective opportunity for qualified review, authority to act, time
to harm, reversibility, integration with clinical systems or devices, persistence of memory or
state, and ability to change after deployment. These properties determine whether an AI system
merely communicates, supports a device function, directs care, or participates in an action with
clinical consequences.

positions.stakeholder_concern: When a manufacturer supplies an evaluated AI capability but a healthcare institution controls data, prompts, workflows, identities, tools, and connected-device access, it is unclear which local changes are mere deployment configuration versus modifications to a device function, who must validate the integrated function, and what evidence parties must exchange.
positions.requested_fda_action: Explicitly address scope questions: what facts make a hospital-deployed assistant become, contain, or materially modify a device function; how to identify the responsible manufacturer and regulated system boundary when multiple organizations shape behavior; when local configuration requires manufacturer review, supplemental validation, or new submission; and minimum evidence exchange among manufacturers, model providers, institutions, and connected-device vendors while preserving beneficial local innovation.
positions.public_summary: VivaSecuris asks FDA to go beyond the discussion paper by clarifying shared responsibility in deployed systems: what local configuration turns a hospital-deployed assistant into or modifies a device function, how the regulated boundary and responsible manufacturer are identified, and what evidence parties must exchange.
positions.supporting_text:
Shared-responsibility question exposed by service delivery
When a manufacturer supplies an evaluated AI capability but a healthcare institution configures
its data, prompts, workflows, identities, tools, and connected-device access, FDA should clarify
which changes remain deployment configuration, which create a modification to a medical-device
function, who must validate the integrated function, and how the parties exchange the evidence
needed to maintain accountability.
VivaSecuris recommends that FDA explicitly address the following scope questions:
  What facts cause a hospital-deployed assistant to become, contain, or materially modify a
medical-device function?
  How should the responsible manufacturer and regulated system boundary be identified when
several organizations control behavior-shaping components?

VIVASECURIS  |  FDA-2026-N-7874
Public Comment — Generative AI-Enabled Medical Devices
  When does local configuration—including prompts, retrieval, workflow logic, role permissions,
tools, and device access—require manufacturer review, supplemental validation, or a new
regulatory submission?
  What minimum evidence must manufacturers, model providers, healthcare institutions, and
connected-device vendors exchange to validate and monitor the integrated function?
  How should FDA preserve beneficial local innovation while preventing unassessed changes from
silently altering intended use, authority, or clinical risk?

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket observability could become disproportionate or intrude on privacy. The passage is truncated, so the full rationale and scope of the concern are not stated.
positions.requested_fda_action: Structure postmarket monitoring so that it is proportionate to risk and privacy preserving, with routine evidence focused on artifacts such as configuration identifiers, policy results, uncertainty ranges, and safety-control information (text incomplete).
positions.public_summary: Comment accepts postmarket performance monitoring but asks that observability be proportionate and privacy preserving, with routine evidence centered on configuration identifiers, policy results, uncertainty ranges, and safety-control information. The passage is truncated, limiting interpretation.
positions.supporting_text:
Postmarket observability should be proportionate and privacy preserving. Routine evidence can
emphasize configuration identifiers, policy results, uncertainty ranges, safety-control

positions.stakeholder_concern: GenAI systems generate new sensitive derived data (conversations, inferred symptoms or diagnoses, risk classifications, summaries, embeddings, retrieved context, agent memory, tool results, feedback, safety interventions, audit records) that may reveal or amplify clinically significant facts even when the source record is already governed, and a generic privacy statement does not address this.
positions.requested_fda_action: For data practices materially affecting device safety or effectiveness and within FDA's authority, FDA should ask sponsors to document an explicit data lifecycle: each data class, its necessity, storage location, access rights, downstream recipient systems, persistence duration, and procedures for correction, retention, archiving, and deletion.
positions.public_summary: Commenter adds a consideration to FDA's postmarket questions: GenAI creates new sensitive derived data (inferences, embeddings, agent memory, audit records). Where such data practices materially affect device safety or effectiveness, FDA should require sponsors to document an explicit data lifecycle rather than generic privacy statements.
positions.supporting_text:
Additional consideration related to Questions 18 and 21. Data collected or created by GenAI requires an explicit lifecycle, not a generic privacy statement.
GenAI systems can create new sensitive information even when the source record is already governed. Conversations, inferred symptoms or diagnoses, risk classifications, summaries, embeddings, retrieved context, agent memory, tool results, feedback, safety interventions, and audit records may reveal or amplify clinically significant facts. For data practices materially affecting device safety or effectiveness and within FDA's authority, FDA should ask sponsors to identify each data class, why it is necessary, where it is stored, who can access it, which downstream systems receive it, how long it persists, and how it is corrected, retained, archived, or deleted.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Data handling around GenAI devices—prompts, outputs, embeddings, memory, caches, backups, and supplier-held copies—can expose patients and corrupt clinical records if erroneous derived inferences propagate as durable truth, and if patient interactions or safety investigations are silently reused for model training or analytics.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect manufacturers to implement enforceable data governance: purpose limitation and minimization, separation of data categories, identity-bound and time-bounded authorization for every read, write, inference, retrieval, export, and deletion, defined retention and verified deletion, provenance and correction propagation, governed secondary use, and contractual plus technical supplier boundaries covering retention, human review, subprocessors, incident response, and migration.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that GenAI device oversight include explicit data governance controls: data minimization and separation, identity-bound and time-limited authorization for all actions, defined retention and verified deletion, provenance and correction propagation, restrictions on secondary use for training, and contractual and technical supplier boundaries.
positions.supporting_text:
Purpose limitation and minimization: collect and derive only the information necessary for the authorized function, safety monitoring, and legally required records.
  Separation: distinguish patient content, operational state, model context, long-term memory, quality evidence, cybersecurity evidence, and de-identified aggregate metrics so each can receive appropriate access and retention controls.
  Identity and authorization: bind every read, write, inference, retrieval, export, and deletion to an authenticated human or machine identity, permitted purpose, patient scope, and time-bounded authority.
  Retention and deletion: define limits for prompts, outputs, caches, embeddings, memory, backups, replicas, and supplier-held copies; verify deletion or justified archival rather than relying on user-interface disappearance, subject to applicable record-retention, investigation, litigation-hold, and data-integrity obligations.
  Correction and provenance: preserve the source and transformation history of derived information and propagate corrections so an erroneous inference does not become durable clinical truth across systems.
  Secondary use: do not silently use patient interactions, clinical content, or safety investigations for model training, product improvement, or unrelated analytics. Any authorized reuse should be separately governed, transparent, and technically enforceable.
  Supplier boundaries: contracts and technical controls should address model-provider retention, human review, abuse monitoring, support access, regional storage, subprocessors, incident response, and termination or migration.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that privacy protection and safety surveillance are not inherently in conflict, and that postmarket monitoring can retain enough attributable evidence to reconstruct the cause of a serious failure without indefinite retention of all raw conversational data.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect sponsors to justify the minimum evidence needed for causal reconstruction of failures, keep content separated from metadata, and permit controlled re-identification only when authorized for patient care, safety investigation, or regulatory obligations.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses postmarket monitoring data practices, arguing privacy and safety are compatible: sponsors should justify the minimum evidence needed to reconstruct serious failures, separate content from metadata, and allow re-identification only when authorized for care, safety investigation, or regulatory purposes.
positions.supporting_text: Privacy and safety should not be framed as opposites. A system can preserve enough attributable evidence to investigate a serious failure without retaining every raw conversation indefinitely. Sponsors should justify the minimum evidence needed for causal reconstruction, protect content separately from metadata, and support controlled re-identification only when authorized for patient care, safety investigation, or regulatory obligations.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Periodic reassessment alone is insufficient; a broad set of technical, operational, and clinical events can change device behavior and should trigger re-evaluation, and cadence should not be fixed arbitrarily.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt both periodic and event-triggered postmarket reassessment, with an enumerated trigger list (model or model-provider changes; prompt, retrieval, orchestration, guardrail, tool, interface, or infrastructure changes; new populations or sites; distribution shift; novel failure modes; cybersecurity events; control degradation; complaint/adverse-event patterns; practice changes) and cadence justified by inherent risk, exposure, rate of change, and time to detect harm.
positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's postmarket reassessment approaches but urges reassessment be both periodic and event-triggered, listing triggers (model or provider changes, pipeline or infrastructure changes, new sites or populations, distribution shift, cybersecurity events, complaint patterns) with cadence justified by risk, exposure, change rate, and detection time.
positions.supporting_text:
Question 19. Reassessment should be both periodic and event-triggered.
Relevant triggers include model or model-provider changes; prompt, retrieval, orchestration, guardrail, tool, interface, or infrastructure changes; new user populations or sites; distribution shift; novel failure modes; cybersecurity events; control degradation; complaint or adverse-event patterns; and changes in clinical practice. Cadence should be justified by inherent risk, exposure, rate of change, and time to detect harm.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Machine-based supervisory agents could create circular assurance if the supervisor shares failure modes with the monitored model, such as when another instance of the same model family reviews its output.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that supervisory agents have a defined, narrower role, independent or diversely implemented failure modes where risk warrants and practicable, restricted privileges, validated detection and interruption performance, protected inputs, and a safe failure state, with auditing and periodic re-evaluation of supervisory actions, failures, overrides, and missed detections.
positions.public_summary: Accepts that machine-based supervisory agents can assist postmarket monitoring, but asks FDA to require safeguards against circular assurance: narrower supervisor roles, independent or diverse failure modes, restricted privileges, validated detection and interruption performance, protected inputs, safe failure states, and audited, periodically re-evaluated supervisory actions.
positions.supporting_text:
Question 20. Machine-based supervisory agents can assist monitoring but must not create circular assurance.
A supervisor should have a defined, narrower role; failure modes that are independent or diversely implemented relative to the monitored component where risk warrants and practicable; restricted privileges; validated detection and interruption performance; protected inputs; and a safe failure state. A model should not be considered independently supervised merely because another instance of the same model family reviews its output. Supervisory actions, failures, overrides, and missed detections should be audited and periodically re-evaluated.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Multiple ecosystem participants (clinicians, institutions, societies, model providers, standards bodies) can usefully contribute postmarket signals, adjudication, benchmarks, and deployment context, but responsibility for acting on that information must not become diffuse.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the manufacturer as the accountable party for aggregating and triaging shared signals, making risk decisions, taking corrective action, and regulatory reporting, and expect data-sharing agreements that specify provenance, timeliness, minimum data fields, privacy protections, and closure of feedback loops.
positions.public_summary: Endorses multi-stakeholder contributions to postmarket monitoring (signals, adjudication, benchmarks, deployment context) but asks FDA to keep manufacturers accountable for aggregation, triage, risk decisions, corrective action, and reporting, supported by data-sharing agreements specifying provenance, timeliness, minimum fields, privacy, and feedback closure.
positions.supporting_text:
Question 21. Shared ecosystem participation should enrich evidence without diffusing manufacturer accountability.
Clinicians, healthcare institutions, professional societies, model providers, and standards bodies can contribute signals, adjudication, benchmarks, and deployment context. The manufacturer should remain responsible for aggregation, triage, risk decisions, corrective action, and regulatory reporting. Data-sharing agreements should specify provenance, timeliness, minimum fields, privacy protections, and feedback closure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Safety-relevant information about GenAI-enabled devices moves across hospital, cloud, model-provider, manufacturer, and device boundaries, and transport encryption alone does not establish that the sender was authorized, that the data are semantically valid, or that the recipient may use them for the stated purpose.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should expect each consequential cross-boundary exchange to carry sender/recipient identity, permitted purpose, patient or device scope, schema and clinical meaning, source and transformation provenance, applicable AI-SBOM configuration, integrity and freshness, privacy classification, retention, and onward-use restrictions.
positions.public_summary: Comment urges FDA to address safety-relevant information exchanged across hospital, cloud, model-provider, manufacturer, and device boundaries. It asks that each consequential exchange preserve identity, permitted purpose, scope, clinical meaning, provenance, AI-SBOM configuration, integrity, privacy, retention, and onward-use limits, noting encryption alone is insufficient.
positions.supporting_text: FDA should recognize that safety-relevant information may cross hospital, cloud, model-provider, manufacturer, and device boundaries. Each consequential exchange should preserve sender and recipient identity, permitted purpose, patient or device scope, schema and clinical meaning, source and transformation provenance, applicable AI-SBOM configuration, integrity and freshness, privacy classification, retention, and onward-use restrictions. Transport encryption is necessary but does not establish that the sender was authorized, the information was semantically valid, or the recipient may use it for the proposed purpose.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that FDA could effectively mandate a specific privacy-preserving technology, when multiple mechanisms (local or federated evaluation, aggregation, pseudonymization, confidential computing, secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, selective disclosure, or protected case-level access) may satisfy the same evidentiary needs depending on the use case.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should define the required properties of the evidence itself and remain technology-neutral, treating advanced cryptography as an optional implementation mechanism rather than a precondition for compliance.
positions.public_summary: Commenter asks FDA to define required properties of evaluation evidence rather than prescribe a particular privacy technology, noting that local or federated evaluation, pseudonymization, cryptographic methods, differential privacy, or protected case-level access may each suffice; advanced cryptography should be optional, not required.
positions.supporting_text: FDA should specify the required evidence properties rather than prescribe one privacy technology. Depending on the use case, sponsors may use local or federated evaluation, aggregation, pseudonymization, confidential computing, secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, differential privacy, selective disclosure, or protected case-level access. Advanced cryptography should be treated as an optional implementation mechanism, not a prerequisite for compliance.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that seemingly minor or low-level changes (e.g., to tool selection, retrieved evidence, interaction state, or guardrail behavior) can be clinically material, so classifying changes by component type would miss safety-relevant impacts.
positions.requested_fda_action: Base change control on impact pathways and verified configuration lineage: have sponsors classify changes by affected competency, hazard, control, population, and workflow, tie the premarket competency baseline to a minimum re-evaluation set per impact pathway, and allow PCCPs to specify change envelopes, trigger categories, affected evidence modules, acceptance thresholds, rollout constraints, and rollback criteria without prespecifying future model weights.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's premarket-baseline and PCCP change-control direction but asks that changes be classified by impact pathway—affected competency, hazard, control, population, workflow—rather than component type, with verified configuration lineage and PCCP-defined change envelopes, thresholds, rollout constraints, and rollback criteria.
positions.supporting_text:
Questions 22–24. Change control should be based on impact pathways and verified configuration lineage.
A change can be low-level yet clinically material because it alters tool selection, retrieved evidence, interaction state, or guardrail behavior. Sponsors should classify changes by affected competency, hazard, control, population, and workflow—not solely by component type. The premarket competency baseline should identify the minimum re-evaluation set for each plausible impact pathway.
  PCCPs may define change envelopes, trigger categories, affected evidence modules, acceptance thresholds, rollout constraints, and rollback criteria even when exact future model weights cannot be specified.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Changes to third-party foundation models can occur without the device manufacturer's knowledge or consent, and manufacturers may lack contractual leverage, version stability, or rollback capability to detect and respond to such changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect manufacturers to secure contractual terms (advance notice, version pinning or controlled rollout, change documentation, retained access to prior versions, incident cooperation, safety-relevant audit information), implement technical detection controls (signed artifacts, version attestation, behavioral canaries, reproducible test suites, deployment manifests), and maintain an exit strategy when a provider cannot support required transparency, stability, or rollback.
positions.public_summary: On FDA's question about third-party model changes, the commenter lists mechanisms: contractual advance notice, version pinning or controlled rollout, change documentation, retained prior-version access, incident cooperation and audit rights; technical detection via signed artifacts, attestation, behavioral canaries and reproducible tests; plus a provider exit strategy.
positions.supporting_text:
Third-party model contracts should require advance notice where feasible, version pinning or controlled rollout, change documentation, continued access to the prior version for investigation/rollback, incident cooperation, and safety-relevant audit information.
  Technical controls should detect unannounced changes through signed artifacts, version attestation, behavioral canaries, reproducible test suites, and deployment manifests.
  A manufacturer should maintain an exit strategy when a foundation-model provider cannot support required transparency, stability, or rollback.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A voluntary Foundation Model Master File is only useful to device sponsors if its contents are kept current, versioned, and contractually referenced, and if it discloses enough safety-relevant detail (limitations, failure modes, subgroup results, update and deprecation terms) for sponsors to manage risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish the voluntary Foundation Model MAF with a defined content set covering model identity and lineage, supported uses, architecture, training-data provenance, healthcare-relevant and subgroup evaluations, limitations and failure modes, safety constraints, cybersecurity practices, update/notification commitments, deprecation and rollback terms, and audit signals, while permitting tiered disclosure that protects proprietary information.
positions.public_summary: Supports a voluntary Foundation Model Master File if contents are versioned, updateable, and contractually referenced. Specifies content including lineage, training-data provenance, healthcare and subgroup evaluations, failure modes, cybersecurity, update notification, and rollback terms, and asks FDA to allow tiered disclosure protecting proprietary details.
positions.supporting_text:
Question 25. A voluntary Foundation Model Master File can be useful if its contents are versioned, updateable, and contractually referenced.
A Foundation Model MAF should include model identity and lineage; intended supported uses; architecture summary; training-data provenance at an appropriate level; healthcare-relevant evaluations; subgroup results; known limitations and failure modes; safety constraints; cybersecurity practices; update policy and notification commitments; deprecation and rollback terms; and available audit signals. FDA should permit tiered disclosure so proprietary details can remain protected while sponsors receive the safety information necessary to manage risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A voluntary Foundation Model MAF alone would not document the full composed medical-device function; the commenter is concerned that model-level disclosures must be integrated into a sponsor-maintained inventory covering fine-tunes, prompts, retrieval sources, tools, agents, orchestration, runtime dependencies, safety policies, identity/authority relationships, competency evidence, and change lineage.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat the MAF as an input to, not a substitute for, a sponsor-maintained AI-SBOM that supplements existing design, product-BOM, hardware, software, supplier, and section 524B cybersecurity SBOM records, referencing existing and protected supplier records by stable identifiers rather than duplicating or publicly disclosing them, provided the sponsor can obtain timely safety-relevant information.
positions.public_summary: Supports Foundation Model MAFs only as an input to a broader, sponsor-maintained AI-SBOM covering models, fine-tunes, prompts, retrieval, tools, agents, orchestration, authority relationships, and change lineage, integrated with existing design, supplier, and 524B cybersecurity records via stable identifiers, allowing referenced protected supplier records.
positions.supporting_text: The MAF should feed, but not replace, a sponsor-maintained AI-SBOM for the complete medical-device function. The AI-SBOM should supplement applicable existing design, product-BOM, hardware, software, supplier, and section 524B cybersecurity-SBOM records. It should identify the model and fine-tunes; prompts and configuration; retrieval sources and embedding components; tools, sensors, actuators, and external services; agents, memory, and orchestration; runtime and infrastructure dependencies; safety policies; identity and authority relationships; competency evidence; and applicable change lineage. Existing component records should be referenced by stable identifiers rather than copied. Protected supplier records may be referenced rather than publicly disclosed, provided the sponsor can obtain timely safety-relevant information.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Evaluating agentic GenAI devices only on output quality is insufficient because risk arises from the scope of authority, multi-step action sequences, persistent state, and downstream consequences, including manipulation through retrieved content and tool outputs.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should require a declared authority envelope specifying permitted tools, data, targets, actions, clinical contexts, and autonomy levels, and set acceptance criteria covering planning and tool use plus refusal, interruption, recovery, authorization, state integrity, and resistance to indirect prompt injection.
positions.public_summary: Comment on agentic devices argues evaluation must extend beyond output quality. It asks FDA to require a declared authority envelope (tools, data, targets, actions, contexts, autonomy levels) and acceptance criteria covering refusal, interruption, recovery, authorization, state integrity, and resistance to indirect prompt injection.
positions.supporting_text:
Question 26. Agentic devices require evaluation of authority, sequences, state, and consequences—not only output quality.
For an agentic device, FDA should require a declared authority envelope identifying permitted tools, data, targets, actions, clinical contexts, and autonomy levels. Acceptance criteria should include correct planning and tool use, but also refusal, interruption, recovery, authorization, state integrity, and resistance to indirect prompt injection through retrieved content and tool outputs.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic systems can take autonomous multi-step actions in which authority is poorly bounded and failures compound across tools, memory, and services; testing focused on single outputs would miss these failure modes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect agentic devices to implement verifiable identity and defined authority for every agent, model, tool, dataset, user, and approving human; authenticated checkpoints for high-consequence or irreversible actions absent a justified evaluated autonomous pathway; model-independent tool controls (least privilege, parameter constraints, rate limits, transaction boundaries); immediate containment and safe-state reversion; and testing of compounding errors, confused-deputy behavior, stale or poisoned memory, tool substitution, partial failure, race conditions, and retry behavior.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses agentic devices with concrete controls beyond FDA's general framing: verifiable identity and bounded authority for agents, tools and approvers; authenticated checkpoints for high-consequence or irreversible actions absent an evaluated autonomous pathway; model-independent tool limits; containment and safe-state reversion; and testing of compounding and
positions.supporting_text:
Every agent, model, tool, service, dataset, policy, user, and approving human should have a verifiable identity and defined authority.
  High-consequence or irreversible actions should require an explicit, authenticated checkpoint unless a justified autonomous pathway has been evaluated.
  Tools should enforce least privilege, parameter constraints, rate limits, and transaction boundaries independently of the model.
  The system should support immediate containment: revoke authority, isolate components, pause actions, preserve evidence, and revert to a safe state.
  Testing should cover multi-step compounding errors, confused-deputy behavior, stale or poisoned memory, tool substitution, partial failure, race conditions, and repeated retry behavior.

positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt or accommodate a technology-neutral 'auditable lifecycle assurance case': a structured, versioned argument linking intended-use claims to hazards, risk controls, competency requirements, test assets, results, clinical confirmation, authorized configuration, deployment evidence, postmarket signals, and change decisions.
positions.public_summary: Proposes, as a supplement to FDA's competency-based approach, a technology-neutral 'auditable lifecycle assurance case': a structured, versioned argument linking intended-use claims to hazards, controls, competency requirements, test assets, clinical confirmation, authorized configuration, deployment evidence, postmarket signals, and change decisions.
positions.supporting_text:
Appendix A - Auditable Lifecycle Assurance Case
The proposed auditable lifecycle assurance framework is a technology-neutral evidence architecture for GenAI-enabled medical devices. Its purpose is to make safety claims continuously attributable to the system that was actually evaluated and deployed.
A.1 Core assurance object
The assurance case
A structured, versioned argument linking an intended-use claim to hazards, risk controls, competency requirements, test assets, results, clinical confirmation, authorized configuration, deployment evidence, postmarket signals, and change decisions.

positions.supporting_text:
A.3 AI System Bill of Materials (AI-SBOM)
The AI-SBOM is a supplemental, versioned description of the behavior-shaping AI system configuration. It should be linked to applicable existing design, product-BOM, supplier, and cybersecurity-SBOM records. It must not replace those records or become a second, conflicting inventory. positions.requested_fda_action: Define layered content for foundation model disclosure files covering model, data/knowledge, configuration, tool and agent, evidence and change, and data-governance elements, including supplier notices, impact analyses, deployment manifests, rollback state, and accountable data custodians.

positions.supporting_text:
Model layer: foundation model, weights or service version, fine-tunes, adapters, quantization, safety models, and integrity identifiers.
  Data and knowledge layer: training/evaluation provenance at an appropriate level, retrieval indexes, clinical sources, embedding models, freshness, population coverage, and known limitations.
  Configuration layer: system prompts, templates, sampling parameters, context limits, policies, guardrails, and user-interface behavior.
  Tool and agent layer: tools, external APIs, sensors, actuators, agents, memory, orchestration, roles, permissions, delegation, and approval checkpoints.
  Evidence and change layer: intended-use claims, competency tests, thresholds, results, monitoring requirements, supplier notices, impact analyses, deployment manifests, and rollback state.
  Data-governance layer: data classes; collection and inference purposes; storage locations; access policy; retention and deletion rules; correction propagation; training or secondary-use status; transfer restrictions; and accountable data owners or custodians.

positions.stakeholder_concern: For medical-device functions distributed across systems and organizations, clinical meaning, authority, and provenance can be lost when information crosses boundaries, and machine-initiated control commands carry greater consequence than observations. The commenter treats these exchange-layer details as part of the device assurance case.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect assurance cases to include a technology-neutral 'assurance exchange envelope' documenting authenticated sender/recipient and human or machine authority, permitted purpose and scope limits, data schema/uncertainty/timestamp metadata, provenance including AI-SBOM configuration and integrity proofs, and resulting actions or escalations. Apply stronger requirements to control commands: patient-context binding, replay/freshness protection, least privilege, independent parameter constraints, device-state checks, required human approval, acknowledgment, and safe timeout or rollback.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that assurance cases for distributed device functions specify a technology-neutral exchange envelope documenting sender, human or machine authority, permitted purpose, data meaning, provenance and AI-SBOM configuration, with stricter safeguards for control commands, including human approval, least privilege, and safe rollback.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter appears concerned that evaluation limited to premarket benchmarking and clinical confirmation does not cover the full lifecycle, including frozen/attested system configuration and supplier dependencies, defined authority envelopes and prohibited transitions, verified deployment conditions, runtime policy enforcement, signal triage, and safe retirement.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a structured set of lifecycle gates (scope, configuration, competency, deployment, runtime, signal, change, retirement) in which prespecified tests and thresholds, adversarial testing, and clinical confirmation sit alongside configuration attestation, monitoring, rollback, and impact-classified change evidence deltas with staged rollout.
positions.public_summary: Proposes extending FDA's competency-based and change-control approach into eight lifecycle gates: scope and authority envelope, frozen and attested configuration with supplier dependencies, prespecified benchmarking and clinical confirmation, deployment verification, runtime policy enforcement, signal triage, impact-classified change evidence with staged rollout, and safe retirement.
positions.supporting_text:
A.5 Lifecycle gates
1. Scope gate: Define intended use, users, environments, authority envelope, prohibited transitions, and risk profile.
2. Configuration gate: Freeze and attest the complete evaluated system configuration and supplier dependencies.
3. Competency gate: Prespecify tests and thresholds; execute benchmarking, adversarial testing, and clinical confirmation.
4. Deployment gate: Verify the deployed configuration, policies, monitoring, interruption, rollback, and operator readiness.
5. Runtime gate: Continuously enforce authorization and safety policies; capture proportionate causal evidence.
6. Signal gate: Triage drift, failures, complaints, incidents, subgroup changes, and cybersecurity findings.
7. Change gate: Classify impact, select evidence delta, approve, stage rollout, verify, and preserve rollback.
8. Retirement gate: Revoke identities and authority, preserve required records, migrate safely, and communicate residual risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Postmarket monitoring and auditability need a defined evidence record, but auditability should not depend on indiscriminate retention of protected health information or full prompts; safety-relevant metadata can be separated from encrypted or access-controlled content.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that risk tiering alone does not specify how much and what kind of evidence is expected, particularly as functions move from non-directive information toward action-taking and autonomous operation.

Presented as illustrative, aligned to existing authorities, not a new classification scheme.

positions.supporting_text:
Appendix B — Least-Burdensome Implementation
The auditable lifecycle assurance framework can be implemented incrementally and should reuse evidence already produced under design controls, risk management, cybersecurity, software lifecycle, clinical evaluation, postmarket surveillance, CAPA, supplier management, and PCCP processes. FDA should specify required relationships and outcomes, not a proprietary data model or platform.
  Permit modular evidence updates so an unchanged clinical component does not require full resubmission when an unrelated infrastructure component changes.
  Allow cryptographic hashes, signed manifests, and protected references where retaining raw clinical content would create privacy or security risk.
  Encourage machine-readable evidence packages while retaining human-readable summaries and regulator access to underlying evidence.
  Use common event and provenance concepts to reduce duplicative logs across quality, cybersecurity, and AI governance systems.

positions.supporting_text:
CDRH’s discussion paper correctly recognizes that GenAI-enabled devices challenge static, output-centric evaluation. Competency assessment is a strong foundation. To remain reliable across deployment, modification, third-party model changes, and autonomous action, that foundation should be connected to a continuously auditable assurance case.
VivaSecuris recommends that FDA explore an auditable lifecycle assurance framework through public workshops and a voluntary pilot. The pilot should include supplemental AI-SBOM concepts linked to applicable existing design, product-BOM, supplier, and cybersecurity-SBOM records; deterministic governance of probabilistic behavior; privacy-preserving postmarket observability; and safe assurance exchange across manufacturers, healthcare institutions, model providers, and connected devices.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts the consequence axis but argues the device activity axis is insufficient because both axes characterize only the output and resulting clinical harm, not the system architecture and operating environment that determine whether an incorrect, degraded, or manipulated output actually reaches the patient.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework beyond output type and consequence to represent architectural and deployment-environment factors that govern whether erroneous, degraded, or manipulated outputs propagate to patients.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's consequence axis as well-constructed but considers the device activity axis insufficient. Argues both axes describe only outputs and resulting clinical harm, omitting the system architecture and operating environment that determine whether incorrect, degraded, or manipulated outputs reach patients.
positions.supporting_text:
The consequence axis is appropriate and well-constructed. The device activity axis, as currently framed, is insufficient.

Both axes describe the output of a GenAI-enabled software function and the clinical harm that follows from relying on it. Neither axis describes the architecture and operating environment that determine whether an incorrect, degraded, or manipulated output reaches the patient in the first place.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the two-axis framework grades only the content of an output and not the architecture or containment of the system producing it; because GenAI-enabled functions, especially agentic ones that call tools, retrieve from external sources, and interoperate with other software, are not bounded at release as deterministic SaMD was, the framework will systematically underestimate risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Incorporate system architecture and containment (tool use, external retrieval, interoperability) as an explicit risk determinant in the risk framework, rather than assessing only the device activity and the consequence of an incorrect output.
positions.public_summary: Argues FDA's two-axis framework is incomplete because it grades output content but not system architecture or containment. Notes that agentic functions using tools, external retrieval, and software interoperation are not bounded at release, and contends the framework would systematically underestimate their risk.
positions.supporting_text: For deterministic Software as a Medical Device, that omission was tolerable, because functionality was bounded at release. For GenAI-enabled functions — particularly agentic ones that call tools, retrieve from external sources, and interoperate with other software — the architecture is itself a risk determinant. A framework that grades only what the function says, and not the containment of the system that says it, will systematically underestimate risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates the two-axis framing does not capture all risk-relevant dimensions, particularly reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, output traceability, the intended user's interpretive capacity, and how tightly a GenAI function is architecturally connected to other systems and tools.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework to include these additional dimensions, including architectural connectedness and agentic coupling assessed through boundary definition on a shared-artifact test, East-West controls, a tool and action inventory with least privilege, and detection and containment evidence.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the two-axis risk framework but recommends adding dimensions: reversibility, downstream safeguards, time pressure, output traceability, user interpretive capacity, and architectural connectedness/agentic coupling—assessed via boundary definition, East-West controls, least-privilege tool and action inventories, and detection and containment evidence.
positions.supporting_text:
Recommendation: Dimensions to consider:
• Reversibility of the resulting action
• Availability and effectiveness of downstream safeguards
• Time pressure of the deployment setting
• Traceability of the output to primary source material
• Interpretive capacity of the intended user
• Architectural connectedness and agentic coupling (Boundary definition on a shared-artifact test, East-West controls, Tool and action inventory with least privilege, Detection and containment evidence)

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter points to two architectural failures in an agent evaluation environment: mislabeling an environment as 'isolated' when a shared cache/artifact store bridged the boundary, and leaving lateral (East-West) agent-to-agent traffic unsegmented and unmonitored, which allowed agents to collaborate, share capability, and persist through remediation. The concern is proportionality: if a well-resourced organization made these basic boundary-definition and segmentation errors, less-resourced digital health firms, health system innovation groups, and single-product startups are likely to fare worse, and to do so inside clinical workflows.
positions.requested_fda_action: The passage implies CDRH should treat containment-boundary definition and segmentation/monitoring of agent-to-agent (East-West) traffic as safety-relevant considerations for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, and should account for the limited infrastructure capability of less-resourced developers deploying such agents in clinical settings. No specific regulatory mechanism is stated in the passage.
positions.public_summary: Commenter highlights two architectural failures in agent containment: environments called 'isolated' while sharing a cache reachable from both sides of a boundary, and unsegmented, unmonitored agent-to-agent traffic enabling collaboration and persistence through remediation. Argues less-resourced developers will fare worse inside clinical workflows.
positions.supporting_text:
Two foundational failures are visible, and both are architectural rather than novel:

An incorrect definition of "connected." The environment was documented as isolated because it had no direct internet route. It nonetheless shared a cached artifact intermediary with the internet. A shared artifact, file store, registry, or cache that is reachable from both sides of a boundary is a connection. Enterprise Architecture has held this position for decades; the evaluation environment's design did not.

Unmanaged East-West traffic. Lateral, peer-to-peer traffic between agent workloads was neither segmented nor monitored, which permitted independent agents to collaborate, share capability, and persist through remediation.

The relevance to CDRH is proportionality. If an organization with this concentration of technical talent and capital defeated its own containment boundary through basic segmentation and boundary-definition errors, then less-resourced innovators — small digital health firms, health system innovation groups, single-product startups — will not do better. They will do considerably worse, and they will do it inside clinical workflows.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that introducing a new "non-directive" versus "action-directing" taxonomy is difficult to delineate and would be contested at the margins for years, increasing the risk that manufacturers misread regulatory intent.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should build on its existing benefit-risk vocabulary (the Factors to Consider guidance for PMA and De Novo classifications) rather than create new terminology, and treat directiveness not as a new category but as a modifier of an existing factor — the probability of a harmful event.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts assessing directiveness as relevant to risk but opposes a new taxonomy, arguing new terms would be contested and could cause manufacturers to misread regulatory intent. Recommends treating directiveness as a modifier of the existing benefit-risk factor of probability of harm.
positions.supporting_text:
Response 1: Build on existing terminology rather than creating a new vocabulary
Defining the line between "non-directive" and "action-directing" is genuinely difficult, and a new taxonomy will be litigated at the margins for years. CDRH already has settled vocabulary in Factors to Consider When Making Benefit-Risk Determinations in Medical Device Premarket Approval and De Novo Classifications (FDA). Novel terminology increases the risk that manufacturers misread regulatory intent; reusing established terms reinforces it.

Recommendation 1: do not treat directiveness as a new category, Treat it as a modifier of an existing factor — the probability of a harmful event.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that fixed Instructions for Use delivered once assume a static user, and that categorical proxies such as patient versus HCP or generalist versus specialist are too coarse to capture actual variation in user knowledge, since some patients become expert in their condition while others defer entirely.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit, and at higher risk levels require, affirmation of user knowledge and competency as a gating precondition to enabling a GenAI function, with depth of affirmation scaled to risk (mere acknowledgment for low-consequence informational outputs; confirmed understanding of output ranges, failure modes, and escalation conditions for functions such as insulin titration), plus re-affirmation at defined intervals or after updates.
positions.public_summary: Argues that one-time Instructions for Use and categorical patient/HCP or generalist/specialist labels are too coarse to reflect actual user knowledge. Recommends FDA permit, and at higher risk levels require, risk-scaled affirmation of user competency to unlock functions, with periodic or post-update re-affirmation.
positions.supporting_text:
The current model — a fixed Instructions for Use, delivered once, with no affirmation of competency — assumes a static user. Categorical proxies such as patient versus HCP, or generalist versus specialist, are coarse and do not reflect how people actually engage with their care. Some patients become deeply expert in their own condition; others defer entirely to the medical establishment. A single label cannot distinguish them.
Recommendation 2: permit and, at higher risk levels, require affirmation of user knowledge and competency as a gating precondition to enabling the function, with the depth of affirmation scaled to the device's risk level. A low-consequence informational function may need only acknowledgment. A function directing insulin titration should confirm that the specific user understands the correct output range, the failure modes, and the conditions requiring escalation, before that capability unlocks — and should re-affirm on a defined interval or when the function is updated.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to FDA framing that treats patients as the class lacking domain knowledge and treats professional credentials as a proxy for the capability to detect erroneous outputs; competence varies within any credentialed population, so lowering assessed risk for HCP-facing functions assumes an error-detection ability the patient safety literature does not support.
positions.requested_fda_action: Stop using credential status (patient vs. HCP, or generalist vs. specialist) as the basis for shifting risk, and instead base risk assessment on demonstrated error-detection capability rather than an assumed capability inferred from credentials.
positions.public_summary: Objects to FDA's framing that patients lack domain knowledge while credentialed clinicians can independently evaluate outputs. Argues competence varies within credentialed groups and that reducing assessed risk for HCP-facing functions based on credentials alone assumes error-detection ability unsupported by patient safety evidence.
positions.supporting_text:
The question is framed around users "who lack the domain knowledge to independently evaluate an output," with patients as the implied class. We object to that framing as both inaccurate and counterproductive.
The framing treats a credential as a proxy for a capability. It is not. Competence within any credentialed population is a distribution, not a constant... A framework that shifts risk downward for HCP-facing functions on the strength of the credential alone assumes an error-detection capability that the patient safety literature does not support.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to a regulatory framing that presumes patients lack the knowledge to evaluate clinical outputs, citing evidence that patient activation, patient–professional partnership, and shared decision-making improve self-management, knowledge, decisional conflict, and satisfaction, with activation contributing most for people with lower numeracy and health literacy. It also warns that such a hierarchical model reinforces deference dynamics that patient safety efforts have worked to dismantle.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should not treat patient-facing GenAI outputs as inherently higher risk on the premise that patient knowledge is absent, and should ground any risk assessment for patient-facing functions in the evidence on patient activation and shared decision-making.
positions.public_summary: Comment challenges any framework presuming patients cannot evaluate clinical information, citing evidence that patient activation and shared decision-making improve knowledge and self-management, especially for lower-literacy patients, while acknowledging heterogeneous effects on hard clinical endpoints; warns hierarchical assumptions reinforce deference dynamics.
positions.supporting_text:
Patient activation — the knowledge, skills, and confidence to engage in one's own care — is associated with better outcomes, and contributes more for people with lower numeracy and health literacy than for those with higher skills (CDC). Patient–professional partnership improves self-management, which in turn improves health-related quality of life (International Journal of Nursing Studies), and shared decision-making is consistently associated with improved patient knowledge, reduced decisional conflict, and higher satisfaction (Frontiers in Public Health).
We note candidly that effects on hard clinical endpoints are heterogeneous across the shared decision-making literature (Medical Decision Making). The defensible claim is not that engagement is uniformly curative. It is that a hierarchical model which treats patient knowledge as absent is contradicted by the evidence and reinforces the same deference dynamics that patient safety programs have spent twenty-five years trying to dismantle.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter objects to assuming that patients lack and HCPs possess relevant domain knowledge, and to treating credential labels (patient vs. HCP, generalist vs. specialist) as proxies for the user competency that actually drives risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Replace categorical user classification with demonstrated, device-specific competency affirmation scaled to risk; require evaluation across the real distribution of user knowledge; grant mitigation credit for traceability, stated uncertainty, and named escalation triggers, but not for disclaimers.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts risk-scaled user considerations but rejects FDA's categorical patient/HCP and generalist/specialist distinctions, urging device-specific competency affirmation, evaluation across the real distribution of user knowledge, and mitigation credit for traceability, stated uncertainty, and escalation triggers rather than disclaimers.
positions.supporting_text: Remove the presumption that patients lack domain knowledge and HCPs possess it. Replace categorical user classification with demonstrated, device-specific competency affirmation scaled to risk. Grant mitigation credit for traceability, stated uncertainty, and named escalation triggers, and none for disclaimers. Require evaluation across the real distribution of user knowledge rather than across credential labels.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter warns that assumptions about the deployment environment can be wrong and that GenAI behavior can change, citing an OpenAI example; a device capable of migrating between non-directive and action-directing information is treated as inherently higher risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Scale oversight to the type of information provided—low oversight for low-risk information, high for high-risk—and apply a high oversight burden whenever a GenAI function can migrate in its behavior during use.
positions.public_summary: Commenter agrees risk should scale with the type of information provided, but adds that any GenAI function capable of migrating in behavior during an exchange should carry a high oversight burden, noting environmental assumptions can prove wrong.
positions.supporting_text: OpenAI demonstrated how fast this can go wrong when the assumption about the environment is wrong.  Risk should always be based on the type of information provided.  If the information is low risk, then the oversight burden is lower.  If the risk is high, the oversight burden should be high. If the GenAI can migrate, then the oversight burden should be high, as AI can change behavior.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that how under-escalation and over-escalation errors are weighted should depend on the knowledge and competency of the user receiving the output, cross-referencing the questions on directiveness and patient- versus HCP-facing outputs.
positions.requested_fda_action: Tie the weighting of escalation error directions to user knowledge and competency, consistent with the considerations raised in Questions 2 and 3.
positions.public_summary: Brief comment on escalation error trade-offs: the relative weight given to under- and over-escalation should depend on the user's knowledge and competency, cross-referencing FDA's questions on output directiveness and patient- versus clinician-facing information. No further detail provided.
positions.supporting_text: The weight should be relevant to the user knowledge and competency (See question #2 and #3)

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that GenAI device standards developed by FDA in isolation could diverge from those of other jurisdictions, increasing developer burden and limiting global interoperability.
positions.requested_fda_action: Engage with international regulatory counterparts (including the European Medicines Agency and authorities in Japan, China, Canada, and South Korea) when developing standards, and pursue harmonized approaches to GenAI regulation where feasible.
positions.public_summary: The commenter recommends that FDA draw on the experience of international regulators, including those in Europe, Japan, China, Canada, and South Korea, and pursue harmonized GenAI standards where feasible, arguing cross-jurisdictional consistency would reduce developer burden and support interoperability.
positions.supporting_text: Learning from international counterparts: FDA also learn lessons in developing standards from to international regulatory counterparts, including the European Medicines Agency, Japan, China, Canada, South Korea, and others to promote harmonized approaches to GenAI regulation where feasible. Consistency across jurisdictions will reduce developer burden, improve patient safety, and support global interoperability.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that GenAI-enabled devices may be designed and monitored without direct patient input, leading to systems that do not reflect real-world patient needs, fail to support autonomy, and rest on unfounded assumptions about patient capabilities and how patients respond to information.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should encourage device developers to involve patients directly in AI development, governance, monitoring, and evaluation, so that patient-centered design and patient engagement are built into the lifecycle of GenAI-enabled devices.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA encourage developers to involve patients directly in GenAI device development, governance, monitoring, and evaluation, arguing patient engagement helps devices reflect real-world needs, support autonomy, and avoid unfounded assumptions about patient capabilities and responses to information.
positions.supporting_text: Emphasize patient-engagement and patient-centered design: FDA should encourage developers of GenAI‑enabled devices to incorporate patients directly into AI development, governance, monitoring, and evaluation. Patient engagement is essential for ensuring that GenAI systems reflect real‑world needs, support autonomy, and avoid assumptions about patient capabilities and likely responses to information.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that GenAI risks are evolving and uncertain, so oversight cannot rest on technical evaluation alone and requires organizational governance within developer organizations. It also sees a need for ethics competency inside FDA's own review process.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should emphasize strong internal governance structures at developing organizations and encourage developers to obtain legal, ethical, and clinical consultation, especially for high-risk or patient-facing functions. FDA should also staff its review processes with bioethics, digital ethics, and responsible AI expertise where appropriate.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA emphasize strong internal governance at developer organizations, encouraging legal, ethical, and clinical consultation for high-risk or patient-facing GenAI functions, and that FDA add bioethics, digital ethics, and responsible AI expertise to its own review processes.
positions.supporting_text: Governance: Given the evolving and uncertain nature of GenAI risks, FDA should emphasize the importance of strong governance structures within developing organizations. Developers should be encouraged to seek legal, ethical, and clinical consultation when appropriate, particularly for high‑risk or patient‑facing functions. In addition, FDA should incorporate ethics expertise within its own review processes when appropriate, including staff trained in bioethics, digital ethics, and responsible AI.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that upstream conditions in the GenAI supply chain affect downstream device risk, so oversight limited to the device manufacturer's submission is insufficient. Using a food safety analogy, it contends that safety must be addressed across the entire GenAI lifecycle, from model developer to end user.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should adopt a 'developer-to-user' lifecycle perspective for GenAI analogous to the 'farm-to-fork' approach in foods, and work collaboratively with other federal agencies, academia, and the private sector to foster governance, safety, and effectiveness for GenAI systems and components used or adapted in regulated devices.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges FDA to look beyond device-level review of foundation models and adopt a "developer-to-user" lifecycle approach, analogous to farm-to-fork food safety, arguing upstream GenAI components affect downstream risk and require collaboration with other agencies, academia, and industry.
positions.supporting_text: A useful analogy is food safety: FDA does not regulate how lettuce is grown, but FDA and the US Department of Agriculture and others regulate safety across the entire farm‑to‑fork supply chain because upstream conditions affect downstream risk. Similarly, if GenAI systems and components will be used or adapted for FDA‑regulated software and devices, FDA will need to work directly and collaboratively with other federal agencies, academia, and the private sector to foster governance, safety, and effectiveness across the GenAI lifecycle. FDA should adopt a developer-to-user perspective for GenAI that parallels the farm-to-fork approach for foods.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the two-axis framework as a reasonable starting point but argues it captures only consequence and activity, omitting upstream model risks (hallucinations, bias, contaminated or incorrect training data, opaque provenance, adversarial prompts, security vulnerabilities) and dynamic lifecycle risks (drift, degradation, missed updates, shifting use contexts), and that it is utilitarian rather than reflecting governance, ethical, privacy, confidentiality, and transparency duties.
positions.requested_fda_action: Replace the two-axis model with a three-layer risk framework: Layer 1 functional (consequence and activity, as currently proposed), Layer 2 model risks (hallucination, bias, data contamination, adversarial prompts, hacking and manipulation), and Layer 3 lifecycle risks (drift, degradation, update needs, stability).
positions.public_summary: Commenter calls FDA's two-axis risk model a useful starting point but incomplete, saying it omits hallucinations, bias, contaminated training data, opaque provenance, security vulnerabilities, and dynamic lifecycle risks. Proposes a three-layer framework adding model-risk and lifecycle-risk layers to the functional axes.
positions.supporting_text:
Pages 4–6 and Discussion Question 1: Limitations of the Two‑Axis Model: The two-axis model discussed by FDA is a good starting point for discussion but does not capture such upstream risks as hallucinations, algorithmic bias and incorrect data. While these axes capture autonomy and harm severity, they do not account for upstream risks such as hallucinations, algorithmic bias, incorrect or contaminated training data, or opaque model provenance. The model is also primarily utilitarian, emphasizing consequences but not reflecting governance priorities, ethical guardrails, or healthcare duties such as privacy, confidentiality, and transparency. In addition, GenAI risks are not static. They may change as models are updated or not updated, as models drift, as data degrades, or as context and use‑cases shift. A static two‑axis model cannot capture these dynamic, lifecycle‑dependent risks, underscoring the need for a more expansive and adaptive regulatory framework.

Instead of a two-axis model, I would suggest a three-layer model:
Layer 1, Functional: Consequences (same as current graph/model) and Activity (same as current graph/model).
Layer 2, Model Risks: addresses hallucinations, biases, data contamination, poor or incorrect training data, susceptibility to adversarial prompts; and vulnerability to hacking, model manipulation, or other security threats.
Layer 3, Lifecycle Risks: model drift, degradation, need for updates, stability.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that disclaimers such as 'talk to your doctor' or 'I am not a medical professional' do not meaningfully reduce the directiveness or risk of patient-facing outputs, because patients are unlikely to reliably seek clinician input and are more likely to cross-reference the output with another AI tool.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should treat action-directing outputs as higher-risk regardless of whether disclaimers or referral statements are included.
positions.public_summary: Endorses CDRH's consideration that disclaimers do not make patient-facing outputs less directive, arguing patients are more likely to consult another AI tool than a clinician. Asks FDA to classify action-directing outputs as higher-risk regardless of accompanying disclaimer language.
positions.supporting_text: Action-taking and Action-directing functions: The paper states that “CDRH is also considering whether a patient facing informational function may not become any less directive because it includes a ‘talk to your doctor’ or an ‘I am not a medical professional’ statement in addition to the ‘action-directing’ information.” The assumption that patients will reliably seek clinician input is unrealistic. The more likely outcome is that patients will simply consult another AI model or tool to cross‑reference the first output. FDA should treat action‑directing outputs as higher‑risk regardless of disclaimers.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that risk from informational outputs depends on how outputs are worded, specified, personalized, framed, and how much underlying data is accessible, and that patient-facing and provider-facing functions warrant different output designs.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should assess informational functions using specified output modifiers—wording/tone, specificity, personalization, transparency and data access, and context/framing—differentiated for patients versus providers, with patient outputs kept plain-language and non-directive while allowing full optional patient access to underlying data, uncertainty indicators, and model limitations.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's continuum view of directiveness and adds specific output modifiers—wording/tone, specificity, personalization, transparency/data access, and framing—differentiated for patients versus clinicians. Recommends patient outputs be plain-language and non-directive, with optional full access to underlying data, uncertainty indicators, and limitations.
positions.supporting_text:
Patient‑Facing Informational Functions: Patient‑facing functions should provide clear, accessible, bottom‑line information that supports autonomy and shared decision‑making. Interfaces may be simplified, graphical, or user‑friendly, but patients should have full optional access to underlying data, uncertainty indicators, and model limitations.
Health Provider‑Facing Informational Functions
Provider functions may be more complex, detailed, and data‑rich. Clinicians may need intermediate outputs, confidence scores, model rationales, and contextual factors that would not benefit many patients. These functions support clinical judgment, diagnostic reasoning, and safe integration of GenAI outputs into care (page 8). Outputs can be more directive because they are interpreted within the clinician’s professional judgment and scope of practice.
FDA can consider the following factors when assessing patient‑facing versus provider‑facing informational functions and the potential risks associated with each.
• Wording and tone: For patients, wording should be plain-language and non-directive. For providers, wording should be technical and precise.
• Specificity: For patients, the output should be general with options and ranges. For providers, outputs should be clinically-based with detailed parameters.
• Personalization: For patents, output should be tailored but non-directive. For providers, output should support clinical judgment for specific cases.
• Transparency and data access: For patients: A simplified interface, but with full optional access to underlying data, uncertainty indicators, and model limitations to support autonomy and shared decision-making. For providers: Full access to all data
• Context and framing: For patients, Emphasis on choices, risks, benefits, alternatives, and shared decision‑making. For providers, the focus can be on clinical factors, next steps/workflows and potential comorbidities.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Patients receiving GenAI-generated clinical information may lack context to judge output reliability, but safeguards should protect them without curtailing autonomy or access. The commenter also notes patients and providers may not know when a model has changed and performance may differ.
positions.requested_fda_action: Encourage specific output-level safeguards for patient-facing functions: uncertainty indicators or ranges, shared decision-making prompts to consult a provider, reminders to recheck or update information, explicit statements that outputs are not a diagnosis, and notifications when a model has been changed, retrained, or updated.
positions.public_summary: Responding on patient-facing risks, the commenter supports FDA encouraging safeguards that preserve patient autonomy and access, and proposes specific measures: uncertainty indicators, prompts to discuss findings with a provider, recheck reminders, explicit non-diagnosis statements, and notifications when the underlying model is updated or retrained.
positions.supporting_text:
Safeguards to Mitigate Risk Without Underestimating Patient Capability
FDA could encourage safeguards that protect patients while preserving autonomy and access:
• Uncertainty indicators: Clear statements such as “These results may be uncertain” or presentation of broad ranges.
• Shared decision‑making prompts. For example: “Discuss these findings with your healthcare provider.”
• Reminders about rechecking results: Prompts indicating when information should be rechecked or updated.
• Clarification that information presented is not a diagnosis: Reinforcing that outputs are informational and do not replace clinical evaluation.
• Model update notifications: Indicators when a model has been changed, retrained, or updated, so patients and providers understand when performance may differ.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views FDA's described range of clinical confirmation approaches as strong but incomplete for GenAI-specific failure modes, including hallucination, bias across subgroups, drift after updates, setting-specific variability, and user over-reliance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the list of clinical confirmation methods to include hallucination and adversarial stress testing, bias/fairness/representativeness evaluation, pre- and post-update drift and stability analysis, testing across varied clinical settings and workflows, and human factors testing of comprehension, over-reliance, safeguards, and uncertainty indicators.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's proposed range of clinical confirmation approaches but calls it incomplete, urging FDA to add hallucination and adversarial stress testing, bias and representativeness evaluation, drift and post-update stability analysis, testing across varied clinical settings, and human factors testing of over-reliance and uncertainty communication.
