positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's focus on third-party model changes but urges FDA to expect specific safeguards — version identification, advance change notification, rollback capability, and audit logs — and to confirm that manufacturers remain accountable for device clinical behavior when upstream models change.
positions.supporting_text:
“The foundation model changed” cannot be a liability shield.

A manufacturer cannot credibly guarantee safety if the model underneath its device can change without notice. FDA should expect contractual and technical guardrails — version identification, advance change notification, rollback capability, and audit logs — so a manufacturer marketing a device built on someone else's model still owns that device's clinical behavior.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the Foundation Model MAF content areas (training-data provenance, known limitations, safety-relevant behaviors, update policies) as sound, but argues voluntary participation is insufficient because foundation-model developers have limited incentive to disclose their own weaknesses, particularly for the highest-risk systems.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the voluntary MAF concept but pair it with contractual disclosure requirements for medical-device use of foundation models and FDA authority to request additional information when necessary, so that information material to evaluating a regulated device cannot remain proprietary.
positions.public_summary: Supports the Foundation Model MAF content concept but considers voluntary disclosure inadequate for highest-risk systems, since model developers have limited incentive to reveal weaknesses. Asks FDA to add contractual disclosure requirements for medical-device use and authority to request further information.
positions.supporting_text:
Voluntary disclosure won't be enough on its own for the highest-risk systems.

A Foundation Model MAF covering training-data provenance, known limitations, safety-relevant behaviors, and update policies is a good concept — but foundation-model developers have limited incentive to volunteer their own weaknesses. Pair the voluntary MAF with contractual disclosure requirements for medical-device use, plus FDA authority to request more when necessary. A foundation model doesn't need FDA approval to exist — but once it materially shapes a regulated device's behavior, the information needed to evaluate that device cannot stay proprietary.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that agentic AI shifts the regulatory question from whether a system can recommend an action to whether it can execute a sequence of actions, and that oversight should therefore turn on the scope of action the agent is permitted to take rather than only its reasoning or output.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an explicit five-level 'Clinical Agency Ladder' (Level 0 Information, Level 1 Recommendation, Level 2 Supervised Action, Level 3 Bounded Autonomy, Level 4 Autonomous Clinical Practice) with evidence requirements that increase sharply at each level.
positions.public_summary: Supports addressing agentic devices but proposes FDA regulate by what an agent is permitted to execute, not only what it can reason about, via an explicit five-level Clinical Agency Ladder from information through autonomous practice, with sharply escalating evidence requirements per level.
positions.supporting_text:
Regulate what the agent is allowed to do — not just what it can reason about.

Agentic AI changes the question from “can it recommend an action” to “can it execute a sequence of them.” I propose an explicit Clinical Agency Ladder, with evidence requirements climbing sharply at each level:
• Level 0 — Information: generates or retrieves information.
• Level 1 — Recommendation: recommends a clinical action.
• Level 2 — Supervised Action: executes actions subject to defined human oversight.
• Level 3 — Bounded Autonomy: independently executes predefined clinical workflows within a narrow scope.
• Level 4 — Autonomous Clinical Practice: independently makes and executes clinically consequential decisions within its licensed scope.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that a static, one-time authorization does not fit GenAI-enabled devices, whose permitted scope, population, environment, and autonomy level need to be explicitly bounded and continuously verified rather than fixed at clearance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a 'Clinical AI License' framework defined by eight elements (scope, competency, population, environment, autonomy, monitoring, revalidation, accountability) and operated through nine staged phases from competency examination and clinical confirmation to supervised deployment, provisional and independent authorization, continuous monitoring, revalidation, and scope expansion or restriction.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a competency-based approach but proposes recasting it as a 'Clinical AI License' defined by eight elements—scope, competency, population, environment, autonomy, monitoring, revalidation, accountability—operated through nine staged phases, with authorization expandable, restrictable, or suspendable based on demonstrated performance. Characterized as dynamic, not lower, standard.
positions.supporting_text:
They can be integrated into one framework: a Clinical AI License, tied to eight elements.
• Scope — exactly what the system is permitted to do.
• Competency — what level of performance it has demonstrated.
• Population — which patients it has demonstrated competence for.
• Environment — where it has demonstrated competence.
• Autonomy — what level of clinical action it may perform without human intervention.
• Monitoring — how continued competence is measured.
• Revalidation — what events require renewed evaluation.
• Accountability — who is responsible for keeping the system within its licensed boundaries.
Operationally, this runs as nine stages: Development → Competency Examination → Clinical Confirmation → Supervised Clinical Deployment → Provisional Authorization → Independent Authorization → Continuous Monitoring → Revalidation → Expansion or Restriction. A system demonstrating superior performance can earn expanded scope; a system demonstrating degradation can have its scope restricted or its authorization suspended. This is not a lower regulatory standard. It is a dynamic one.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues acceptance criteria should be anchored to an explicit, quantified specialty-specific human-clinician baseline, with the level of required performance tied to whether the device operates under supervision or unsupervised, and a floor below which no clinical deployment is permitted.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt tiered numeric thresholds: provisional authorization at or above 50% of the specialty-specific human-clinician baseline with mandatory supervision, independent unsupervised authorization at or above 100% of that baseline, and no clinical deployment below 50%. The commenter presents the threshold as falsifiable and open to challenge.
positions.public_summary: Proposes explicit numeric acceptance criteria benchmarked to specialty-specific clinician performance: provisional, supervised authorization at 50% or more of that baseline; unsupervised authorization at 100% or more; no clinical deployment below 50%. Offers the threshold as deliberately falsifiable and open to challenge.
positions.supporting_text:
A concrete threshold, stated plainly: Provisional Authorization should require performance at or above 50% of the specialty-specific human-clinician baseline, under mandatory supervision. Independent Authorization should require performance at or above 100% of that baseline, unsupervised. Below 50%, a model does not deploy in any clinical capacity.

This number is deliberately falsifiable and open to challenge — that is the point.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a regulatory framework could treat current clinical workflow as a permanent ceiling rather than a floor, making a generative AI system that outperforms the human standard of care harder to deploy than the less effective care it would replace.
positions.requested_fda_action: Anchor the framework in a principle that regulatory requirements not impose greater deployment barriers on a GenAI system than on the less effective standard of care it is measured against, with the test being better outcomes plus reasonable assurance of safety.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges FDA to adopt an anchoring principle: where a generative AI system outperforms the human standard of care it is compared against, regulatory requirements should not make it harder to deploy than existing care. Current workflow should be a floor, not a ceiling.
positions.supporting_text:
One principle should anchor this entire rulemaking: if a generative AI system produces better outcomes than the human standard of care it is measured against, the regulatory framework must not make that safer technology harder to deploy than the less effective one it replaces.

Healthcare already carries enormous institutional, financial, and legal inertia. A regulatory framework that quietly treats today's clinical workflow as a permanent ceiling on tomorrow's patient outcomes — rather than a floor to be exceeded — will have failed the only test that should matter: better outcomes with reasonable assurance of safety.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that risk should be organized around the degree of clinical agency a function exercises rather than around the underlying device or model architecture. The passage is a fragment and does not elaborate further.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make clinical agency the central axis of the risk framework, rather than device architecture.
positions.public_summary: In a brief fragment, the commenter urges FDA to organize its risk framework around a function's clinical agency rather than its device or model architecture. No further detail or supporting rationale appears in the passage.
positions.supporting_text: and treat clinical agency, not device architecture, as the central axis of risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A federal licensing-style framework for autonomous clinical AI collides with state regulation of the practice of medicine, an objection the commenter notes has been raised publicly (Federation of State Medical Boards) and acted on by at least one state board.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should state, before autonomous systems are deployed, which resolution it intends: either confining federal authority to the narrow question of whether a system may act autonomously at all (leaving human clinicians' decisions to state law), or having state boards accommodate the federal authorization as they do DEA registration.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses autonomous GenAI devices, arguing a federal authorization to act autonomously conflicts with state practice-of-medicine regulation. Asks FDA to declare in advance whether its authority is limited to permitting autonomy alone or whether state boards should accommodate it, as with DEA registration.
positions.supporting_text:
This framework does not resolve one live objection, and should not pretend to: the Federation of State Medical Boards has publicly stated that AI is not ready to be licensed like a physician, and states — not FDA — traditionally regulate the practice of medicine.

A federal Clinical AI License, as proposed here, needs one of two resolutions to survive that objection. Either FDA authority is limited to a narrow, explicit question — whether a system may act autonomously at all — leaving every diagnosis and treatment decision by a human clinician untouched by this framework and by state practice-of-medicine law; or state medical boards reconcile to it the way they already reconcile to DEA registration and federal prescribing authority alongside their own licensure. FDA should take a position on which path it intends before an autonomous system is deployed and a state board intervenes — as one already has.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that frameworks stated only in the abstract cannot be acted upon, and that authorization decisions need concrete, testable performance thresholds benchmarked to specialty-specific human clinician performance and tied to the level of human supervision required.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt tiered numeric acceptance criteria referenced to a specialty-specific human-clinician baseline: performance at or above 50% of that baseline for authorization under mandatory supervision, at or above 100% for unsupervised independent authorization, and no clinical deployment below 50%; treat the specific figures as falsifiable and open to refinement by sponsors, specialty societies, and FDA.
positions.public_summary: Commenter proposes concrete, falsifiable acceptance thresholds pegged to specialty-specific clinician baselines: at or above 50% permits authorization only under mandatory supervision, at or above 100% permits unsupervised authorization, and below 50% permits no clinical deployment. Figures are offered for testing and refinement.
positions.supporting_text:
horization should require performance at or above 50% of the specialty-specific human-clinician baseline, under mandatory supervision. Independent Authorization should require performance at or above 100% of that baseline, unsupervised. Below 50%, a model does not deploy in any clinical capacity.
This number is deliberately falsifiable and open to challenge — that is the point. A specific threshold gives sponsors, specialty societies, and FDA something concrete to test, argue with, and refine, rather than a framework everyone can agree with in the abstract and no one can act on.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a risk framework that does not explicitly account for a device's capacity to take action, rather than only generate information, will under-scrutinize systems that can act.
positions.requested_fda_action: Add clinical agency — the extent to which a GenAI device can act versus only provide information — as a core dimension of the risk framework, with greater regulatory scrutiny for devices that can act.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA's risk framework explicitly include clinical agency as a core dimension, so that GenAI devices capable of taking action receive greater scrutiny than those that only generate information. Accepts the framework's direction but seeks this added dimension.
positions.supporting_text: 2. Make clinical agency a core risk dimension — an AI that can act should face more scrutiny than one that can only speak.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states, without elaboration, that a competency-based evaluation model combining device benchmarking with clinical confirmation is an appropriate foundation for evaluating GenAI-enabled devices.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt the competency-based evaluation approach of benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation as described in the discussion paper.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses FDA's proposed competency-based evaluation framework, describing benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation as the right foundation for assessing GenAI-enabled devices. The brief statement offers no requested modifications, conditions, or supporting detail.
positions.supporting_text: 3. Adopt competency-based evaluation — benchmarking plus clinical confirmation is the right foundation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a binary authorization decision would exclude GenAI tools that are not yet capable of independent operation but could be used safely under clinical supervision, and that clinical authority should be tied to demonstrated competence rather than granted or withheld at once.
positions.requested_fda_action: Create a graduated autonomy pathway in which GenAI-enabled devices earn increasing clinical authority as they demonstrate competence, and establish a supervised clinical deployment mode so devices not ready for independent practice remain eligible for supervised clinical use.
positions.public_summary: Commenter proposes that FDA go beyond a binary authorization model by creating a graduated autonomy pathway, where GenAI devices gain clinical authority as competence is demonstrated, plus a supervised clinical deployment category allowing use of devices not yet ready for independent operation.
positions.supporting_text:
4. Create graduated autonomy — AI should earn increasing clinical authority through demonstrated competence.
5. Establish supervised clinical deployment — "not ready for independent practice" should not mean "not eligible for clinical use."

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a one-time premarket authorization treats a GenAI device's competence as permanently established, whereas competence should be shown on an ongoing basis after deployment.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make authorization dynamic, so that a device's competence must be continuously demonstrated through ongoing postmarket evaluation rather than assumed to persist from the initial authorization.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA treat authorization as dynamic rather than one-time, requiring GenAI device competence to be continuously demonstrated after deployment instead of assumed to persist from initial premarket review. The brief statement does not detail specific monitoring mechanisms.
positions.supporting_text: 6. Make authorization dynamic — competence should be continuously demonstrated, not permanently assumed.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that reassessment of GenAI-enabled devices after deployment may lack clearly defined, objective conditions for when revalidation is required.
positions.requested_fda_action: Establish objective triggers for revalidation, specifying that model changes, performance degradation, and new indications each require reassessment.
positions.public_summary: The commenter recommends that FDA define objective triggers for post-deployment revalidation, stating that model changes, performance degradation, and new indications should each require reassessment. The brief recommendation does not elaborate on cadence, thresholds, or evidence scaling.
positions.supporting_text: 7. Establish objective revalidation triggers — model changes, performance degradation, and new indications should all trigger reassessment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter appears concerned that review and evaluation capacity is limited, but that involving independent third parties could erode FDA's final decision-making role.
positions.requested_fda_action: Engage qualified independent third parties to expand assessment capacity within a competency-based approach, while structuring that involvement so FDA retains ultimate authority over device decisions.
positions.public_summary: The commenter endorses using independent third parties to expand evaluation capacity under the competency-based approach, but conditions this on arrangements that preserve FDA's ultimate decision-making authority rather than transferring it. The passage offers no further detail on qualifications or scope.
positions.supporting_text: 8. Use independent third parties to add capacity without diluting FDA's ultimate authority.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that distributing postmarket and ecosystem responsibilities across multiple parties could create regulatory ambiguity about who is accountable.
positions.requested_fda_action: Preserve clear manufacturer accountability when structuring shared roles across the ecosystem, ensuring shared responsibility does not translate into unclear regulatory obligations.
positions.public_summary: Brief statement endorsing retention of clear manufacturer accountability, cautioning that shared responsibility across ecosystem participants should not result in regulatory ambiguity about who is answerable. No specific mechanisms or elaboration are provided in the passage.
positions.supporting_text: 9. Maintain manufacturer accountability — shared ecosystem responsibility should never become shared regulatory ambiguity.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states that a device manufacturer cannot control aspects of an underlying foundation model that it cannot observe, implying that voluntary or limited disclosure leaves manufacturers unable to evaluate the device built on the model.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require foundation-model transparency at a level sufficient for evaluation of the device built on that model, rather than relying on disclosure that does not support such evaluation.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA require foundation-model transparency sufficient to evaluate the device built on it, arguing manufacturers cannot control what they cannot see. This goes beyond FDA's proposed voluntary Foundation Model Master File disclosure approach.
positions.supporting_text: 10.Require foundation-model transparency sufficient to evaluate the device built on it — a manufacturer cannot control what it cannot see.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that the relevant risk driver for agentic GenAI devices is the scope of clinical authority the agent is permitted to exercise, rather than the sophistication of its reasoning or model capability alone.
positions.requested_fda_action: Frame regulatory treatment of agentic AI around the clinical authority delegated to the agent (what actions it can take), not solely around its reasoning or capability characteristics.
positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA base regulation of agentic GenAI devices on the scope of clinical authority the agent is permitted to exercise, rather than on reasoning capability alone. Brief statement; no further detail on implementation is provided.
positions.supporting_text: 11.Regulate agentic AI according to clinical authority, not just reasoning capability.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that using clinician performance as the comparator could function as an upper limit on what devices are expected or permitted to achieve, rather than as a baseline reference.
positions.requested_fda_action: Set comparators and acceptance criteria so that human clinician performance serves as a reference point rather than a ceiling, and recognize or reward devices that demonstrate clinical outcomes superior to human performance.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts clinician-based comparators but asks FDA to treat human performance as a reference point rather than an upper limit, so that devices demonstrating superior clinical outcomes are recognized and rewarded. Brief statement without supporting detail or proposed methods.
positions.supporting_text: 12.Reward superior clinical outcomes — human performance should be a reference point, not a ceiling.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that conventional device software testing is not sufficient for GenAI, which produces variable outputs, interacts dynamically, operates in open-ended situations, evolves, and increasingly acts autonomously, but views FDA's proposed elements as currently disconnected.
positions.requested_fda_action: Integrate competency-based evaluation, clinical confirmation, postmarket monitoring, independent evaluation, and agentic AI oversight into a single coherent framework modeled on how clinical competence is managed: define competencies, test knowledge, supervise practice, progressively grant autonomy, license independent practice, monitor performance, and restrict practice when competence lapses.
positions.public_summary: Agrees traditional device testing is insufficient for GenAI and endorses FDA's exploration of competency-based evaluation, clinical confirmation, postmarket monitoring, independent evaluation, and agentic AI approaches, but urges FDA to unify them using the clinical model of graduated, monitored, revocable autonomy.
positions.supporting_text:
GenAI differs from conventional medical-device software because it produces variable outputs, interacts dynamically with users, operates across open-ended situations, evolves over time, and increasingly takes autonomous action. FDA is right that traditional testing methodologies may not be sufficient, and right to explore competency-based evaluation, clinical confirmation, postmarket monitoring, independent evaluation, and new approaches to agentic AI.
The next step is to connect these ideas. The United States already has a mature system for managing clinical competence under uncertainty: we establish competencies, test knowledge, supervise practice, progressively grant autonomy, license independent practice, monitor performance, and restrict practice when competence is no longer demonstrated.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees with the two-axis framework but is concerned it treats autonomy as risk-raising without symmetrically crediting mitigations; two devices with identical capability should not be treated identically when one routes every consequential output through an accountable licensed reviewer.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly in the risk framework that a named human-in-the-loop who reviews the basis for an output and signs or declines it, as well as the reversibility of the resulting action, are first-class risk-lowering variables that move a device down the effective-risk surface.
positions.public_summary: Endorses the two-axis risk framework but asks FDA to make it symmetrical: explicitly treat a named human reviewer who signs or declines consequential outputs, and the reversibility of resulting actions, as first-class risk-lowering variables rather than only sorting risk upward for autonomy.
positions.supporting_text: 1. Endorse the two-axis risk framework — and make a named human-in-the-loop and reversibility first-class, risk-lowering variables, not only a way to sort risk upward. The Activity axis rightly treats fully-autonomous action as higher-risk than an informational, non-directive output. We encourage the framework to state explicitly the mirror image: inserting a qualified human who reviews the basis for an output and signs — or declines — it before it becomes consequential is a mitigation that moves a device down the effective-risk surface, just as autonomy moves it up. Two devices with identical raw capability should not carry identical regulatory risk if one routes every consequential output through an accountable licensed reviewer and the other acts on its own. The reversibility of the action deserves the same first-class treatment. Making these explicit gives developers a concrete, safety-promoting design target rather than a penalty to be discovered late.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The paper treats HCP-facing use as lower risk because a clinician can catch incorrect outputs, but does not tie this to the statutory independent-review criterion, leaving developers to discover the clinical-decision-support boundary case by case.
positions.requested_fda_action: Explicitly connect the risk framework to the independent-review criterion in section 520(o)(1)(E), naming a design pattern in which a qualified professional can independently review the basis for a recommendation and does so before acting, as a distinct lower-risk class.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the risk framework's logic that HCP-facing use lowers risk, but asks CDRH to make the clinical-decision-support boundary explicit by tying it to the statutory independent-review criterion (section 520(o)(1)(E)), so developers can design toward a clear, predictable lower-risk category.
positions.supporting_text: 2. Make the clinical-decision-support boundary explicit in the framework. The paper notes that HCP-facing use lowers risk because a clinician can catch an incorrect output. We encourage CDRH to connect this directly to the statutory independent-review criterion at section 520(o)(1)(E): when a device is designed so that a qualified professional can independently review the basis for its recommendation, and does so before acting, it occupies a distinct, lower-risk class. Naming that "name-the-human" design pattern in the framework would let developers build toward a clear line, rather than discovering it case by case, and would reward exactly the architecture the paper's safety logic favors.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter cautions, citing Vaccaro et al. (2024), that adding a human reviewer to an already-strong model does not reliably improve task accuracy and can sometimes reduce it, so oversight should not be treated as a performance safeguard; the human's role is ownership and answerability for consequences, which a benchmark score cannot confer.
positions.requested_fda_action: Keep the competency-based framework but benchmark the model alone on its own performance, while requiring clinical confirmation to measure the human-AI team as actually deployed, and state explicitly that the human's function is accountability rather than an assumed accuracy gain.
positions.public_summary: Supports the competency-based approach but urges FDA to benchmark the model alone and use clinical confirmation to evaluate the human-AI team as deployed, citing evidence that human review does not reliably improve accuracy; the human's role is accountability, not added performance.
positions.supporting_text: 3. In competency-based evaluation, score the human–AI team as it will be deployed — and be precise that the human's role is accountability, not a guarantee of higher accuracy. The analogy to how clinicians are trained and credentialed is apt. We add one caution from the evidence: adding a human reviewer to an already-strong model does not reliably raise task accuracy, and on some decision tasks can lower it (Vaccaro et al., Nature Human Behaviour, 2024). The right inference is not "remove the human" — it is that the human's function in a regulated device is ownership of and answerability for the consequence, which no benchmark score confers. So benchmark the model honestly on its own, but let clinical confirmation measure the team as actually deployed.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter endorses the inclusion of safety competencies—recognizing safety-critical situations and escalating, and calibration, uncertainty, and clinical deferral—in the benchmarking structure, framing reliable handoff to a human as safety-critical behavior rather than a shortcoming in autonomy.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the described safety behavior competencies (escalation, and calibration/uncertainty/clinical deferral) as elements of the benchmarking framework.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports the discussion paper's proposed safety competencies for benchmarking, specifically recognizing and escalating safety-critical situations and calibration, uncertainty, and clinical deferral, characterizing reliable handoff to a human clinician as demonstrating safety-critical behavior rather than a failure of autonomy.
positions.supporting_text: The paper's safety competencies for recognizing safety-critical situations and escalating, and for calibration, uncertainty, and clinical deferral, are exactly right: a device that reliably knows when to hand off to a human is demonstrating the safety-critical behavior, not failing to be autonomous.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and drift monitoring are appropriate and that responsibility can realistically be distributed across manufacturers, clinicians, and institutions, but argues this only works if a durable, privacy-preserving record of who reviewed each output and what they decided travels with the determination.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should expect shared postmarket responsibility to be backed by a portable, tamper-evident, PHI-free record of human review decisions; the commenter offers as an example signed, timestamped attestations whose fingerprints are anchored to an external tamper-evident ledger so determinations and human sign-off can be independently verified later.
positions.public_summary: Endorses the paper's postmarket approaches—re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, drift monitoring—and shared manufacturer/clinician/institution responsibility, but adds that it works only with a portable, privacy-preserving, tamper-evident record of human review decisions. Offers signed, ledger-anchored attestations as one illustrative pattern.
positions.supporting_text: 4. Postmarket "shared-ecosystem responsibility" works only with a portable, tamper-evident record of who reviewed what and what they decided. The paper's call for periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and drift / performance-degradation monitoring is well-placed, and distributing responsibility across manufacturers, clinicians, and institutions is realistic. In practice it functions only if a durable, privacy-preserving record of the human decision travels with the determination. We build and operate one such pattern: each reviewed output becomes a signed, timestamped, PHI-free attestation whose fingerprint is anchored to an external, tamper-evident ledger, so a determination and its human sign-off can be independently verified after the fact without exposing patient data. We offer the pattern, not a product, as one concrete way to make shared postmarket responsibility auditable

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees agentic systems warrant elevated scrutiny for reduced human review, but argues that abstract autonomy-level labels are a weaker basis for oversight than a functional check at each consequential or hard-to-reverse action, and notes such labels are less robust to prompt injection.
positions.requested_fda_action: Anchor agentic oversight to a functional, local test: at each consequential or difficult-to-reverse action, require that a named, qualified licensed human reviews the basis for the action and is accountable for it, rather than relying on autonomy-level classifications alone.
positions.public_summary: Agrees agentic systems merit elevated scrutiny, but proposes oversight be tied to a functional checkpoint — a named, qualified human reviewing and accountable for each consequential or hard-to-reverse action — rather than abstract autonomy-level labels, citing scalability and prompt-injection robustness.
positions.supporting_text: 5. For agentic systems, anchor oversight to whether a named, licensed human signs the consequential action — not to autonomy in the abstract. The paper is right to give agentic AI elevated scrutiny for its "reduced opportunity for human review." We suggest the operative test be functional and local: at each point where the system takes an action that is consequential or difficult to reverse, is there a qualified human who reviews the basis and is accountable for it? Oversight tied to that checkpoint scales across architectures and is more robust to prompt injection than autonomy-level labels alone.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter wants it to remain unambiguous that a foundation model master file does not constitute device authorization and does not shift responsibility away from the entity deploying the device. Accountability should rest with the deploying party and the licensed clinician who signs off on consequential outputs.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain and keep central the stated principle that a Foundation Model MAF is not a device approval and that the deploying sponsor remains responsible for the device, with accountability located in the deployer and the licensed human endorsing the output.
positions.public_summary: Endorses the paper's stated principle that a foundation model master file is not a device approval and the deploying sponsor remains responsible, urging FDA to keep this central and to place accountability with the deployer and the licensed clinician signing consequential outputs.
positions.supporting_text: The paper's own principle — that a foundation-model master file is not a device approval, and that the sponsor deploying the device remains responsible for it — is exactly right, and we encourage CDRH to keep it central: the party who deploys the AI, and the licensed human who signs the consequential output, are where accountability must sit.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts that many generative functions (retrieval, drafting, summarization, triage) are well suited to automation and should be regulated lightly, but is concerned that consequential clinical or coverage decisions could be automated on the basis of performance scores alone rather than human accountability.
positions.requested_fda_action: Keep the risk framework light-touch for low-consequence automation tasks, but for consequential clinical or coverage decisions require an accountable, licensed human who reviews the basis of the output, signs it, and answers for the outcome — treating this as a durable requirement rather than something satisfied by higher benchmark performance.
positions.public_summary: Supports a light-touch risk framework for automatable generative functions such as retrieval, drafting, summarization and triage, but argues that consequential clinical or coverage decisions require an accountable licensed human who reviews the basis, signs, and answers for the outcome — not merely higher performance scores.
positions.supporting_text: A great deal of what a generative model does — retrieval, drafting, summarization, triage — is genuinely well suited to automation, and the framework should keep that path light. The narrow, load-bearing exception is the consequential clinical or coverage decision, where the durable requirement is not a better score but an accountable, licensed human who reviews the basis, signs, and answers for the outcome.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that AI should augment rather than indiscriminately replace clinicians' clinical judgment, and that clinical applications carry risks tied to the seriousness of the decision, patient vulnerability, and consequences of error.
positions.requested_fda_action: Allow appropriate automation of low-risk administrative functions (scheduling, documentation assistance, workflow management, patient navigation, certain operational communications), while regulating clinical applications in proportion to decision seriousness, patient vulnerability, and potential consequences of error.
positions.public_summary: Supports risk-proportionate regulation but urges FDA to distinguish low-risk administrative functions, which should benefit from automation, from clinical applications, which should be regulated according to decision seriousness, patient vulnerability, and consequences of error, with AI strengthening rather than replacing clinical judgment.
positions.supporting_text: AI should be used to strengthen healthcare professionals mdash;not indiscriminately replace their clinical judgment. Low-risk administrative functions, including scheduling, documentation assistance, workflow management, patient navigation, and certain operational communications, should benefit from appropriate automation. Clinical applications, however, must be regulated according to the seriousness of the decision, the vulnerability of the patient, and the potential consequences of an error.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that GenAI-enabled outputs affecting pediatric patients and other vulnerable populations carry heightened risk and should not be validated or overseen at the same level as outputs for the general population.
positions.requested_fda_action: Apply stricter validation standards to GenAI-enabled functions used in decisions involving pediatric and other vulnerable populations, and require enhanced human oversight for those uses.
positions.public_summary: Commenter asks FDA to differentiate risk and evidence expectations by population, applying stricter validation standards and enhanced human oversight to GenAI-enabled functions informing decisions about pediatric patients and other vulnerable groups. The passage does not otherwise evaluate FDA's proposed framework.
positions.supporting_text: Decisions involving pediatric patients and other vulnerable populations must be subject to stricter validation standards and enhanced human oversight.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that higher-risk clinical activities—diagnosis and differential diagnosis, prescribing and medication changes, treatment planning, referrals, emergency triage, and escalation decisions—could be carried out by GenAI with reduced or absent human review. It maintains that responsibility for such care must stay with a qualified healthcare professional.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that GenAI outputs in these higher-risk categories always be reviewed and approved by a licensed clinician, with AI limited to an informing role. Ensure oversight expectations keep accountability for higher-risk care with an appropriately qualified healthcare professional.
positions.public_summary: Commenter asks FDA to require licensed clinician review and approval for GenAI involvement in diagnosis, prescribing, treatment planning, referrals, triage, and escalation decisions, with AI limited to an informing role and responsibility for higher-risk care remaining with a qualified professional.
positions.supporting_text: AI-supported diagnosis and differential diagnosis, prescribing and medication changes, treatment planning, referrals, emergency triage, and escalation decisions should always require review and approval by a licensed clinician. ... AI may inform these decisions, but responsibility for higher-risk care must remain with an appropriately qualified healthcare professional.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that a credible regulatory framework cannot rely on manufacturer self-assessment alone, and that independent evaluation must occur both before market entry and on an ongoing basis.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require independent premarket testing of GenAI-enabled devices and recurring third-party audits as mandatory elements of the framework, rather than optional or voluntary involvement.
positions.public_summary: The commenter states that a credible framework should mandate independent premarket testing and recurring third-party audits, going beyond FDA's exploration of whether and how independent third parties might participate. No detail is provided on qualifications, scope, or independence criteria.
positions.supporting_text:
A credible regulatory framework should require each of the following:

• Independent premarket testing and recurring third-party audits;

positions.stakeholder_concern: The passage, a fragment of a list of recommended safeguards, indicates concern that postmarket oversight of GenAI outputs requires a durable, auditable record linking inputs, outputs, actions, the specific model version, and the human reviewers involved.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require permanent, tamper-resistant decision logs capturing inputs, generated outputs, actions taken, the model version in use, and the individuals responsible for review as part of postmarket monitoring expectations.
positions.public_summary: In a list of recommended safeguards, the commenter calls for permanent, tamper-resistant decision logs recording inputs, outputs, actions taken, the model version involved, and the individuals responsible for review. The passage is a fragment; broader position on FDA's postmarket approaches is not stated.
positions.supporting_text: • Permanent, tamper-resistant decision logs showing the inputs used, outputs generated, actions taken, model version involved, and individuals responsible for review;

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that postmarket surveillance should be continuous and should span not only accuracy and model drift but also bias, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and unequal outcomes across patient populations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Ensure postmarket monitoring expectations cover continuous tracking of accuracy, bias, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, model drift, and disparities in outcomes among patient subpopulations, rather than periodic performance checks alone.
positions.public_summary: In a brief listing, the commenter calls for continuous postmarket monitoring covering accuracy, bias, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, model drift, and unequal outcomes across patient populations—broader and more continuous than periodic re-benchmarking alone. The passage does not elaborate further.
positions.supporting_text: • Continuous monitoring for accuracy, bias, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, model drift, and unequal outcomes among patient populations;

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket oversight of AI-enabled functions lacks binding reporting duties and rapid mechanisms to stop unsafe outputs, and that obligations on both developers and healthcare organizations may go unenforced.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require mandatory incident reporting and defined procedures for immediately disabling, rolling back, or recalling unsafe AI functions, and impose meaningful financial penalties, corrective-action requirements, and FDA enforcement when developers or healthcare organizations fail to comply.
positions.public_summary: Commenter urges stronger postmarket obligations than described: mandatory incident reporting, defined procedures to immediately disable, roll back, or recall unsafe AI functions, plus financial penalties, corrective actions, and FDA enforcement against both developers and healthcare organizations that fail to comply.
positions.supporting_text:
• Mandatory incident reporting and defined procedures for immediately disabling, rolling back, or recalling unsafe AI functions; and

• Meaningful financial penalties, corrective-action requirements, and FDA enforcement when developers or healthcare organizations fail to meet these obligations.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a device validated at authorization may drift or degrade due to software updates, new data, third-party foundation model changes, altered clinical environments, or expanded agentic capabilities, so one-time evaluation is insufficient.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require lifecycle oversight in which every material change is documented and assessed, and, where the change could affect clinical performance or patient safety, independently revalidated before broader deployment.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports lifecycle oversight but urges FDA to go beyond quality-system-managed change control: every material change—software updates, new data, third-party foundation model changes, altered clinical settings, or expanded agentic capabilities—should be documented, assessed, and independently revalidated before broader deployment where patient safety could be affected.
positions.supporting_text: Oversight must continue throughout the full life cycle of an AI system. A model that performed safely during its original evaluation may change because of software updates, new data, changes to an underlying foundation model, altered clinical environments, or expanding agentic capabilities. Every material change should be documented, assessed, and—when it could affect clinical performance or patient safety—independently revalidated before broader deployment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that when multiple parties—technology developers, device manufacturers, healthcare organizations, and clinical users—are involved, accountability can be shifted among them after an adverse event, leaving responsibility unresolved.
positions.requested_fda_action: Ensure responsibility is clearly assigned by defining legal and operational responsibilities for each participant across validation, deployment, monitoring, cybersecurity, clinician training, patient disclosure, and incident response.
positions.public_summary: Addressing postmarket roles, the commenter urges that responsibility be explicitly assigned so developers, manufacturers, healthcare organizations, and clinicians cannot shift accountability after adverse events, with defined legal and operational duties for validation, deployment, monitoring, cybersecurity, training, patient disclosure, and incident response.
positions.supporting_text: Responsibility must also be clearly assigned. Technology developers, medical-device manufacturers, healthcare organizations, and clinical users should not be permitted to shift accountability to one another following an adverse event. Each participant should have defined legal and operational responsibilities governing validation, deployment, monitoring, cybersecurity, clinician training, patient disclosure, and incident response.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that patients may not know when AI materially influences their care and may lack practical avenues to obtain human review, correct errors, or raise concerns; disclosures placed in technical documentation or terms of service are seen as inadequate.
positions.requested_fda_action: Ensure patient-facing safeguards are part of the framework: notification when AI materially influences care, a route to request human review, mechanisms to correct inaccurate information, and the ability to report concerns without losing treatment access, with transparency written to be understandable to patients and clinicians.
positions.public_summary: Commenter addresses patient-facing safeguards, urging that patients be able to know when AI materially influences care, request human review, correct inaccurate information, and report concerns without losing treatment access, with transparency understandable to patients and clinicians rather than buried in technical or legal documents.
positions.supporting_text: Patients must retain meaningful rights within an AI-enabled healthcare system. They should be able to understand when AI materially influences their care, request appropriate human review, correct inaccurate information, and report concerns without losing access to treatment. Transparency must be understandable to patients and clinicians—not buried within technical documentation or lengthy terms of service.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter finds the activity/consequence axes useful but notes that systems falling in the same cell of the matrix can still present materially different risks.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expand the risk framework to also account for reversibility, time to correction, error detectability, traceability to data and system versions, safeguard independence, exposure before containment, and stability of the population and workflow.
positions.public_summary: Considers FDA's activity and consequence axes useful but insufficient, since devices in the same risk cell can differ materially. Asks FDA to add dimensions including reversibility, time to correction, error detectability, version and data traceability, safeguard independence, exposure before containment, and population and workflow stability.
positions.supporting_text: The proposed activity and consequence axes are useful, but systems in the same cell can present different risks. FDA should also consider reversibility, time to correction, error detectability, traceability to data and system versions, safeguard independence, exposure before containment, and stability of the population and workflow.

positions.stakeholder_concern: An output labeled as informational may function as action-directing in practice; features such as personalization, urgency, repeated recommendations, confidence presentation, defaults, omission of alternatives, and automated tool use can shift a function along the directiveness continuum regardless of how the interface describes it.
positions.requested_fda_action: Assess directiveness based on the device's observed behavior rather than interface labeling or sponsor characterization, and treat the listed output and interaction features as modifiers that can move an ostensibly informational function toward action direction.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses assessing directiveness, arguing it should be determined by a device's observed behavior rather than interface labels. It identifies personalization, urgency, repeated recommendations, confidence presentation, defaults, omitted alternatives, and automated tool use as features that can shift apparently informational outputs toward action direction.
positions.supporting_text: Directiveness should be judged by observed behavior, not interface labels. Personalization, urgency, repeated recommendations, confidence presentation, defaults, omitted alternatives, and automated tool use can move an apparently informational function toward action direction.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter indicates that evaluation of multi-turn conversational GenAI devices must address behaviors that emerge over the course of an exchange, not just single-output performance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify that multi-turn evaluation covers context accumulation or loss, escalation, refusal, interruption, and safe stop behaviors.
positions.public_summary: Comment addresses multi-turn conversational evaluation, recommending that testing specifically cover context accumulation or loss, escalation, refusal, interruption, and safe-stop behaviors. It does not state a broader view on FDA's proposed approach to characterizing emergent conversational intended use.
positions.supporting_text: Multi-turn evaluation should cover context accumulation or loss, escalation, refusal, interruption, and safe stop.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a single benchmark score cannot substantiate competency, and that claims lack meaning without specified population, setting, user, workflow, input distribution, reference standard, acceptance criteria, failure rules, denominators, uncertainty, version, and exclusions. Robustness to degraded or unusual inputs and run-to-run consistency are also treated as unaddressed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require competency to be demonstrated through structured, fully specified evidence for each claim rather than one benchmark score, and require testing with missing, contradictory, shifted, adversarial, and low-quality inputs plus repeated-run and equivalent-input testing.
positions.public_summary: Accepts a competency-based evaluation framework but argues a single benchmark score is insufficient. Asks FDA to require per-claim specification of population, setting, user, workflow, inputs, reference standard, acceptance criteria, uncertainty, and version, plus testing of degraded, adversarial, and repeated inputs.
positions.supporting_text: Competency should be supported by structured evidence rather than one benchmark score. Each claim should identify the population, setting, user, workflow, input distribution, reference standard, acceptance criteria, failure rules, denominators, uncertainty, version, and exclusions. Testing should include missing, contradictory, shifted, adversarial, and low-quality inputs, plus repeated-run and equivalent-input testing.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Performance on public benchmarks may not correspond to performance in the actual clinical operating environment, so treating benchmark results as predictive of real-world safety and effectiveness is not warranted.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to affirmatively justify why a chosen benchmark represents the device's intended use and to characterize how the benchmark's data distribution differs from the intended operating environment, rather than presuming predictive validity.
positions.public_summary: The commenter agrees benchmark results should not be presumed to predict clinical performance and asks FDA to require sponsors to justify a benchmark's relevance to the intended use and to document differences between benchmark data and the real operating environment.
positions.supporting_text: Public benchmark performance should not be presumed to predict clinical performance. Sponsors should explain why a benchmark represents the intended use and where its distribution differs from the operating environment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned about the lack of independence when a sponsor controls benchmark test construction, tuning, scoring, and interpretation, which can undermine the credibility of benchmark-based evidence.
positions.requested_fda_action: Where sponsors control the benchmarking process, FDA should consider requiring or accepting independence safeguards such as external adjudication, preregistration, blinded evaluation, locked test sets, or qualified reproduction of results.
positions.public_summary: Comment accepts benchmark-based evaluation but notes that sponsor control over test construction, tuning, scoring, and interpretation warrants safeguards, suggesting external adjudication, preregistration, blinded evaluation, locked test sets, or qualified reproduction may be appropriate in such cases.
positions.supporting_text: When a sponsor controls test construction, tuning, scoring, and interpretation, external adjudication, preregistration, blinded evaluation, locked tests, or qualified reproduction may be appropriate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Synthetic data has legitimate but bounded utility; relying on it alone risks unsupported conclusions about real-world prevalence, subgroup performance, workflow effects, clinical performance, and benefit-risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: Recognize synthetic data as appropriate for schema testing, fault injection, specified rare cases, and reproducibility, while requiring that it not by itself establish prevalence, workflow effects, subgroup or clinical performance, or benefit-risk.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts synthetic data for limited purposes—schema testing, fault injection, specified rare cases, and reproducibility—but states it should not on its own establish real-world prevalence, workflow effects, subgroup or clinical performance, or benefit-risk conclusions.
positions.supporting_text: Synthetic data can support schema testing, fault injection, specified rare cases, and reproducibility. It should not, by itself, establish real-world prevalence, workflow effects, subgroup performance, clinical performance, or benefit-risk.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Pooling synthetic-input and real-patient performance results could produce misleading single performance estimates when the two datasets do not measure the same quantity under comparable conditions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that synthetic and real-data performance results be reported separately, permitting combination only when they estimate the same quantity under compatible conditions.
positions.public_summary: On combining evidence, the commenter states that synthetic-data and real-data performance results should be reported separately unless both estimate the same quantity under compatible conditions, setting a narrower condition for pooling than FDA's open-ended question implies.
positions.supporting_text: Synthetic and real-data results should remain separate unless they estimate the same quantity under compatible conditions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that reliance on postmarket monitoring could displace evidence that should be generated before patients are exposed to a device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Permit greater premarket uncertainty only under explicit conditions: failures are promptly detectable, consequences are limited or reversible, exposure is bounded, and containment measures are feasible; otherwise require the premarket evidence.
positions.public_summary: Accepts that greater premarket uncertainty may sometimes be tolerated, but only where failures are promptly detectable, consequences limited or reversible, exposure bounded, and containment feasible. Emphasizes that postmarket monitoring should not replace evidence required before a device is used.
positions.supporting_text: Postmarket monitoring should not substitute for evidence needed before use. Greater residual uncertainty may be acceptable only when failures are promptly detectable, consequences are limited or reversible, exposure is bounded, and containment is feasible.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter appears concerned that postmarket approaches such as re-benchmarking or clinician review are insufficient unless embedded in a structured lifecycle program with defined baselines, denominators, indicators, thresholds, ownership, and response actions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify that credible lifecycle monitoring programs include a versioned baseline; denominator and deployment-context data; performance, safety, data-quality, and process indicators; investigation thresholds; incident linkage; assigned review ownership; and rules for rollback, suspension, or reassessment.
positions.public_summary: Endorses lifecycle postmarket evaluation but specifies required components beyond FDA's listed approaches: a versioned baseline; denominator and deployment-context data; performance, safety, data-quality, and process indicators; investigation thresholds; incident linkage; defined review ownership; and rollback, suspension, or reassessment rules.
positions.supporting_text: A credible lifecycle program should include a versioned baseline; denominator and deployment-context data; performance, safety, data-quality, and process indicators; investigation thresholds; incident linkage; review ownership; and rollback, suspension, or reassessment rules.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that reassessment triggers must cover the full range of components and contextual factors that can alter a GenAI device's behavior, not only changes to the model itself, and that operational failure signals be recognized as prompts for review.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should define reassessment as triggered by material changes across the model, prompts, retrieval corpus, orchestration, tools, guardrails, interface, intended use, users, population, workflow, source data, or clinical practice, and additionally by new safety signals, subgroup degradation, unexplained output shifts, repeated tool failures, and loss of traceability.
positions.public_summary: Comment endorses periodic reassessment but proposes broader triggers than FDA describes: material changes to model, prompts, retrieval corpus, orchestration, tools, guardrails, interface, intended use, users, population, workflow, source data, or clinical practice, plus safety signals, subgroup degradation, unexplained output shifts, tool failures, and lost traceability.
positions.supporting_text: Reassessment should follow material changes in the model, prompts, retrieval corpus, orchestration, tools, guardrails, interface, intended use, users, population, workflow, source data, or clinical practice. New safety signals, subgroup degradation, unexplained output shifts, repeated tool failures, and lost traceability should also trigger review.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Third-party foundation model changes may go undetected if manufacturers rely on model names or release labels rather than verifiable version tracking, leaving device behavior to shift without assessment.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect manufacturers to maintain versioned dependency inventories with contractual and technical controls covering change and incident notification, version identification, impact assessment, and rollback or version pinning, supported by detection methods such as regression and canary testing, runtime fingerprints, shadow evaluation, and output-distribution monitoring; where a dependency cannot be detected, assessed, or controlled, permitted use should be narrowed and safeguards strengthened.
positions.public_summary: Commenter supports controls for third-party foundation model changes but urges specifics: versioned dependency inventories instead of model names or release labels; change, incident, and rollback provisions; and detection via regression, canary, shadow testing and output monitoring. Uncontrollable dependencies should narrow permitted use.
positions.supporting_text: Manufacturers using third-party foundation models should maintain a versioned dependency inventory rather than rely on a model name or release label. Controls should support change notice, version identification, incident notification, impact assessment, and rollback or pinning where feasible. Regression tests, canary testing, runtime fingerprints, shadow evaluation, and output-distribution monitoring can help detect change. If a dependency cannot be adequately detected, assessed, or controlled, that uncertainty should narrow permitted use and strengthen safeguards.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Evaluating only the quality of agentic outputs is insufficient; the safety of multi-step action sequences, authorization limits, failure recovery, and the integrity of human checkpoints must also be assessed, including exposure to prompt injection and stale or adversarial tool results.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt acceptance criteria for agentic devices that cover tool selection and parameters, authorization boundaries and least privilege, approval before irreversible actions, interruption, timeout, rollback and recovery, logging, partial failure handling, prompt injection resistance, and refusal when authority or confirmation is absent; require that human oversight occur before consequential actions, with sufficient information for the reviewer and no ability for the system to bypass or pressure the checkpoint.
positions.public_summary: Agrees agentic devices need additional evaluation, but asks FDA to specify criteria beyond output quality: action-sequence safety, tool selection, authorization limits and least privilege, approval before irreversible actions, rollback, logging, prompt-injection resistance, and human checkpoints that occur before action and cannot be bypassed.
positions.supporting_text: Agentic systems require evaluation of output quality and action-sequence safety. Criteria should address tool selection, parameters, authorization boundaries, least privilege, stale or adversarial results, approval before irreversible actions, interruption, timeout, rollback, recovery, prompt injection, logging, partial failure, and refusal when authority or confirmation is missing. Oversight is meaningful only when it occurs before the consequential action, the reviewer has the information needed to decide, and the system cannot bypass or pressure the checkpoint.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that aggregate calibration, benchmark capability, and monitoring metrics can mask failures in intended-use relevance, discrimination, threshold behavior, and performance in clinically important strata, and that negative or missing evidence may be lost over the product life cycle.
positions.requested_fda_action: Strengthen the framework with structured risk modifiers, traceable competency evidence, explicit reporting of uncertainty, and versioned lifecycle decision records, and require that null, adverse, conflicting, blocked, and unavailable evidence remain visible throughout the product life cycle.
positions.public_summary: Accepts FDA's general direction but asks for structured risk modifiers, traceable competency evidence, explicit uncertainty, and versioned lifecycle decision records, warning that calibration, benchmarks, and monitoring can hide failures in intended-use relevance, discrimination, thresholds, and important subgroups; negative or missing evidence should stay visible.
positions.supporting_text: FDA's framework would be strengthened by structured risk modifiers, traceable competency evidence, explicit uncertainty, and versioned lifecycle decision records. Calibration, benchmark capability, and monitoring should not conceal failures in intended-use relevance, discrimination, threshold behavior, or clinically important strata. Null, adverse, conflicting, blocked, and unavailable evidence should remain visible throughout the product life cycle.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter views the two-axis framework as a useful, intuitive primary heuristic but is concerned that adding dimensions directly would create an unmanageable multi-dimensional matrix, while important risk-relevant factors (traceability, reversibility, time pressure, downstream safeguards, user capability, execution authority) would otherwise go unaddressed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the two-axis structure and incorporate the listed additional factors as risk modifiers that adjust placement within the framework and the strength of associated controls, rather than as new axes.
positions.public_summary: Supports retaining FDA's two-axis risk framework as a primary heuristic rather than expanding it into a multi-dimensional matrix, but asks FDA to operationalize traceability, reversibility, time pressure, downstream safeguards, user capability/setting, and execution authority as risk modifiers affecting placement and controls.
positions.supporting_text:
The proposed two-axis framework - device activity on one axis and consequence of relying on an incorrect output on the other - is a useful primary heuristic. It is intuitive, clinically meaningful, and readily scalable from non-directive informational functions to fully autonomous action-taking functions. FDA should retain the two axes rather than converting the framework into an unmanageable multi-dimensional matrix. [1]
... Additional dimensions should function as risk modifiers that influence placement within the framework and the strength of associated controls. Particularly important modifiers include:
• Traceability: whether a consequential output can be linked to the patient or encounter, source information or evidence, model/configuration state, and primary materials on which it relied.
• Reversibility: whether an incorrect action can be promptly reversed without lasting harm.
• Time pressure: whether meaningful human review is feasible before harm can occur.
• Downstream safeguards: whether an independent mechanism can constrain, intercept, escalate, or block an unsafe action.
• User capability and setting: whether the output is delivered to a patient, generalist, specialist, or another system that may have different ability to independently evaluate it.
• Execution authority: whether the function merely provides information, strongly directs action, or can itself cause a consequential action to occur.
These modifiers can be operationalized without changing the basic two-axis structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees that GenAI-enabled in vitro diagnostic, measurement, and signal-processing functions warrant special risk consideration because users often cannot directly assess such outputs and therefore cannot recognize or avoid reliance on an incorrect result.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain and continue to treat the limited user-verifiability of in vitro diagnostic, measurement, and signal-processing outputs as a distinct risk consideration within the risk framework.
positions.public_summary: Endorses FDA's identification of GenAI-enabled in vitro diagnostic, measurement, and signal-processing functions as raising special risk considerations, because users generally cannot directly assess those outputs and so cannot recognize or avoid relying on incorrect results.
positions.supporting_text: FDA also appropriately identifies GenAI-enabled in vitro diagnostic, measurement, and signal-processing functions as presenting special risk considerations because their outputs may not be directly assessable by the user, limiting the user's ability to recognize and avoid reliance on an incorrect output. [1]

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that risk and assurance requirements should account for how much clinically relevant system state (external models, tools, clinical data sources, institutional policy, changing configuration) lies outside the sponsor's direct control, a dimension not captured by device activity and consequence of an incorrect output alone.
positions.requested_fda_action: Scale assurance proportionately: allow comparatively conventional competency and lifecycle controls for bounded, recommendation-only functions, while requiring substantially stronger provenance, configuration-lineage, authorization, and postmarket controls for high-consequence agentic functions dependent on external components, consistent with a least-burdensome approach that seeks the minimum information and control functions needed for the device's actual risk profile.
positions.public_summary: Accepts risk-proportionate regulation but urges FDA to add a dimension: how much clinically relevant system state lies outside sponsor control.
positions.supporting_text: The amount and type of assurance should also be proportionate to the extent to which clinically relevant system state lies outside the sponsor's direct control. A bounded, recommendation-only function may be adequately addressed through comparatively conventional competency and lifecycle controls, whereas a high-consequence agentic function dependent on external models, tools, clinical data sources, institutional policy, or changing configuration may warrant substantially stronger provenance, configuration-lineage, authorization, and postmarket controls. This is consistent with a least-burdensome approach: the objective is not maximum control for every device, but the minimum information and control functions necessary to address the relevant safety and effectiveness questions for the device's actual risk profile. [15]

positions.stakeholder_concern: Assessing directiveness based on wording or disclaimers could understate risk, since outputs labeled informational may in practice narrow users toward a specific clinical action; specificity, personalization, imperative strength, confidence presentation, urgency, suppression of alternatives, consequence of the implied action, and repetition across multi-turn interactions all matter.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define directiveness functionally rather than lexically, using the test of what a reasonable intended user is likely to do because of the output, and have risk analysis reflect functional directiveness even when the interface labels output as informational.
positions.public_summary: Supports FDA's directiveness continuum but urges functional rather than word-based assessment. Recommends judging risk by what a reasonable intended user would likely do, weighing specificity, personalization, imperative strength, confidence, urgency, suppressed alternatives, consequence, and reinforcement across multi-turn exchanges, regardless of informational labeling.
positions.supporting_text:
Directiveness should be assessed functionally rather than lexically. The presence or absence of words such as "recommend," "consider," or "talk to your doctor" should not determine risk by itself. Relevant characteristics include specificity, personalization, imperative strength, confidence presentation, temporal urgency, the degree to which alternatives are suppressed, the clinical consequence of the implied action, and whether the output is repeated or reinforced across a multi-turn interaction.
A useful principle is to ask what a reasonable intended user is likely to do because of the output. If the practical effect of an informational function is to narrow the user toward a specific clinical action, the risk analysis should reflect that functional directiveness even when the interface labels the output as informational.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter accepts that patient-facing functions may need distinct safeguards where safe use depends on clinical knowledge patients cannot be expected to have, but is concerned that treating patient-facing status as automatically higher risk would be inaccurate.
positions.requested_fda_action: Assess risk for patient-facing functions based on the output, context, likely downstream action, health-literacy demands, escalation pathways, and the patient's ability to recognize uncertainty or error, rather than by user type alone, and recognize safeguards such as calibrated uncertainty communication, clear scope boundaries, structured escalation for high-risk symptoms, prevention of unsupported specificity, and interface design that reduces automation bias without undermining patient autonomy.
positions.public_summary: Agrees patient-facing functions may need distinct safeguards where safe use requires clinical knowledge patients lack, but argues patient-facing status should not automatically mean higher risk. Recommends risk be based on output, context, downstream action, health literacy, escalation pathways, and error recognition.
positions.supporting_text:
Patient-facing functions may require different safeguards when safe use depends on clinical knowledge that the intended patient population cannot reasonably be expected to possess. However, patient-facing status should not automatically be treated as higher risk. Risk should depend on the output, context, likely downstream action, health-literacy demands, availability of escalation pathways, and the patient's ability to recognize uncertainty or error.
Useful safeguards can include calibrated uncertainty communication, clear scope boundaries, structured escalation for high-risk symptoms, prevention of unsupported specificity, and user-interface designs that reduce automation bias without undermining patient autonomy.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Risk depends on whether the intended user can independently evaluate an output within the device's operating domain, not on a categorical generalist/specialist label; generalists may gain access to expertise, but safeguards should increase where safe use requires specialist-level interpretation the user likely lacks.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat the generalist/specialist distinction as a context modifier rather than a categorical risk classification, and require sponsors to characterize the expected user, required domain knowledge, intended degree of independent review, and escalation conditions—with any needed specialist review built into the workflow rather than conveyed only through labeling.
positions.public_summary: Accepts considering generalist versus specialist users but urges FDA to treat it as a context modifier rather than a categorical risk label, keyed to whether the intended user can independently evaluate outputs. Asks that required specialist review be embedded in workflow, not labeling.
positions.supporting_text:
The distinction should be treated as a context modifier rather than a categorical risk label. The relevant issue is whether the intended user can independently evaluate the output within the domain in which the device is operating.
